status: Zero-error obstructions are known, and Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), in the open-problems section of [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115), explicitly conjecture a remaining non-condensing barrier.
solved_when: An answer is given in the constant-rate regime: either an explicit deterministic condenser that nontrivially raises the entropy rate while permitting small smoothing error, or a proof that no such condenser exists (the conjectured non-condensing barrier).
why: A resolution would explain a fundamental difference between one-bit and longer-block contributions to entropy in this adversarial model.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115), open-problems section.

title: G18. Seedless samplable condensing beyond black-box assumptions
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Can we construct seedless condensers for arbitrary efficiently samplable sources starting from standard assumptions like LWE, rather than from specialized or bespoke assumptions — and if so, can such constructions meet the parameters already achieved by the specialized-hashing approaches?
status: Freitag–Silbak–Wichs give near-optimal constructions for specialized hashing and prove a black-box barrier showing that standard game-based assumptions cannot yield such condensers via black-box techniques, motivating a non-black-box approach (Freitag–Silbak–Wichs, 2025, [Seedless Condensers for Efficiently Samplable Sources](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1783)).
solved_when: A seedless condenser for general efficient samplers is constructed from an established assumption such as LWE using non-black-box techniques, matching the parameters of the specialized-assumption constructions (which are near-optimal per Freitag–Silbak–Wichs).
why: It would place the deterministic improvement of algorithmically generated randomness on a conventional, standard cryptographic foundation instead of specialized assumptions.
key_works: Freitag–Silbak–Wichs (2025), [*Seedless Condensers for Efficiently Samplable Sources*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1783).

title: G19. Quasilinear Raz extraction without auxiliary length restrictions
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can Raz's two-source randomness extractor be implemented in quasilinear time over its full original asymmetric regime, rather than only when the second source is at most half the length of the first? Formally, remove the restriction \(n_2\le n_1/2\) and the associated auxiliary-parameter constraints from the quasilinear construction.
status: The 2025 implementation of Foreman–Wooltorton–Milner–Curchin already runs in \(O(n_1\log^2 n_1)\) on its supported parameters; broadening that range beyond \(n_2\le n_1/2\) is explicitly open.
solved_when: The extractor runs in \(O(n_1\log^2 n_1)\) time for all source lengths covered by Raz's original asymmetric regime, with no \(n_2\le n_1/2\) condition or auxiliary-parameter restrictions.
why: It would bring fast extraction to realistic unequal-source configurations currently outside the implementation's reach.
key_works: Foreman–Wooltorton–Milner–Curchod (2025), [*An efficient construction of Raz’s two-source randomness extractor with improved parameters*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15547).

title: G20. Ordinary-to-seedless-nonmalleable extractor conversion
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Does every ordinary two-source or affine extractor admit a generic conversion into a seedless nonmalleable extractor? Concretely, can such a transformation achieve polynomial error loss, constant-factor entropy overhead, and a constant fraction of output length?
status: The question was explicitly posed in 2024 (Li–Zhong, [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108)). Strong dedicated constructions of seedless nonmalleable extractors exist, but none supplies a generic conversion from ordinary extractors.
solved_when: A transformation is given that takes any two-source or affine extractor and produces a seedless nonmalleable extractor with error loss polynomial in the original error, entropy requirements within a constant factor of the original, and output length a constant fraction of the original.
why: A generic conversion would let every advance in ordinary extraction automatically yield tamper-resistant randomness, instead of requiring bespoke nonmalleable constructions for each setting.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108).

title: G21. Negligible-error two-source nonmalleability at polylogarithmic entropy
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can we build a two-source non-malleable extractor with negligible error from two sources of only polylogarithmic entropy, tamper-proof against independent manipulation of each source where at least one tampering function is fixed-point-free?
status: Constructions from 2024 (Li–Zhong, [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108)) achieve either polynomial error with long output, or constant output at logarithmic entropy.
solved_when: An explicit construction exists producing nonconstant output with error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\) from two sources each with polylogarithmic entropy min-entropy, secure against separate tampering functions with at least one fixed-point-free.
why: It would give negligible-error tamper resistance from extremely weak independent sources, the missing regime between current constant-output and polynomial-error results.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108).

title: G24. Short-seed linear extractors with linear output
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can we construct a strong seeded extractor that is linear in the source for every fixed seed, achieving near-optimal seed length and linear output even at very low source entropy?
status: Known linear constructions trade seed length against output length; unrestricted seeded extraction does not settle this linearity-constrained target. For context, Doron–Fridman (2025), [*Bit-Fixing Extractors for Almost-Logarithmic Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.33), Section 2.3 discusses this frontier.
solved_when: A construction exists that is strong, linear in the source for each fixed seed, with seed length \(d=O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\), output length \(m=\Omega(k)\), and working for all entropy thresholds \(k\ge C\log(n/\varepsilon)\).
why: Linearity enables efficient integration with coding, sharing, and algebraic protocols.
key_works: Doron–Fridman (2025), [*Bit-Fixing Extractors for Almost-Logarithmic Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.33), Section 2.3.

title: G25. Optimal-order seeded extraction against unrestricted quantum information
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can a seeded extractor achieve the classical optimum even when the adversary's side information is quantum of unrestricted dimension? Formally: extract Ω(k) bits from X using a seed of length O(log(n/ε)) whenever H_min(X|E) ≥ k ≥ C log(n/ε), with no bound on the dimension of E.
status: Trevisan-style constructions recover nearly all the entropy but require longer seeds; known shorter-seed results impose restrictions on the setting. A 2016 claim of full generality at optimal parameters was withdrawn. (De–Portmann–Vidick–Renner 2012, [*Trevisan's Extractor in the Presence of Quantum Side Information*](https://doi.org/10.1137/100813683); Ben-Aroya–Ta-Shma 2012, [*Better short-seed quantum-proof extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3737); [withdrawn 2016 claim](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04194).)
solved_when: A construction (with explicit constant C) extracts Ω(k) bits with error ε from any n-bit source with H_min(X|E) ≥ k ≥ C log(n/ε), using seed length O(log(n/ε)), against quantum side information E of arbitrary dimension; ideally with an efficient explicit implementation.
why: It would match classical-order extraction parameters against unrestricted quantum storage, giving optimal privacy amplification in the presence of fully general quantum adversaries.
key_works: De–Portmann–Vidick–Renner (2012), [*Trevisan’s Extractor in the Presence of Quantum Side Information*](https://doi.org/10.1137/100813683); Ben-Aroya–Ta-Shma (2012), [*Better short-seed quantum-proof extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.3737); [withdrawn 2016 claim](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04194).

title: R3-005. The three-uniform hypergraph share-size gap
subfield: Round 3
open: When every minimal authorized set has size three, how much information must participants share in the worst case? Determine the optimal worst-case total information ratio, improving the \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) lower bound or the \(O(n^3/\log n)\) upper bound in the long-secret regime.
status: Beimel's 2023 lower bound reaches \(n^{3/2}\) (see [*Lower Bounds for Secret-Sharing Schemes for k-Hypergraphs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2023.16), especially the \(k=3\) case), while decomposition constructions leave a polynomial gap. Large unauthorized sets are allowed, distinguishing this model from slices.
solved_when: The lower and upper bounds match (up to constants), giving the optimal worst-case total information ratio for access structures whose minimal authorized sets all have size three, in the long-secret regime.
why: It quantifies exactly how expensive authorization by triples can be, and closing the gap pins down whether the known decomposition-based constructions are essentially optimal or far from it.
key_works: Amos Beimel (2023), [*Lower Bounds for Secret-Sharing Schemes for k-Hypergraphs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2023.16), especially the \(k=3\) case.

title: R3-008. Duality for perfect nonlinear secret sharing
subfield: Round 3
open: Does an access structure and its dual always share the same optimal maximum-share information ratio when both perfect reconstruction and perfect privacy are required? A single concrete pair with unequal ratios would refute the conjecture.
status: Equality is known to hold for multilinear constructions. Csirmaz's 2019/2021 counterexample achieves almost-perfect sharing on 174 participants, but leaves the perfect model unresolved.
solved_when: Either the equality is proved for all access structures in the perfect model, or an explicit access structure is exhibited whose optimal maximum-share information ratio differs from that of its dual.
why: It settles whether complementing an authorization policy can change its fundamental storage cost, determining the extent to which duality can be exploited to bound or transfer complexity results between structures.
key_works: László Csirmaz (2019; journal 2021), [*Secret Sharing and Duality*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13663); Applebaum–Nir (2021), [*Upslices, Downslices, and Secret-Sharing with Complexity of 1.5ⁿ*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/052/).

title: R3-015. Safe two-scheme key cycles
subfield: Round 3
open: Given any public-key encryption scheme Enc, can one always construct another scheme Enc' that remains secure even when an encryption of Enc's secret key under Enc' and an encryption of Enc''s secret key under Enc are both made public, with the two keys independent? Formally: for every Enc, does there exist Enc' such that publishing Enc'(sk) and Enc(sk') with independent (sk, sk') breaks neither scheme's security?
status: This is Conjecture 2 of Daniele Micciancio's 2025 paper *Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption* (https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1, DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm). It remains open; known counterexamples for cycles where both encryptions use the same scheme do not settle the two-scheme, independent-key case.
solved_when: A construction of Enc' (for arbitrary Enc) with a proof that publishing Enc'(sk) and Enc(sk'), with independent keys, preserves both schemes' security — or a counterexample, i.e., an Enc for which no such Enc' exists.
why: A positive answer would justify the heterogeneous key cycles that arise in composability transformations, allowing security proofs to go through where key-dependency cycles across different schemes currently block them.
key_works: Daniele Micciancio (2025), [*Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1), DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm, Conjecture 2.

title: R3-016. Full composability from ordinary FHE alone
subfield: Round 3
open: Does ordinary fully homomorphic encryption already give fully composable homomorphic encryption, without assuming circular security? Formally, can full composability — the ability to evaluate functions on arbitrary combinations of ciphertexts — be derived from standard FHE definitions alone?
status: The question is explicitly left unresolved in Micciancio (2025), *Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption* (https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1, DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm); fresh-ciphertext correctness alone is known to be insufficient.
solved_when: A proof that ordinary FHE implies fully composable homomorphic encryption with no circular-security hypothesis, or a counterexample separating the two notions, is established.
why: It would close the definitional gap between foundational FHE notions and arbitrary composition of homomorphic computations, so that composability no longer rests on an extra unproven assumption.
key_works: Daniele Micciancio (2025), [*Fully Composable Homomorphic Encryption*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/1/1), DOI:10.62056/ak5wl86bm.

title: R3-017. Unbounded-circuit KDM security from ordinary LWE
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we build public-key encryption from ordinary LWE that remains secure when the encrypted messages are key-dependent — even for arbitrarily large circuits chosen adaptively, and for any number of keys, without fixing any bound in advance?
status: The distinction between bounded and unbounded KDM security dates to 2010 (Barak–Haitner–Hofheinz–Ishai). Kitagawa–Matsuda's 2020 amplification supports arbitrary numbers of keys but still requires an a priori circuit-size bound; circular-secure, circuit-private FHE gives the unbounded form under additional assumptions.
solved_when: A scheme based on ordinary LWE is proven KDM-secure for every polynomial-size key-dependent-message circuit, with the scheme fixed independently of the circuit-size bound and the number of keys, and with adaptive choices of circuits allowed.
why: It would remove a predetermined complexity ceiling from applications that encrypt key-dependent data, letting security scale with the computation actually performed rather than a bound fixed at setup.
key_works: Boaz Barak, Iftach Haitner, Dennis Hofheinz and Yuval Ishai (2010), [*Bounded Key-Dependent Message Security*](https://iftachh.github.io/MyHomepage/papers/BoundedKDM/boundedkdm.pdf); Fuyuki Kitagawa and Takahiro Matsuda (2020), [*Circular Security Is Complete for KDM Security*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1060); Benny Applebaum (2014), [*Key-Dependent Message Security: Generic Amplification and Completeness*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-013-9149-6).

title: R3-018. Collision resistance at algebraic degree two
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a collision-resistant hash family shrink its input while each output coordinate is computed by a degree-two polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\)? Equivalently, construct such a shrinking family (even from a specially chosen hard distribution of quadratic maps), or prove that every efficiently sampled quadratic family admits efficient collision finding.
status: Explicitly open since 2017. Degree three is achievable under codeword-hardness assumptions, and random quadratic maps yield universal one-way hashing under a quadratic-system assumption, but they are not known to be collision resistant.
solved_when: Either a shrinking family of quadratic-polynomial hash functions over \(\mathbb F_2\) with a proof of collision resistance is exhibited, or it is shown that for every efficiently sampled family of such maps, collisions can be found efficiently.
why: It determines whether a single multiplication layer suffices to support collision resistance, fixing the minimal algebraic degree — and hence arithmetic complexity — needed for this fundamental primitive.
key_works: Benny Applebaum, Naama Haramaty-Krasne, Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz and Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2017), [*Low-Complexity Cryptographic Hash Functions*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.7).

title: R3-022. Collusion-resistant private puncturing from DCR
subfield: Round 3
open: Can privately constrained PRFs built from decisional composite residuosity be extended to withstand polynomially many colluding constrained keys, so that the punctured points remain hidden under a multi-key privacy definition — all while keeping an exponentially large domain and without recourse to stronger obfuscation or FHE assumptions?
status: The state of the art is a 2025 result of Behera–Meyer–Orlandi–Roy–Scholl, which achieves single-key selective security for polynomially bounded Waring-rank predicates, including puncturing; the multi-key, collusion-resistant extension is the proposed open frontier.
solved_when: A construction from DCR supports polynomially many colluding constrained keys, satisfies a multi-key privacy definition hiding the punctured points, and retains an exponentially large domain without assuming obfuscation or FHE beyond DCR.
why: It would let many independent delegations share a single algebraic PRF family rather than requiring fresh setups per delegator.
key_works: Amik Raj Behera, Pierre Meyer, Claudio Orlandi, Lawrence Roy and Peter Scholl (2025), [*Privately Constrained PRFs from DCR: Puncturing and Bounded Waring Rank*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/230).

title: R3-024. Adaptive registered attribute-weighted sums with unbounded inputs
subfield: Round 3
open: Can one build registered functional encryption for attribute-weighted sums with access control that handles an unbounded number of attribute-value pairs while still allowing the adversary to choose challenge attributes, function registrations, and corruptions adaptively — and keeps ciphertexts compact, with size independent of the public-input length, under standard pairing assumptions?
status: Pal–Schädlich (2026), [*Compact Registered Functional Encryption for Attribute-Weighted Sums with Access Control*](https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000194419), DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-26737-5_11, achieve adaptive IND security for one input pair; their unbounded-input construction requires challenge attributes, registered functions, and corrupted users to be declared upfront. Closing that gap is the proposed target.
solved_when: A construction exists achieving adaptive IND security for attribute-weighted sums with access control, supporting an a priori unbounded number of attribute-value pairs and adaptive challenge attributes, registrations, and corruptions, with ciphertext compactness independent of public-input length, based on standard pairing assumptions.
why: It would allow encrypted records and their access policies to evolve over time without any advance knowledge of future access patterns, enabling dynamic database authorization and adaptive data analysis under evolving policies.
key_works: Tapas Pal and Robert Schädlich (2026), [*Compact Registered Functional Encryption for Attribute-Weighted Sums with Access Control*](https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000194419), DOI:10.1007/978-3-032-26737-5_11.

title: R3-032. Adaptive deletion for arbitrary monotone access structures
subfield: Round 3
open: Can information-theoretic secret sharing with adaptive certified deletion be constructed for every efficiently representable monotone access structure — that is, where an adversary corrupts and deletes shares sequentially while its currently undeleted shares always form an unauthorized set?
status: Explicit since Bartusek–Raizes (2024), who achieve threshold structures; their general-access construction achieves only no-signaling security. Katz–Sela (2025) reiterate the privately verifiable information-theoretic question.
solved_when: A construction exists for every efficiently representable monotone access structure with adaptive certified deletion security, where the adversary may corrupt and delete shares sequentially and its currently undeleted shares remain unauthorized throughout.
why: It would support certified deletion policies based on complex organizational authorization rules, beyond simple threshold requirements.
key_works: James Bartusek and Justin Raizes (2024), [*Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08117); Jonathan Katz and Ben Sela (2025), [*Secret Sharing with Publicly Verifiable Deletion*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1596), [EUROCRYPT slides](https://iacr.org/submit/files/slides/2025/eurocrypt/eurocrypt2025/234/234_slides.pdf).

title: R3-034. Threshold signing keys with certified deletion
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we build a threshold signature scheme in which the quantum signing-key shares can be certifiably deleted, so that unforgeability survives a sequence of compromises as long as too few undeleted shares have accumulated, while authorized parties can still produce independently combinable partial signatures?
status: The problem was explicitly posed in 2024 by Bartusek–Raizes and in Raizes's 2025 thesis (§11.4). It is known that deletion of threshold secret shares alone does not suffice to provide reusable signing on the protected shares. Key works: Bartusek–Raizes (2024), *Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*; Justin Raizes (2025), *Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*; Desmedt–Frankel (1989/1990), *Threshold Cryptosystems*.
solved_when: A construction exists with a formal proof that unforgeability holds against a sequential-compromise (mobile) adversary whenever fewer than the threshold number of undeleted shares remain, with certified deletion of shares, and with non-interactive combinable partial signatures by authorized parties.
why: It would make the retirement or revocation of distributed signing authority cryptographically checkable, rather than merely procedural.
key_works: Bartusek–Raizes (2024), [*Secret Sharing with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08117); Justin Raizes (2025), [*Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*](https://csd.cmu.edu/sites/default/files/phd-thesis/CMU-CS-25-107.pdf), §11.4; Yvo Desmedt and Yair Frankel (1989/1990), [*Threshold Cryptosystems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-34805-0_28).

title: R3-036. Public deletion verification for CE-NIZK without iO
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we build statistically sound NP non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs with certified-everlasting zero knowledge where anyone — not just the verifier — can check that deletion has taken place, without relying on indistinguishability obfuscation? Formally, obtain publicly verifiable deletion for certified-everlasting NIZKs under standard assumptions.
status: The problem is stated explicitly in the September 2026 revision of Pappu's work (Nikhil Pappu, 2025; revised 2026, *Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*, §2.7), where LWE-based constructions achieve only private verification of deletion and a coset-state route using iO is suggested as an approach to public verification.
solved_when: A construction of statistically sound NP NIZK proofs with publicly verifiable deletion and certified-everlasting zero knowledge is given, with security proved without assuming indistinguishability obfuscation.
why: Public verifiability of deletion enables independent audits of data destruction, since third parties can confirm a deletion occurred rather than trusting the original verifier.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-043. Plain-model certified-deniable signatures beyond black-box simulation
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a signature scheme in the plain model — with no idealized oracle — be both unforgeable and certifiably deniable, so that after deletion the retained evidence is simulatable without the signature beyond independently available prior information, using a non-black-box simulator? Or does the impossibility extend to rule out such simulators as well?
status: Çakan–Goyal–Raizes (2024; revised 2025; CRYPTO 2026) give QROM constructions and a plain-model black-box simulation barrier in *How to Delete Without a Trace: Certified Deniability in a Quantum World*; the stronger impossibility for non-black-box simulators is not established. See also Raizes (2025), *Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*, Part III.
solved_when: Either a plain-model signature scheme with certified deniability is constructed whose simulator is non-black-box (and after deletion, retained evidence is simulatable without the signature beyond independently available prior information), or the black-box simulation barrier is extended to an impossibility for non-black-box simulators.
why: It determines whether a verifier can credibly erase evidence of a signed interaction without relying on an idealized oracle such as the QROM.
key_works: Alper Çakan, Vipul Goyal and Justin Raizes (2024; revised 2025; CRYPTO 2026), [*How to Delete Without a Trace: Certified Deniability in a Quantum World*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1832); Justin Raizes (2025), [*Quantum Approaches to Verifiable Deletion*](https://csd.cmu.edu/sites/default/files/phd-thesis/CMU-CS-25-107.pdf), Part III.

title: R3-047. Simultaneous-message QKD with full everlasting security
subfield: Round 3
open: Can two parties who each send a single simultaneous message — with no interaction beforehand or afterward — agree on a shared secret key with standard everlasting security, even agreeing to abort when an active adversary interferes?
status: The problem was posed explicitly in 2025, in §1.3 of Grilo, Malavolta, Walter, and Zhang (2025; proceedings 2026), *Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*. What is currently known for simultaneous messages is only a conditional search guarantee, not full everlasting security; four messages over two rounds suffice to achieve full security.
solved_when: A QKD protocol exists in which the honest parties exchange exactly two simultaneous messages and achieves full everlasting security, including agreement-or-abort under active attacks; today four messages over two rounds are needed for that security level.
why: It would let parties generate keys by sending independently and in parallel, removing the back-and-forth coordination that interactive QKD requires.
key_works: Alex B. Grilo, Giulio Malavolta, Michael Walter and Tianwei Zhang (2025; proceedings 2026), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-048. Positive key rate in two-round EPR-based QKD
subfield: Round 3
open: Can two parties extract a linear number of secret key bits, with standard everlasting security, from n transmitted qubits in just two rounds using EPR pairs and single-qubit measurements?
status: The 2025 computational-monogamy protocol (Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang, 2025; proceedings 2026, "Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution," §1.3) achieves two rounds, but explicitly leaves positive key rate open.
solved_when: A two-round EPR-based protocol with single-qubit measurements is exhibited that achieves standard everlasting security and produces Ω(n) secret key bits from n transmitted qubits.
why: A positive key rate makes the two-round regime practically useful, improving the usable key yield per transmitted qubit rather than yielding only a sublinear or negligible amount of key.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025; proceedings 2026), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-049. Computational monogamy with arbitrary efficient Bob measurements
subfield: Round 3
open: Can computational monogamy of entanglement survive an adversarial recipient — that is, if the BB84 basis is initially computationally hidden but Bob is allowed any efficient basis-dependent POVM (rather than the prescribed basis measurement), while Charlie remains computationally unbounded, is Bob and Charlie's joint guessing probability still negligibly bounded?
status: The problem was made explicit in 2025 by Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang, [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3; their theorem requires Bob's prescribed basis measurement.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that, in the computational-monogamy setting with an initially computationally hidden BB84 basis, allowing Bob any efficient basis-dependent POVM while Charlie remains unbounded still forces their joint guessing probability to be negligible — replacing the current requirement that Bob perform the prescribed basis measurement.
why: It would extend computational monogamy to handle adversarial recipient processing, closing the gap between the idealized measurement model and what a dishonest, quantum-computationally bounded party could actually do.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-050. Computational monogamy with two unbounded measurement stages
subfield: Round 3
open: Can the computational monogamy-of-entanglement game be strengthened so that both Bob and Charlie may use arbitrary unbounded POVMs after an efficient state preparation with a computationally hidden basis? Formally, prove (or rule out) monogamy in the two-unbounded-measurement-stage version of the game.
status: The problem was posed explicitly in 2025 by Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025), *Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*, §1.3; even the weaker variant allowing only efficient arbitrary measurements for Bob remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of computational monogamy is established for the game in which both Bob's and Charlie's measurement stages allow arbitrary unbounded POVMs, with only efficient state preparation and a computationally hidden basis assumed; as an intermediate milestone, even the case restricting Bob alone to efficient arbitrary measurements is resolved.
why: It separates the complexity of preparing a state from the complexity of measuring it, pinning down whether computational monogamy is a property of preparation alone or of the full measurement pipeline.
key_works: Grilo, Malavolta, Walter and Zhang (2025), [*Computational Monogamy of Entanglement and Non-Interactive Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.00791v1), §1.3.

title: R3-051. Two-message QKD in the qubit-by-qubit model
subfield: Round 3
open: Can two-message everlasting-secure quantum key distribution be realized when every state and operation is confined to the qubit-by-qubit model? Formally, construct such a QKD protocol without any coherent joint processing of polynomial-size quantum registers.
status: Malavolta–Walter explicitly posed this restriction in 2023/2024; their OWF-based two-message construction (Robust Quantum Public-Key Encryption with Applications to Quantum Key Distribution, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02999, §1.3) relies on many-qubit superpositions and thus does not meet it.
solved_when: A two-message everlasting-secure QKD protocol is constructed in which all states and operations follow the qubit-by-qubit model, with no coherent joint processing of polynomial-size quantum registers.
why: It would make minimal-interaction QKD compatible with simpler quantum optical hardware, avoiding the need for large coherent quantum processing.
key_works: Giulio Malavolta and Michael Walter (2023; revised 2024), [*Robust Quantum Public-Key Encryption with Applications to Quantum Key Distribution*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02999), §1.3.

title: R3-057. Statistical randomized encodings of degree two
subfield: Round 3
open: Does every finite Boolean function admit a statistical randomized encoding whose output coordinates are quadratic polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) in the input and random bits? Equivalently, is degree two sufficient for statistical randomized encodings of all Boolean functions?
status: Degree three is known to suffice, while known perfect-privacy lower bounds do not settle the statistical relaxation; this boundary is explicitly identified in the literature, notably in Applebaum (2017), *Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*, §4.1, and Halevi, Ishai, Kushilevitz and Rabin (2023), *Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*.
solved_when: A proof that every finite Boolean function has such a degree-at-most-two statistical randomized encoding, or a counterexample function for which no such encoding exists.
why: A positive answer would lower the algebraic complexity of information-theoretically secure computation, simplifying constructions that currently require degree-three encodings.
key_works: Benny Applebaum (2017), [*Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2017/067/), §4.1; Shai Halevi, Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz and Tal Rabin (2023), [*Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/870).

title: R3-058. Statistical randomized encodings of locality three
subfield: Round 3
open: Does every finite Boolean function admit a statistically private randomized encoding in which each output bit depends on at most three input-or-randomness bits?
status: Locality four is achievable, while locality two is insufficient in general; the intermediate statistical case of locality three remains unresolved in the cited treatment (Applebaum 2017, *Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*, §4.1).
solved_when: A construction of statistical randomized encodings of locality three for all Boolean functions is given, or a function family is exhibited that admits no statistically private encoding of locality three.
why: It pinpoints the smallest local operation that still supports general private encodings, sharpening the boundary between locality four (achievable) and locality two (impossible).
key_works: Benny Applebaum (2017), [*Garbled Circuits as Randomized Encodings of Functions: A Primer*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2017/067/), §4.1.

title: R3-061. One-round framing-free distributed ZK
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a distributed zero-knowledge proof with strong completeness against malicious verifiers be achieved in a single round in the ideal-coin-tossing model? Formally: obtain a one-round information-theoretic distributed ZK proof with strong completeness, or prove that two rounds are necessary, while keeping verification communication independent of the statement circuit size.
status: Hazay–Venkitasubramaniam–Weiss (2023; journal 2026, [*Your Reputation's Safe with Me: Framing-Free Distributed Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09576-7), §1.3) obtain two rounds for appropriately robustly encoded statements and \(k>6t+2\); they explicitly leave round optimality open.
solved_when: Either a one-round information-theoretic distributed ZK proof with strong completeness against malicious verifiers is constructed in the ideal-coin-tossing model with verification communication independent of statement circuit size, or a lower bound proving two rounds are necessary is established.
why: It makes private input certification compatible with a workflow of one upload followed by verification, rather than multi-round interaction.
key_works: Carmit Hazay, Muthuramakrishnan Venkitasubramaniam and Mor Weiss (2023; journal 2026), [*Your Reputation’s Safe with Me: Framing-Free Distributed Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09576-7), §1.3.

title: R3-063. Polynomial-loss reduction from local sources to local NOBF sources
subfield: Round 3
open: Can every \(d\)-local source of min-entropy \(k\) — where each output bit depends on at most \(d\) uniform input bits — be reduced to a distribution exponentially close to a mixture of \(d\)-local nonoblivious bit-fixing sources that retains \(\Omega(k/\operatorname{poly}(d))\) entropy, or is such a reduction impossible?
status: Explicitly posed in 2022. The best known reduction retains \(\Omega(k/(2^d d^2))\) entropy, an exponential loss in \(d\). See Omar Alrabiah, Eshan Chattopadhyay, Jesse Goodman, Xin Li and João Ribeiro (2022), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 2 and §1.2; DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2022.10.
solved_when: A reduction from every \(d\)-local source of min-entropy \(k\) to a distribution exponentially close to a mixture of \(d\)-local nonoblivious bit-fixing sources retaining \(\Omega(k/\operatorname{poly}(d))\) bits of entropy is given — with \(\operatorname{poly}(d)\) a polynomial in the locality parameter \(d\) — or a proof that no such reduction exists.
why: A positive answer would extend local-source extraction to regimes of growing locality, where the current exponential-in-\(d\) entropy loss in reductions blocks progress.
key_works: Omar Alrabiah, Eshan Chattopadhyay, Jesse Goodman, Xin Li and João Ribeiro (2022), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 2 and §1.2; DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2022.10.

title: R3-064. Sharp low-weight Chevalley–Warning bounds for quadratic systems
subfield: Round 3
open: How small can a nonzero common zero of a system of \(m\) quadratic polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) be, when all the polynomials vanish at the origin and \(2m<n\)? Determine the sharp \(n,m\)-dependent upper bound on its minimum Hamming weight — in particular, can a linear-in-\(m\) bound remain necessary even as \(n/m\) grows?
status: The 2022 low-weight Chevalley–Warning theorem of Alrabiah, Chattopadhyay, Goodman, Li and Ribeiro ([*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 4 and §1.2) gives an \(O(m)\) bound; tightness for quadratic systems remains explicitly unresolved.
solved_when: An upper bound on the minimum Hamming weight of such a nonzero common zero is established, matching the problem's \(2m<n\) regime, together with matching examples showing whether linear dependence on \(m\) is or is not necessary when \(n/m\) grows.
why: The bound controls the algebraic obstructions to randomness extraction from local sources and underpins the complexity of solving sparse polynomial systems.
key_works: Alrabiah, Chattopadhyay, Goodman, Li and Ribeiro (2022), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Extract from Local Sources*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13725), Theorem 4 and §1.2.

title: R3-066. Exponentially small error for random constant-degree sumset extractors
subfield: Round 3
open: Do most degree-\(d\) polynomials extract from sumset sources with exponentially small error, even when the degree \(d\) is a fixed constant? Formally, prove that at entropy \(k = Cdn^{C/d}\) the error is \(2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}\), with a small constant entropy rate serving as a concrete milestone.
status: Posed in 2025 (Alrabiah, Goodman, Mosheiff and Ribeiro (2025), *Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*, Theorem 2 and §7). For even \(d\), the best general bound requires \(k = O(d(n/\varepsilon^2)^{2/d})\), which rules out the exponentially small error regime at fixed degree.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that most degree-\(d\) polynomials extract from sumset sources at entropy \(k = Cdn^{C/d}\) with error \(2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}\), including for fixed \(d\); a first milestone is achieving error \(2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}\) at a small constant entropy rate.
why: It would deliver strong statistical security while keeping the algebraic degree of the extractor independent of the error parameter.
key_works: Alrabiah, Goodman, Mosheiff and Ribeiro (2025), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10297), Theorem 2 and §7.

title: R3-073. Lifting group-product generators to arbitrary group-valued blocks
subfield: Round 3
open: Can the group-product-to-block-product reduction be lifted from Boolean-valued block functions to blocks that map arbitrarily into the group? That is, extend the reduction to products \(\prod_i h_i(x_{I_i})\) where each \(h_i\) is an arbitrary group-valued map on a disjoint block of input bits, while preserving near-optimal seed dependence on block width, block count, and error for a fixed noncommutative mixing group such as the quaternions.
status: The 2025 reduction of Chin Ho Lee and Emanuele Viola handles \(g_i^{f_i(x_{I_i})}\) with Boolean \(f_i\) ([*Pseudorandom Bits for Non-Commutative Programs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.9), Theorem 10 and §1.2); extending the block's range to the entire group is explicitly open.
solved_when: A reduction is constructed for \(\prod_i h_i(x_{I_i})\) with arbitrary group-valued \(h_i\) on disjoint blocks, for a fixed noncommutative mixing group such as the quaternions, achieving near-optimal seed dependence on block width, block count, and error.
why: It removes the Boolean-exponent restriction from algebraic derandomization, allowing the reduction to handle general group-valued functions rather than only \(g_i^{f_i(x_{I_i})}\) with Boolean \(f_i\).
key_works: Chin Ho Lee and Emanuele Viola (2025), [*Pseudorandom Bits for Non-Commutative Programs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.9), Theorem 10 and §1.2.

title: M08. Circuit-linear communication with only one honest participant
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can constant-round malicious secure computation tolerating a single honest party achieve communication linear in the circuit, independent of the number of parties? Formally, is there a constant-round protocol for dishonest-majority MPC with \(n-1\) corruptions and communication \(O(|C|\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))+\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda)\), under weak assumptions such as ordinary oblivious transfer and without stronger general-purpose primitives?
status: Current round-collapsing results require a constant honest fraction. A 2024 DDH-based construction (Goyal et al., 2024, [Dishonest Majority Constant-Round MPC with Linear Communication from DDH](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1466)) tolerates \(n-1\) corruptions but retains an \(O(|C|n)\) circuit term; round-collapsing techniques toward minimal assumptions appear in Goyal–Li–Ostrovsky–Song (2025/2026, [Towards Building Scalable Constant-Round MPC from Minimal Assumptions via Round Collapsing](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/508)).
solved_when: A constant-round maliciously secure MPC protocol tolerating \(n-1\) corruptions is constructed with communication \(O(|C|\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))+\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda)\), relying only on weak assumptions such as ordinary OT and avoiding stronger general-purpose primitives.
why: A solution would determine whether almost-total collusion inherently imposes per-gate communication proportional to the party count, resolving a basic scalability question for secure computation.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2024), [*Dishonest Majority Constant-Round MPC with Linear Communication from DDH*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1466); Goyal–Li–Ostrovsky–Song (2025/2026), [*Towards Building Scalable Constant-Round MPC from Minimal Assumptions via Round Collapsing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/508).

title: M09. Adaptivity-preserving compression of MPC rounds
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can the number of rounds in a general MPC protocol be collapsed while still tolerating adversaries who corrupt parties adaptively during the protocol (without erasures) and keeping communication nearly linear in the circuit size? Formally, is there a round-compression compiler whose security loss is an explicit function of when and how many parties are corrupted?
status: This is currently a proposed compiler target. Existing round-collapse results do not establish the full combination of adaptivity, erasure-freeness, and near-linear communication sought here.
solved_when: A compiler exists that compresses rounds, preserves erasure-free adaptive security with communication near-linear in the circuit size, and comes with an explicit security loss bound depending on corruption timing and count.
why: Without it, parties compromised mid-computation are outside the threat model of existing constant-round protocols; such a theorem would make round-efficient MPC safe against realistic, ongoing compromise.
key_works: Goyal–Li–Ostrovsky–Song (2025/2026), [*Towards Building Scalable Constant-Round MPC from Minimal Assumptions via Round Collapsing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/508); Canetti et al. (2002), [*Universally Composable Two-Party and Multi-Party Secure Computation*](https://doi.org/10.1145/509907.509980).

title: M10. Efficient guaranteed output delivery from OWFs without random oracles
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Match constant-round honest-majority MPC with guaranteed output delivery and circuit-linear-in-\(n\) communication using ordinary OWFs in the standard model.
status: Li–Song’s 2026 protocol achieves the relevant combination in the random-oracle model, with communication \(O(|C|n\lambda+Dn^3\lambda^3+W_I\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda))\).
why: Would place low-latency, availability-preserving MPC on an explicit minimal assumption.
key_works: Li–Song (2026), [*Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296).

title: M11. Guaranteed output delivery without the depth surcharge
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can constant-round honest-majority MPC with guaranteed output delivery achieve communication that does not grow with the multiplicative depth of the computed circuit — or is there an inherent price for depth that any such protocol must pay?
status: The September 2026 Li–Song revision achieves constant rounds and linear communication in Minicrypt, but still incurs the \(Dn^3\lambda^3\) depth-surcharge term for guaranteed output delivery [Li–Song (2026), *Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*, https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296].
solved_when: Either a constant-round honest-majority MPC protocol with guaranteed output delivery removes the \(Dn^3\lambda^3\) communication term, or a lower bound is proved showing that depth-dependent communication of this order is unavoidable for such protocols.
why: Without an answer, deep computations pay a substantial extra communication cost merely to be guaranteed completion, so circuits of large depth remain disproportionately expensive to compute securely.
key_works: Li–Song (2026), [*Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296).

title: M12. Network-agnostic MPC with near-quadratic setup
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can perfectly secure MPC that tolerates both synchronous and asynchronous adversaries be realized with only near-quadratic circuit-independent communication? Formally, reduce the setup overhead of network-agnostic MPC to \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) bits while keeping computation polynomial and the corruption thresholds optimal.
status: Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song's October 2026 revision achieves \(O((|C|n+(D+C_I)n^2+n^6)\log n)\) bits under the optimal threshold \(n>2\max(t_s,t_a)+\max(2t_a,t_s)\).
solved_when: A perfectly secure network-agnostic MPC protocol is given whose circuit-independent communication cost is \(\widetilde O(n^2)\), with polynomial computation and corruption thresholds matching the optimal bound \(n>2\max(t_s,t_a)+\max(2t_a,t_s)\).
why: It would remove an enormous startup cost from protocols designed for settings where network timing is uncertain.
key_works: Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song (2026), [*Perfectly Secure Network-Agnostic MPC Comes for Free*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/377).

title: M13. Responsive network-agnostic secure computation
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can a multiparty computation protocol achieve optimal network-agnostic resilience and perfect privacy while its latency tracks actual message delays during fast executions, yet remain secure when delays are arbitrary? In particular, can responsiveness be realized separately across preprocessing, evaluation, and reconstruction?
status: This is a proposed strengthening of the 2026 feasibility theorem of Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song (2026), *Perfectly Secure Network-Agnostic MPC Comes for Free* (https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/377); responsiveness is required to cover preprocessing, evaluation, and reconstruction separately. Related lines include optimistically responsive consensus and failure-detector hierarchies.
solved_when: A protocol exists combining optimal network-agnostic resilience, perfect privacy, and responsiveness — with running time governed by actual (not worst-case) message delays during fast executions — while preserving security under arbitrary delays, with responsiveness achieved in each of preprocessing, evaluation, and reconstruction.
why: It would let applications exploit fast networks for speed without having to trust those networks to stay fast, since security degrades gracefully to the asynchronous setting.
key_works: Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song (2026), [*Perfectly Secure Network-Agnostic MPC Comes for Free*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/377).

title: M14. Asynchronous weighted and fluid MPC
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can we build maliciously secure MPC for asynchronous networks in which the set of participants changes over time with unequal weights, and where output delivery is still guaranteed? In particular, the goal is to characterize how much honest-weight overlap between successive committees is necessary and sufficient for such a construction.
status: Almashaqbeh–Ghude's 2026 work combines weighted participation, dynamic membership, and guaranteed delivery, but only under synchrony ([*MPC with Weighted and Fluid Participation*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1375)).
solved_when: A construction exists that achieves maliciously secure MPC with changing weighted membership and guaranteed output delivery in an asynchronous network, together with a characterization of the required honest-weight overlap between successive committees.
why: Long-running computations often involve organizations with unequal trust, resources, and availability; a solution tells us how such parties can join and leave securely without a synchrony assumption.
key_works: Almashaqbeh–Ghude (2026), [*MPC with Weighted and Fluid Participation*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1375).

title: M15. Near-linear private-state handover between weighted committees
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can a committee hand its entire private MPC state over to a successor committee at essentially the cost of the state itself — that is, using only \(O(S+n\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))\) field elements to transfer an \(S\)-element state among \(n\) parties — while achieving malicious security and proactive refresh whenever the weighted participation has a fixed positive honest-weight margin?
status: This is a proposed efficiency target beyond the 2026 feasibility results of Almashaqbeh–Ghude (2026), [*MPC with Weighted and Fluid Participation*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1375), which established weighted proactive sharing and state handover without near-linear communication.
solved_when: A protocol transfers an \(S\)-element private MPC state using \(O(S+n\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))\) field elements, with malicious security and proactive refresh, proven secure under a fixed positive honest-weight margin.
why: It would make committee rotation affordable for large persistent private states, so long-lived weighted-participation MPC systems can rotate membership without paying communication proportional to the full state times the committee size.
key_works: Almashaqbeh–Ghude (2026), [*MPC with Weighted and Fluid Participation*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1375).

title: M16. Asynchronous MPC within tenfold synchronous throughput overhead
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: How close can asynchronous MPC come to its synchronous counterpart in real throughput? Concretely, build an asynchronous MPC protocol with guaranteed delivery tolerating \(t<n/3\) Byzantine faults whose total throughput cost is within a factor of ten of a matched synchronous implementation for \(n=32,64,128\), accounting for preprocessing and adversarial delays.
status: This is a proposed moonshot benchmark with no existing demonstrations. On the theory side, Goyal–Liu-Zhang–Song (2024), [*Towards Achieving Asynchronous MPC with Linear Communication and Optimal Resilience*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/243), give linear-amortized communication, and Meng et al. (2026), [*RondoMPC*](https://eprint.iacr.org/1261), improve practical preprocessing; together these mark the relevant starting points.
solved_when: A demonstrated asynchronous MPC protocol with guaranteed delivery at \(t<n/3\) achieves throughput within \(10\times\) of a matched synchronous implementation at \(n=32\), \(n=64\), and \(n=128\), with the comparison including preprocessing and adversarial delays.
why: It would quantify—and potentially sharply reduce—the practical cost of removing synchrony assumptions, telling practitioners whether asynchrony is genuinely affordable.
key_works: Goyal–Liu-Zhang–Song (2024), [*Towards Achieving Asynchronous MPC with Linear Communication and Optimal Resilience*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/243); Meng et al. (2026), [*RondoMPC*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1261).

title: M17. Communication-optimal asynchronous identifiable abort
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: What is the true communication and latency cost of achieving identifiable abort in asynchronous MPC, once correctness and input loss are relaxed enough to permit improved corruption thresholds? Determine tight bounds for both measures in this relaxed setting.
status: Appan–Heath–Ren (2026, [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455)) establish feasibility boundaries; the quantitative frontier remains open.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for communication and latency in asynchronous MPC with identifiable abort under the relaxed correctness and input-loss definitions permitting improved corruption thresholds.
why: It pins down the precise price of accountability when guaranteed output delivery is unattainable — the number real deployments must budget for attributing fault.
key_works: Appan–Heath–Ren (2026), [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455).

title: M18. Low-overhead protection against super-rushing
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can synchronous malicious MPC protocols be compiled so they remain secure against adversaries who get to see some next-round messages before committing to all of their current-round ones, while preserving resilience and near-linear communication? The compiled protocol must also allow event-driven advancement, without reintroducing round-end waiting or global synchronization barriers.
status: The 2025 foundational work of Asharov–Chandramouli–Cohen–Ishai (2025), [*Peeking Into the Future: MPC Resilient to Super-Rushing Adversaries*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1394), proves that substantial secret-sharing and triple-based protocol families resist super-rushing; no general preservation theorem follows.
solved_when: A compilation of synchronous malicious MPC exists that tolerates super-rushing adversaries, preserves the original resilience and near-linear communication, and permits event-driven execution without round-end waiting or global synchronization barriers.
why: It closes a concrete mismatch between round-based security proofs and event-driven implementations, where messages can be processed as they arrive rather than at round boundaries.
key_works: Asharov–Chandramouli–Cohen–Ishai (2025), [*Peeking Into the Future: MPC Resilient to Super-Rushing Adversaries*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1394).

title: M20. Adversarial scheduling corpus for MPC implementations
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can we build a corpus of executable scheduling tests that exposes when MPC implementations diverge from their proofs — distinguishing rushing, super-rushing, input exclusion, and incorrect abort attribution? Each test should carry minimized failing traces and the proof-model metadata needed to pin down which semantic guarantee is violated.
status: Currently a proposed data target, motivated by documented mismatches between MPC implementations and their proofs and by recent distinctions in asynchronous correctness, including Asharov et al. (2025), [*Peeking Into the Future*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1394) and Appan–Heath–Ren (2026), [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455). No corpus exists yet.
solved_when: A released corpus of executable scheduling tests exists that distinguishes rushing, super-rushing, input exclusion, and incorrect abort attribution, with each failing trace minimized and annotated with proof-model metadata.
why: It turns semantic security regressions in MPC implementations into reproducible, checkable events rather than anecdotal reports, so mismatches between implementations and proofs can be systematically detected and minimized.
key_works: Asharov et al. (2025), [*Peeking Into the Future*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1394); Appan–Heath–Ren (2026), [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455).

title: M25. Function-specific trusted-party size complexity
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: How much trusted-party computation does each functionality genuinely require to achieve fairness or guaranteed output delivery in the presence of a dishonest majority? The goal is a classification of functionalities by the minimum size of a trusted party invoked only once.
status: The problem stands as a proposed classification program extending the 2022 general bounds of Ishai et al. (2022), [*Fully-Secure MPC with Minimal Trust*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1248); useful direct-sum and composition theorems are currently missing.
solved_when: For each functionality, its minimum once-invoked trusted-party size for fairness and for guaranteed delivery against dishonest majorities is characterized, together with the supporting direct-sum and composition theorems that make the classification usable.
why: A solution would separate functions that demand substantial trusted intervention from those that need very little, giving a function-specific measure of unavoidable trust in secure computation.
key_works: Ishai et al. (2022), [*Fully-Secure MPC with Minimal Trust*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1248).

title: M26. Tight delay–security tradeoffs for fair coin tossing
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can fair multiparty coin tossing be achieved through delays alone, and if so, at what exact cost in sequential delay, total work, and the adversary's ability to parallelize? In particular, determine the optimal such tradeoffs for the setting with \(n-1\) corruptions.
status: Ball–Christ–Dodis–Garg (2026), in [*Fair Multiparty Coin Tossing from Minimal Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/931), establish an existence equivalence with delay functions; the tight quantitative reductions remain a separate open target.
solved_when: The delay–security tradeoff is quantitatively tight: optimal bounds on sequential delay, total work, and adversarial parallelism are established for delay-enabled fair multiparty coin tossing, including the case of \(n-1\) corruptions.
why: A tight characterization would tell us exactly when timed computation can economically replace stronger honesty assumptions in fair coin tossing protocols.
key_works: Ball–Christ–Dodis–Garg (2026), [*Fair Multiparty Coin Tossing from Minimal Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/931).

title: M27. Large-party rational coin-tossing classification
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Which utility matrices allow a coin-tossing protocol in which, for any number of parties, no coalition of up to \(n-1\) parties can profitably deviate — and how does the answer change once deviations go beyond the semi-malicious model?
status: Wang–Wu's October 2026 preprint ([*Game-Theoretically Fair Coin Toss from Random Walk Against \(n-1\) Corruptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2405)) identifies sufficient and impossible regimes and gives a complete three-party characterization; the general-party classification remains open.
solved_when: A complete classification of the utility matrices admitting cooperative-strategy-proof coin tossing for arbitrary \(n\) against \(n-1\) corruptions is given, together with an extension of the classification to deviations beyond semi-malicious behavior.
why: It settles when economic incentives alone can sustain shared randomness among mutually distrustful parties, even in the face of near-total collusion.
key_works: Wang–Wu (2026), [*Game-Theoretically Fair Coin Toss from Random Walk Against \(n-1\) Corruptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2405).

title: M31. Near-linear honest-verifier-to-malicious-verifier compilation
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Compile efficient honest-verifier ZK into malicious-verifier ZK with near-linear prover and communication overhead and constant additive rounds, stating the privacy notion and extra assumptions.
status: Proposed efficiency target. HV-SZK equals SZK is established, and OWFs already give computational ZK for NP.
why: Would preserve the practical advantage of specialized honest-verifier protocols.
key_works: Goldreich–Sahai–Vadhan (1998), [*Honest-Verifier Statistical Zero-Knowledge Equals General Statistical Zero-Knowledge*](https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~/oded/PSX/gsv.pdf); Vadhan (2006), [*An Unconditional Study of Computational Zero Knowledge*](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539705447207).

title: M33. Exact rounds for fully black-box nonmalleable ZK from OWFs
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: How many messages are really needed to build fully black-box simulation-extractable nonmalleable zero knowledge from one-way functions alone? In particular, do five messages suffice when only delayed-input one-many security is required?
status: Constant-round fully black-box feasibility was established in 2024 (Botta–Ciampi–Orsini–Siniscalchi–Visconti, "Black-Box (and Fast) Non-Malleable Zero Knowledge"), but the exact round count remains open; meanwhile, four-round fully black-box ordinary ZK from arbitrary one-way functions runs into an earlier barrier (Hazay–Pass–Venkitasubramaniam, 2020, "Which Languages Have 4-Round Fully Black-Box Zero-Knowledge Arguments from One-Way Functions?").
solved_when: A construction (or matching lower bound) pins down the exact minimum message count for fully black-box simulation-extractable nonmalleable ZK from arbitrary OWFs, specifically resolving whether the five-message, delayed-input one-many regime is achievable.
why: It separates the inherent round cost of nonmalleability itself from the overhead introduced by compilers, telling us which part of current round complexity is unavoidable.
key_works: Botta–Ciampi–Orsini–Siniscalchi–Visconti (2024), [*Black-Box (and Fast) Non-Malleable Zero Knowledge*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/432); Hazay–Pass–Venkitasubramaniam (2020), [*Which Languages Have 4-Round Fully Black-Box Zero-Knowledge Arguments from One-Way Functions?*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-45727-3_20).

title: M35. Four-round statistical nonmalleable ZK under full concurrency
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can four-round statistical non-malleable zero knowledge be achieved when many proofs run concurrently and the adversary acts as both prover and verifier across adaptive statements? Formally, extend the four-round construction to fully concurrent many-many executions with a unified simulation-extraction guarantee.
status: The recent four-round theorem of Kiyoshimawa (2025/2026) [Four-round Statistical Non-malleable Zero-knowledge](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1787) establishes delayed-input one-many security, and that guarantee does not automatically imply full concurrency. Earlier constant-round concurrent non-malleable ZK was studied by Yan–Deng–Sun (2018) [Concurrent Non-Malleable Zero-knowledge and Simultaneous Resettable Non-malleable Zero-knowledge in Constant Rounds](https://doi.org/10.1186/s42400-018-0014-7).
solved_when: A four-round statistical non-malleable zero-knowledge protocol is proved secure under fully concurrent many-many executions with adaptive statements and a single unified simulation-extraction definition.
why: Real proof services face adversaries interacting in many sessions at once, as both provers and verifiers; without a concurrent guarantee, security proven in isolated or one-many settings may not hold when these interactions overlap.
key_works: Kiyoshima (2025/2026), [*Four-round Statistical Non-malleable Zero-knowledge*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1787); Yan–Deng–Sun (2018), [*Concurrent Non-malleable Zero-knowledge and Simultaneous Resettable Non-malleable Zero-knowledge in Constant Rounds*](https://doi.org/10.1186/s42400-018-0014-7).

title: M36. Negligible nonmalleability error in three-round weak ZK
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can a three-round weak zero-knowledge argument in the plain model achieve negligible nonmalleability error while keeping its weak-ZK quantifier precisely stated?
status: A September 2026 preprint (Zhang et al. (2026), [*Three-Round Weak Non-Malleable Zero-Knowledge Argument*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1964)) obtains three rounds with weak ZK and parameterized inverse-polynomial nonmalleability error from primitives including OT and circuit-private FHE; negligible error remains open.
solved_when: A construction of three-round plain-model weak-ZK arguments is given whose nonmalleability error is negligible (not merely parameterized inverse-polynomial), with the weak-ZK quantifier explicitly retained and stated.
why: It would strengthen tamper resistance of these arguments without adding interaction.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), [*Three-Round Weak Non-Malleable Zero-Knowledge Argument*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1964).

title: M39. Randomness generation secure under partial resets
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can the partial-key-reset-secure pseudorandomness required for strong resettable NIZK be instantiated under familiar standard-model assumptions — or failing that, can the required related-key security notion itself be weakened?
status: The October 2026 revision (Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), [Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036)) provides generic defenses but identifies partial-reset PRF security as an unresolved assumption-level issue.
solved_when: An explicit construction of the needed partial-reset PRF security is given from a standard, familiar assumption, or the related-key security requirement is formally weakened while still sufficing for strong resettable NIZK.
why: It would convert the currently generic reset defense into an efficiently justified, concretely instantiated construction.
key_works: Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), [*Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036).

title: M40. End-to-end partial-reset experiments
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can a zero-knowledge prover safely reuse parts of its randomness across resets — fault injections and VM rollbacks — without paying for it in proof size or verification cost? Concretely, can selective reuse of prover masks and keys be benchmarked end-to-end so that it acts as a defense with unchanged proof size and verification and under 10% prover overhead, across three proof architectures?
status: Proposed experimental target; no experiments yet. The 2026 work of Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), *Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses* (https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036), gives the attacks and a generic randomness-generation defense.
solved_when: Experiments demonstrate, under fault injection and VM rollback, a defense based on selective reuse of prover masks and keys that keeps proof size and verification unchanged and incurs under 10% prover overhead, evaluated across three proof architectures.
why: Ordinary transcript-validity tests do not reveal many reset-induced witness leaks, so without such end-to-end experiments these vulnerabilities go undetected in practice.
key_works: Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), [*Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036).

title: M48. Extractability-preserving robust ZK combiners
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can zero-knowledge proof systems be combined so that adaptive simulation extractability is preserved whenever the designated components supply extraction and the others supply privacy — even under correlated malicious setups?
status: Currently this is a proposed strengthening of the 2025 robust-ZK combination theorem for thresholds \(t_s+t_z>n\), following Applebaum–Kachlon (2025), [*How to Share an NP Statement or Combiners for Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/334).
solved_when: A combination construction (or theorem) is given that preserves adaptive simulation extractability under the stated component split and correlated malicious setups, strengthening the 2025 robust-ZK combination theorem for thresholds \(t_s+t_z>n\).
why: A solution would let applications diversify their underlying assumptions across components without losing knowledge-soundness guarantees, enabling threshold trust in extraction.
key_works: Applebaum–Kachlon (2025), [*How to Share an NP Statement or Combiners for Zero-Knowledge Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/334).

title: M50. Ordinary OWFs from high-error private-coin ZK
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Does a constant-round private-coin zero-knowledge proof for NP with high error — where the completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge errors sum to at most \(1 - 1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\) — already imply the existence of ordinary one-way functions? Formally, derive ordinary OWFs from such proofs under the assumption \(NP \not\subseteq ioP/poly\).
status: The 2026 result of Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer (2026), [*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651), gives ordinary OWFs for public-coin proofs but only auxiliary-input OWFs for private coins.
solved_when: Ordinary one-way functions are derived from constant-round private-coin NP zero-knowledge proofs with completeness, soundness, and ZK errors summing to at most \(1 - 1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), under the assumption \(NP \not\subseteq ioP/poly\).
why: It would identify the weakest meaningful private-coin privacy guarantee that already forces cryptographic hardness.
key_works: Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer (2026), [*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651).

title: M51. High-error ZK-to-OWF implications beyond constant rounds
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Does every polynomial-round public-coin zero-knowledge proof whose combined completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge errors sum to at most \(1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\) still imply one-way functions? Formally, under the same complexity premise, derive OWFs from polynomial-round public-coin ZK whenever \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_z\le1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\).
status: Constant rounds satisfy the unweighted criterion. For \(m\) messages, the known general criterion is \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+(m-1)\varepsilon_z<1\); removing its message-dependent coefficient remains open.
solved_when: OWFs are derived from polynomial-round public-coin ZK satisfying the unweighted criterion \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_z\le1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), replacing the message-dependent bound.
why: It would show whether interaction dilutes the hardness forced by weak privacy, or whether the implication survives at any polynomial round count.
key_works: Chatterjee–Li–Vasudevan (2026), [*Weak Zero-Knowledge and One-Way Functions*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.5); Chakraborty et al. (2026), [*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651).

title: M52. Machine-checkable MPC/ZK frontier registry
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can we build a versioned, machine-checkable registry of the MPC and zero-knowledge frontier? The corpus would record, for each theorem, its messages, setup, corruption timing, honesty thresholds, soundness type, simulator quantifiers, and assumption strength, together with checked comparability rules.
status: Proposed data target; nothing built yet. The motivating pattern is that recent advances repeatedly close broad headlines while leaving model-qualified gaps — e.g., Applebaum–Kachlon–Patra (2023), [*The Round Complexity of Statistical MPC with Optimal Resiliency*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/418), and Appan–Heath–Ren (2026), [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455).
solved_when: A versioned theorem corpus exists capturing all the listed dimensions (messages, setup, corruption timing, honesty thresholds, soundness type, simulator quantifiers, assumption strength) and comes with checked comparability rules.
why: It would prevent incorrect "solved" labels and stop the invalid composition of incomparable results, which recent advances make an acute risk as broad headlines get closed while model-qualified gaps remain.
key_works: Applebaum–Kachlon–Patra (2023), [*The Round Complexity of Statistical MPC with Optimal Resiliency*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/418); Appan–Heath–Ren (2026), [*Asynchronous MPC with Abort*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/455).

title: A01. Indistinguishability obfuscation from ordinary LWE
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size classical circuits be built from ordinary LWE alone? That is, without evasive, circular-evasive, succinct-sampling, or other obfuscation-specific assumptions.
status: Open since general-purpose candidates appeared in 2013. Well-founded-assumption constructions, e.g. Jain–Lin–Sahai (2020/2021), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09317), use combinations of assumptions; current lattice-only general candidates remain heuristic, and recent work such as Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932), continues to chip away at the required assumptions.
solved_when: A construction of iO for all polynomial-size classical circuits is given, proved secure under ordinary LWE (standard, non-evasive, non-circular, non-succinct-sampling) with a polynomial-time reduction.
why: It would give a conventional post-quantum foundation for a large fraction of advanced cryptography, replacing bespoke obfuscation-specific assumptions with the most standard lattice assumption.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai (2020/2021), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09317); Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A03. General iO from polynomial-security assumptions
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can general indistinguishability obfuscation be built from assumptions that are hard only against polynomial-time adversaries? More precisely, construct iO without the subexponential hardness currently needed to absorb exponential losses in the security reduction.
status: Short-equivalence-proof promises permit improved reductions, but arbitrary equivalent circuits do not necessarily satisfy those promises; Jain–Jin (2022), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence*](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00100).
solved_when: A construction of general iO is given whose security reduces to assumptions secure against polynomial-time adversaries, with no subexponential hardness requirement.
why: It would ground obfuscation in ordinary cryptographic hardness rather than a much stronger quantitative assumption, aligning iO with the standard regime of cryptographic security.
key_works: Jain–Jin (2022), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence*](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00100).

title: A04. Minimum truth-table savings sufficient to bootstrap XiO
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: How much must an obfuscator shrink a truth table before that compression alone yields full indistinguishability obfuscation — in particular, is a mere polynomial saving such as \(2^n/n^c+\operatorname{poly}(|C|,\lambda)\) enough to bootstrap polynomial-time iO?
status: XiO with \(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\)-type size can be amplified to stronger iO under subexponential XiO and LWE assumptions (Lin–Pass–Seth–Telang 2016, *Indistinguishability Obfuscation with Non-trivial Efficiency*, https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/006); polynomial savings remain a strictly weaker, unresolved starting point.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that XiO with size \(2^n/n^c+\operatorname{poly}(|C|,\lambda)\) implies polynomial-time iO, under whatever assumptions are made explicit in the proof.
why: It would pin down the efficiency threshold for a general obfuscation breakthrough, showing that even modest truth-table savings suffice.
key_works: Lin–Pass–Seth–Telang (2016), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation with Non-trivial Efficiency*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/006).
aliases: XiO amplification threshold; exponentially efficient iO.

title: A06. Strong pseudorandom obfuscation from falsifiable assumptions
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
