open: Can stronger variants of pseudorandom obfuscation (PRO) — those powerful enough to support witness encryption with ciphertext size independent of the witness length — be constructed from clearly specified falsifiable assumptions, or is there a fundamental barrier showing this is impossible?
status: The strongest construction in the PRO framework, due to Branco et al. (2024/2025, [*Pseudorandom Obfuscation and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1742)), is heuristic and relies on subexponential and private-coin evasive LWE rather than falsifiable assumptions.
solved_when: Either a construction of the stronger PRO variants supporting witness-size-independent witness encryption is given from clearly specified falsifiable assumptions, or a matching barrier (impossibility proof) is established.
why: It would ground unusually succinct encryption in assumptions with conventional security games, replacing heuristic foundations with ones we can meaningfully test.
key_works: Branco et al. (2024/2025), [*Pseudorandom Obfuscation and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1742).

title: A07. Secret-oblivious private-coin evasive LWE
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Is private-coin evasive LWE secure when the sampler class is secret-oblivious — and if not, can an attacker actually exploit it under the exact restrictions the assumption imposes? A second, sharper form: either prove security for useful classes of secret-oblivious samplers, or exhibit an attack that respects the sampler restrictions exactly.
status: The 2026 Huang–Hung–Yamada correction invalidates a previously claimed obfuscation attack in this regime while leaving the security of the assumption unresolved.
solved_when: Either a security proof is given for useful secret-oblivious sampler classes in private-coin evasive LWE, or an attack is exhibited that satisfies the exact sampler restrictions of the assumption.
why: Several advanced lattice constructions depend on the precise scope of evasive assumptions; pinning down which secret-oblivious samplers are safe determines which of those constructions stand.
key_works: Huang–Hung–Yamada (2026), [*A Note on Obfuscation-Based Attacks on Private-Coin Evasive LWE*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/4/20); Vaikuntanathan–Wee–Wichs (2022), [*Witness Encryption and Null-IO from Evasive LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1140).

title: A08. A viable boundary for differing-inputs obfuscation
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Which restricted classes of circuit samplers still admit differing-inputs obfuscation under standard, falsifiable assumptions once arbitrary correlated auxiliary input is ruled out? Formally, characterize the bounded-input samplers for which such a diO construction can exist in this auxiliary-input-free setting.
status: Versions allowing general auxiliary input face implausibility results (Garg–Gentry–Halevi–Wichs, 2014, *On the Implausibility of Differing-Inputs Obfuscation and Extractable Witness Encryption with Auxiliary Input*). The state of the art as of October 2026 is public-coin diO built from indistinguishability obfuscation plus the knowledge-style KOALA assumption (Chen–Vaikuntanathan, 2026, *Public-coin Differing-input Obfuscation from KOALA and iO*).
solved_when: A characterization is given of the bounded-input circuit samplers admitting diO under conventional falsifiable assumptions in the setting excluding arbitrary correlated auxiliary input — identifying which samplers are in and which are out.
why: It would delineate the meaningful forms of differing-inputs obfuscation that survive the known implausibility barriers, separating what is fundamentally broken from what remains a viable target.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Halevi–Wichs (2014), [*On the Implausibility of Differing-Inputs Obfuscation and Extractable Witness Encryption with Auxiliary Input*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/860); Chen–Vaikuntanathan (2026), [*Public-coin Differing-input Obfuscation from KOALA and iO*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2346).

title: A10. Quasilinear general iO without equivalence-proof promises
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can general-purpose indistinguishability obfuscation be realized with only quasilinear blow-up in code size and evaluation overhead, without requiring the circuits to come equipped with short formal proofs of their equivalence? More precisely, can the quasilinear efficiency regime be achieved for arbitrary circuits, with the dependence on equivalence-proof size eliminated entirely?
status: Ma–Dai–Shi (2025), in [*Quasi-Linear Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/307), achieve overhead quasilinear in both the circuit size and the equivalence-proof size; the dependence on the proof remains.
solved_when: A construction of iO for general circuits is given whose obfuscated-code size and evaluation overhead are quasilinear in the circuit size alone (up to security-parameter factors), with no dependence on the length of any mathematical equivalence proof supplied with the circuit.
why: It would extend the quasilinear-efficiency regime of obfuscation from circuits with short equivalence proofs to arbitrary equivalent programs, making asymptotic efficiency results meaningful without proof-system side conditions.
key_works: Ma–Dai–Shi (2025), [*Quasi-Linear Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/307).

title: A12. Obfuscation-assumption challenge corpus
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can the community produce a machine-readable corpus of obfuscation-assumption challenge families, where each family records its exact sampler restrictions, parameter provenance, known attacks, reduced instances, and reproducible attack costs?
status: A proposed data target with no corpus yet published; recent corrections to evasive-LWE attack claims (Huang–Hung–Yamada (2026), [*A Note on Obfuscation-Based Attacks on Private-Coin Evasive LWE*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/4/20)) illustrate why sampler metadata is essential. Related efforts include reproducible average-case benchmarks and adversarial-instance generation; also relevant is Ragavan–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Bilinear Maps and LPN Variants*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/856).
solved_when: Such a challenge corpus is published with all of the listed metadata — sampler restrictions, parameter provenance, documented attacks, reduced instances, and reproducible attack-cost measurements — for its challenge families.
why: Reliable assumption comparison and cryptanalysis: with sampler metadata attached to every instance, mistaken or overstated attack claims can be caught and reproduced rather than argued in the abstract.
key_works: Huang–Hung–Yamada (2026), [*A Note on Obfuscation-Based Attacks on Private-Coin Evasive LWE*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/4/20); Ragavan–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Bilinear Maps and LPN Variants*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/856).

title: A14. Crossing the linear-collusion ciphertext barrier
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can general-circuit functional encryption be made secure against collusions of size \(Q\) with ciphertexts that grow strictly slower than linearly in \(Q\), starting only from weak assumptions — or can we prove that such compactness is unattainable for restricted functionality classes?
status: Adaptive bounded-collusion FE is known to achieve linear dependence of ciphertext size on \(Q\); improving this to sublinear in the general setting would imply indistinguishability obfuscation. See Ananth–Vaikuntanathan (2019), [*Optimal Bounded-Collusion Secure Functional Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/314).
solved_when: A construction of general-circuit FE from weak assumptions achieves ciphertext size sublinear in the collusion bound \(Q\), or a barrier theorem establishes that sublinear dependence is impossible for a specified restricted functionality class.
why: It answers whether ciphertext compactness itself already demands obfuscation-level power, separating what weak assumptions can achieve from what inherently requires iO.
key_works: Ananth–Vaikuntanathan (2019), [*Optimal Bounded-Collusion Secure Functional Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/314).

title: A15. Fully adaptive circuit ABE from ordinary LWE
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can we build attribute-based encryption for general circuits, assuming only the standard (ordinary) Learning with Errors assumption, that remains secure even when the adversary chooses the challenge attribute and requests decryption keys adaptively after seeing the public parameters? Formally, the goal is a fully adaptively secure circuit ABE scheme whose security reduces to ordinary LWE, with no partitioning fixed before setup and no resort to witness encryption.
status: The current state of the art is an October 2026 output-adaptive ABE, an intermediate notion; fully adaptive constructions based on witness encryption do not settle the question from LWE alone. Key works: Waters–Wichs (2024), [*Adaptively Secure Attribute-Based Encryption from Witness Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1486); Cheng–Goyal (2026), [*Revisiting Partitioning: Output-Adaptive ABE for Circuits from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2305).
solved_when: A construction of circuit ABE from ordinary LWE is given, together with a proof of full adaptive security — i.e., security against adversaries that select challenge attributes and make function-key (decryption key) requests after the public parameters are published.
why: Real authorization requests and policies are chosen after a system is deployed, not fixed before setup, so partially adaptive guarantees do not match how ABE is actually used.
key_works: Waters–Wichs (2024), [*Adaptively Secure Attribute-Based Encryption from Witness Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1486); Cheng–Goyal (2026), [*Revisiting Partitioning: Output-Adaptive ABE for Circuits from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2305).

title: A20. Sublinear collusion dependence in lattice registered FE
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can ciphertext size in lattice-based registered functional encryption for general circuits grow sublinearly in the number of corrupted users \(Q\)? Formally, is there a construction supporting general circuits under explicit lattice assumptions whose ciphertext size is \(o(Q)\) in the collusion parameter?
status: The 2026 construction of Champion–Wu–Yamada (2026), [*Silent Threshold Encryption from Lattices*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1716), achieves \(Q\widetilde O(d)+\ell\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,d,\log N)\) ciphertext size from decomposed LWE in the random-oracle model, leaving the dependence on \(Q\) linear.
solved_when: A registered functional encryption scheme for general circuits, based on explicit lattice assumptions, achieves ciphertext size with sublinear dependence on \(Q\), improving on the current \(Q\widetilde O(d)\) term while retaining the \(\ell\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,d,\log N)\) portion.
why: Collusion bounds currently dominate the compactness budget, so sublinear dependence would directly yield meaningfully smaller ciphertexts under large-scale corruption.
key_works: Champion–Wu–Yamada (2026), [*Silent Threshold Encryption from Lattices*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1716).

title: A22. Adaptive registered ABE with linear CRS in the plain model
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can registered attribute-based encryption for monotone span programs achieve a linear-size common reference string with adaptive security in the plain model, while users generate their keys independently and statelessly?
status: The 2026 linear-CRS construction of Stracovsky–Waters–Wu, *Pairing-Based Registered ABE for Boolean Formulas with a Linear-Size CRS*, achieves static plain-model security under a \(q\)-type assumption and adaptive security in random oracles, but not adaptive plain-model security.
solved_when: A pairing-based registered ABE scheme for monotone span programs is given with a CRS of linear size, proven adaptively secure in the plain model (no random oracles), with independent, stateless user key generation.
why: It would combine compact setup with the realistic setting where keys are registered adaptively after the system is deployed, closing the gap left by current static-security and random-oracle results.
key_works: Stracovsky–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Pairing-Based Registered ABE for Boolean Formulas with a Linear-Size CRS*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1062).

title: A24. Fully adaptive multi-authority circuit ABE from LWE
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can we build multi-authority attribute-based encryption for general circuits, secure against fully adaptive adversaries and malicious authorities, from the plain Learning With Errors assumption — with no random oracles, no central setup authority, and no trusted issuer?
status: No such construction is known. Current frontier results each give up something: the 2025 circuit constructions of Cini–Lai–Woo (2025) ([*Lattice-based Multi-Authority/Client Attribute-based Encryption for Circuits*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/1/4/1)) achieve only very-selective security, rely on stronger assumptions, and restrict how authorities may be corrupted, while earlier work by Datta–Komargodski–Waters (2023) ([*Fully Adaptive Decentralized Multi-Authority ABE*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30620-4_15)) achieved fully adaptive decentralized multi-authority ABE but not for circuits from LWE.
solved_when: A construction is given whose security reduces to standard (ordinary) LWE, supporting arbitrary circuits, with fully adaptive security under malicious (corruptible) authorities, in a decentralized setting without random oracles or any central authority, accompanied by a proof.
why: It would deliver expressive, circuit-level access control in settings where no single party is trusted to issue keys — the trust is genuinely distributed across authorities.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Woo (2025), [*Lattice-based Multi-Authority/Client Attribute-based Encryption for Circuits*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/1/4/1); Datta–Komargodski–Waters (2023), [*Fully Adaptive Decentralized Multi-Authority ABE*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30620-4_15).

title: A26. Compact multi-authority FE across the corruption frontier
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: How efficiently can decentralized multi-authority functional encryption remain when many authorities may be malicious? In particular, determine the tight compactness achievable when tolerating \(\chi\) corrupted authorities, especially for coalitions growing beyond logarithmic size.
status: The 2026 revision of Goyal–Yadugiri (2025/2026), *Decentralized Multi-Authority Functional Encryption with Malicious Authorities from Standard Assumptions*, handles regimes where \(\binom n\chi\) is polynomial; additionally, nontrivial compactness beyond logarithmically many corrupted authorities is known to imply iO.
solved_when: A precise characterization is given of the compactness of decentralized FE tolerating \(\chi\) malicious authorities — matching constructions and lower bounds across the regime, including whether nontrivial compactness beyond logarithmically many corrupted authorities is achievable without implying iO.
why: It clarifies how increasing decentralization changes the cryptographic power required, marking exactly where standard assumptions stop sufficing and indistinguishability obfuscation becomes necessary.
key_works: Goyal–Yadugiri (2025/2026), [*Decentralized Multi-Authority Functional Encryption with Malicious Authorities from Standard Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/412).

title: A28. Function privacy without universal-circuit inflation
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can a compiler take a declared private-key functional-encryption workload and hide not just the messages but the functions being computed, while inflating circuit size by at most \(2\times\)? The compiled scheme should retain adaptive security and the original leakage profile.
status: Proposed engineering target. Generic function-privacy transformations already establish feasibility, e.g., Brakerski–Segev (2014/2015), [*Function-Private Functional Encryption in the Private-Key Setting*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/550).
solved_when: A compilation procedure exists that hides both functions and messages with at most \(2\times\) additional circuit work, preserves adaptive security, and maintains the original leakage profile.
why: Function descriptions can reveal proprietary algorithms or sensitive query intent, so achieving function privacy cheaply makes private-key FE practical without the blowup of universal-circuit techniques.
key_works: Brakerski–Segev (2014/2015), [*Function-Private Functional Encryption in the Private-Key Setting*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/550).

title: A29. Security-model-aware FE and ABE benchmarks
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can we build a benchmarking methodology for functional- and attribute-based encryption that compares constructions only on genuinely equivalent security tasks — tracking, alongside raw performance on identical circuits, the collusion bounds, adaptive versus selective security, attribute visibility, setup assumptions, output range, and parameter-generation costs of each scheme?
status: Proposed data target only; no benchmark yet exists. Existing constructions occupy different points on these axes, making raw throughput comparisons misleading. Key works include Ananth–Vaikuntanathan (2019), *Optimal Bounded-Collusion Secure Functional Encryption* (https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/314), and Cini–Wee (2023/2025), *ABE for Circuits with poly(λ)-Sized Keys from LWE* (https://doi.org/10.1137/24M1636162).
solved_when: A benchmark suite exists that runs identical circuits across FE/ABE implementations while recording, per construction, collusion bounds, adaptive/selective security, attribute visibility, setup assumptions, output range, and parameter-generation costs, so that results are reproducible and comparable across schemes.
why: Without accounting for where schemes sit on these security-model axes, throughput comparisons are misleading; such a suite would make implementation progress measurable across genuinely equivalent tasks.
key_works: Ananth–Vaikuntanathan (2019), [*Optimal Bounded-Collusion Secure Functional Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/314); Cini–Wee (2023/2025), [*ABE for Circuits with poly(\(\lambda\))-Sized Keys from LWE*](https://doi.org/10.1137/24M1636162).

title: A31. Instantiating prime-order generic-group WE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can the generic-group oracle in the Hair–Sahai prime-order witness encryption scheme be replaced by an explicit group, with security reduced to a standard assumption such as DDH or discrete log? In other words, is there a standard-model instantiation of the 2026 prime-order generic-group WE construction?
status: Hair–Sahai (2026) claim unconditional NP witness encryption in the classical generic-group model; this is an oracle-model result, not a standard-model DDH or discrete-log theorem. Key work: Hair–Sahai (2026), [*Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).
solved_when: A concrete prime-order group instantiation of the Hair–Sahai construction is given, together with a security reduction to a conventional (non-oracle) assumption.
why: It would convert a major oracle-model advance into an explicit assumption-based construction usable in practice, and rule out the possibility that the scheme's security is an artifact of the generic-group abstraction.
key_works: Hair–Sahai (2026), [*Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).

title: A32. Concrete parameters for group-based WE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can a witness encryption scheme based on generic groups be run at realistic scale — that is, can we produce a concrete, reproducible implementation that encrypts to actual NP relations and decrypts in practical time? The target is a reproducible candidate for \(10^5\)-gate relations with ciphertexts below 1 GB and encryption/decryption under one hour on a specified workstation, at 128-bit classical attack cost.
status: This is a proposed moonshot; the existing polynomial-time and quasipolynomial generic-security statements for group-based witness encryption do not establish these concrete bounds.
solved_when: A reproducible candidate exists for \(10^5\)-gate relations, with ciphertexts below 1 GB, encryption/decryption below one hour on a specified workstation, and an analysis targeting 128-bit classical attack cost.
why: It would reveal whether the new group-based route to witness encryption can support substantive applications, rather than remaining an asymptotic existence result.
key_works: Hair–Sahai (2026), [*Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275); Jin (2026), [*Witness Encryption for NP from SNARGs and Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2063).

title: A33. Extractable WE from conventional falsifiable assumptions
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can extractable witness encryption be built from a standard, falsifiable assumption such as plain LWE or conventional group assumptions? A first construction may exclude arbitrary correlated auxiliary input, provided any bounded-advice extension it offers is explicitly specified.
status: Impossibility results rule out broad auxiliary-input formulations of extractable witness encryption (Garg–Gentry–Halevi–Wichs, 2014, [*On the Implausibility of Differing-Inputs Obfuscation and Extractable Witness Encryption with Auxiliary Input*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/860)). As of October 2026, unconditional extractability is known only in the generic-group model (Campanelli, 2026, [*A Note on Extractable Witness Encryption in Generic Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2399)).
solved_when: A construction of extractable witness encryption is given whose security reduces to an ordinary, falsifiable assumption (e.g., LWE or standard group assumptions); if the construction does not handle arbitrary correlated auxiliary input, it must state precisely what bounded-advice regime it covers.
why: Extraction is what makes witness encryption usable for applications built on hard *true* statements, where the ciphertext's security must be tied to the infeasibility of producing a witness; without it, those applications lack a soundness guarantee.
key_works: Campanelli (2026), [*A Note on Extractable Witness Encryption in Generic Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2399); Garg–Gentry–Halevi–Wichs (2014), [*On the Implausibility of Differing-Inputs Obfuscation and Extractable Witness Encryption with Auxiliary Input*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/860).

title: A36. Breaking the half-exponent in LWE-based XWE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can we push the encryption exponent for general witness encryption built from standard LWE below 1/2, assuming only ordinary (not stronger) subexponential hardness of LWE? Formally, construct extractable-style witness encryption where the encryption time degrades as \(2^{m^\epsilon}\) for some \(\epsilon < 1/2\), with explicit dependence on the witness size and the underlying LWE security parameters.
status: The \(2^{m/2}\) construction is a verified reference point; arbitrarily small positive exponents remain a stronger, unachieved target. Known obstacles include meet-in-the-middle barriers and questions about fine-grained reductions. Brakerski et al. (2017/2018), [*Non-Trivial Witness Encryption and Null-iO from Standard Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/874).
solved_when: A construction achieves exponent strictly below \(1/2\) — indeed, arbitrarily small positive exponents are the stronger target — from ordinary subexponential LWE, with the encryption exponent's dependence on witness size and security parameters stated explicitly.
why: It would improve the best-known route to witness encryption from weak assumptions, giving meaningful security and efficiency even before a full polynomial-time witness encryption scheme becomes available.
key_works: Brakerski et al. (2017/2018), [*Non-Trivial Witness Encryption and Null-iO from Standard Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/874).

title: A39. Polylogarithmic public tracing from plain WE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can we build publicly traceable broadcast encryption from plain witness encryption with ciphertexts only polylogarithmic in the number of users? Formally, achieve ciphertext size poly(λ, log N) while retaining collusion resistance and applicable independent-key guarantees.
status: The best known result, the September 2026 cutoff-iO construction (Nassar–Waters–Wu, 2026, [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932)), achieves ciphertext size N^ε poly(λ) for every fixed positive ε, from WE plus LWE — subpolynomial in N but not polylogarithmic.
solved_when: A construction from plain WE (plus standard assumptions) achieves ciphertext size poly(λ, log N) for N users, with security parameter λ, preserving collusion resistance and independent-key guarantees.
why: Public traitor tracing would scale to very large populations, where current ciphertext sizes grow polynomially in N.
key_works: Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A41. False-instance versus hard-true-instance WE benchmarks
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can we construct benchmark relations for witness encryption that pair independently verified false instances with hard true instances, together with witness distributions and explicit release-game assumptions? In other words, a family of test relations whose false instances are checkably false and whose true instances are computationally hard to distinguish from false without a witness.
status: A proposed data target; no such benchmarks exist yet. Ordinary WE guarantees secrecy on false instances, while hard true instances require additional reasoning. Related threads include Garg et al. (2025), [*A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364) and Campanelli (2026), [*A Note on Extractable Witness Encryption in Generic Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2399).
solved_when: A set of benchmark relations is published, each with independently checked false instances, hard true instances, an associated witness distribution, and explicitly stated release-game assumptions.
why: Without such benchmarks, application security can be inferred from the wrong witness-encryption definition; ordinary WE secrecy guarantees only apply to false instances, and hard true instances require additional reasoning that currently has no ground truth to test against.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), [*A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364); Campanelli (2026), [*A Note on Extractable Witness Encryption in Generic Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2399).

title: A42. Efficient public certification of condition ciphertexts
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can a special-purpose witness-encryption ciphertext carry a compact public certificate that it indeed encodes the declared payload commitment and condition? The certificate should add at most \(10\times\) overhead to encryption and remain secure against a malicious encryptor.
status: Proposed engineering target. General proofs can certify encryption computations, but the integrated efficient envelope remains to be demonstrated. Related directions include verifiable encryption, proof-carrying data, and malicious-input certification (Garg et al. (2025), [A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364)).
solved_when: A publicly verifiable certification mechanism exists for condition ciphertexts, with total encryption overhead bounded by \(10\times\), and a proof of malicious-encryptor security.
why: Without such certificates, recipients cannot tell what a conditional ciphertext actually promises to release, undermining trust in condition-based encryption systems.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), [*A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364).

title: A43. SNARGs for all NP from polynomially hard LWE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we construct succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for all of NP assuming only polynomial hardness of LWE? More precisely, the goal is a construction with polynomial-time preprocessing and proof length polynomial in the security parameter and logarithmic in the verification time.
status: LWE-based SNARGs are established for P and for special NP languages that admit suitable bounded-space nonmembership proofs (Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956)). The general NP case remains open.
solved_when: A SNARG construction for arbitrary NP languages exists from standard polynomial-hardness LWE, with polynomial preprocessing and proof length polynomial in the security parameter and logarithmic in verification time.
why: It would yield general succinct verification of arbitrary NP computations from a conventional post-quantum assumption, giving quantum-safe delegation and computation checking on standard hardness.
key_works: Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956).

title: A45. Universal SNARGs without formal-correctness promises
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we build universal SNARGs for NP from arbitrary suitable witness encryption or two-message argument systems, without insisting on short correctness proofs in a specified formal system? In other words, is there a construction that avoids the formal-provability requirement entirely rather than merely making it non-explicit?
status: The 2025 universal framework of Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Mathialagan (2025), [*Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718104), uses formal proofs of correctness; non-explicit use of a scheme does not eliminate that logical requirement.
solved_when: A universal NP SNARG is constructed from any suitable witness encryption scheme or two-message argument system, with no requirement that parties produce short correctness proofs in a specified formal system.
why: It would free universal cryptographic constructions from dependence on formal provability, removing a logical bottleneck that currently shapes which schemes can serve as foundations.
key_works: Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Mathialagan (2025), [*Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718104).

title: A46. Remove derandomization from unprovability-based SNARGs
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can a succinct non-interactive argument for NP based on unprovability be built without assuming promise-class derandomization? Formally, eliminate the premise \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) from the 2026 unprovability-based construction while retaining its other explicitly stated premises.
status: The 2026 Hsieh–Jain–Li–Mathialagan construction uses LWE, SXDH, promise-class derandomization (\(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\)), and a formal unprovability assumption involving hard Extended Frege tautologies.
solved_when: An NP-SNARG construction is given that assumes LWE, SXDH, and the formal unprovability assumption involving hard Extended Frege tautologies, but not \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) or any promise-class derandomization premise.
why: It isolates whether derandomization contributes essential cryptographic power to unprovability-based SNARGs, separating that assumption's role from the others.
key_works: Hsieh–Jain–Li–Mathialagan (2026), [*SNARGs for NP from Unprovability of Mathematical Theorems*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/098/).

title: A47. Adaptive public delegation from plain WE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can publicly verifiable, adaptively sound SNARGs for arbitrary NP be built from plain witness encryption together with ordinary LWE, without upgrading the witness encryption to an extractable or obfuscation-based form?
status: Universal constructions currently yield nonadaptive results, and stronger guarantees are known only for restricted languages; positional WE alone does not establish the full target. Related work includes Jin et al. (2025), *Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness*, and Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), *Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs*.
solved_when: A construction is given of publicly verifiable, adaptively sound SNARGs for all of NP whose assumptions are plain WE and standard LWE, with no reliance on extractable WE or iO.
why: It would convert a weaker advanced primitive into broadly usable adaptive delegation, making succinct verification available far beyond the restricted settings currently reachable.
key_works: Jin et al. (2025), [*Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718104); Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A49. Adaptive soundness for shadow-PCP SNARGs
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can the shadow-PCP/function-binding approach to Micali-style SNARGs be made sound against adversaries who choose their statements adaptively, after seeing the setup? A formal strengthening would give adaptively sound SNARGs while preserving standard-model hashing and succinct parameters.
status: A theorem dated September 2026 establishes nonadaptive soundness for this route; adaptive soundness remains open. Key works include Guan–Yogev (2025/2026), [*Micali's SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2328).
solved_when: A construction in the shadow-PCP/function-binding framework is proven adaptively sound, with security holding for statements chosen after setup is published, and with standard-model hashing and succinct parameters retained.
why: Verifiers should remain secure when statements are selected after setup is published; without adaptive soundness, the SNARG is only justified in a weaker, nonadaptive security model.
key_works: Guan–Yogev (2025/2026), [*Micali’s SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2328).

title: A51. Practical two-group-element SNARGs
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can succinct arguments retain proofs of just two source group elements while becoming practical — with quasilinear prover work, tractable CRS generation, and competitive verification on large circuits?
status: The 2025/2026 construction of Arnon–Dujmovic–Yogev (2025/2026), [*Pairing-Based SNARGs with Two Group Elements*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2160), gives two \(\mathbb G_1\) elements in the generic group model plus the random oracle model, including a 768-bit BLS12-381 illustration, but is explicitly not yet concretely efficient.
solved_when: A construction achieves two-source-group-element proofs with quasilinear proving time, tractable CRS generation, and verification competitive on large circuits, demonstrated with concrete efficiency (e.g., matching or improving upon the 768-bit BLS12-381 illustration).
why: It would make ultra-short proofs useful in real deployments rather than serving only as an asymptotic feasibility demonstration.
key_works: Arnon–Dujmovic–Yogev (2025/2026), [*Pairing-Based SNARGs with Two Group Elements*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2160).

title: A53. Quasioptimal concrete delegation from polynomial LWE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we build, from polynomial-strength LWE assumptions, a practical delegation system — a SNARG or IVC for deterministic computations — that is competitive on real hardware? Concretely, this means quasilinear prover overhead, proofs under 1 MB, and verification costing under 1% of recomputation on declared large workloads.
status: A proposed moonshot that deliberately retains polynomial-hardness assumptions rather than pursuing stronger ones. Theoretical LWE-based SNARGs and IVC for P already exist, including Chen–Freitag–Jin–Wichs (2025), [*Unambiguous SNARGs for P from LWE with Applications to PPAD Hardness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718159); what is missing is quasioptimal concrete efficiency.
solved_when: An implemented LWE-based SNARG or IVC for deterministic computations achieves quasilinear prover work, proofs below 1 MB, and verification below 1% of the cost of recomputation on the declared large workloads.
why: It would give a concrete, plausibly post-quantum alternative to pairing- or hash-based delegation, with measured performance rather than asymptotic promises.
key_works: Chen–Freitag–Jin–Wichs (2025), [*Unambiguous SNARGs for P from LWE with Applications to PPAD Hardness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718159).

title: A54. A fully doubly efficient IP equals PSPACE theorem
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we build interactive proofs for arbitrary polynomial-space computations where the honest prover runs in time polynomial in the computation's running time and the verifier runs in time polynomial in the input length — a "fully doubly efficient" IP = PSPACE theorem?
status: Chen–Hong–Kalai–Xi reach \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\) in 2026, improving on the earlier \(n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}\) regime; the general case remains open.
solved_when: An information-theoretic interactive proof exists for general time-T polynomial-space computations, with prover time polynomial in T and verifier time polynomial in the original input length.
why: It would align the cost of honest proving with the cost of the underlying computation throughout PSPACE, making proof-based delegation practical even for the most general computation class.
key_works: Chen–Hong–Kalai–Xi (2026), [*Towards a Doubly Efficient IP=PSPACE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1287).

title: A55. Covert memory checking without read-only reads
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can covert memory checking be made fundamentally cheaper when logical reads are allowed to modify server memory or the checker's private state? Formally, either establish matching overhead lower bounds in this mutable-read setting, or exploit that freedom to beat the current bounds.
status: The 2025 \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) query lower bound of Boyle–Komargodski–Vafa ([*The Complexity of Memory Checking with Covert Security*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/358)) assumes read-only reads and sublinear local storage, leaving the mutable-read case open.
solved_when: Either a lower bound matching the current \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) query bound is proved without the read-only-reads assumption, or a checker circumventing that bound is constructed when reads may be mutable.
why: It determines whether mutable reads enable fundamentally cheaper integrity checking, resolving whether the read-only restriction in current lower bounds is an artifact or essential.
key_works: Boyle–Komargodski–Vafa (2025), [*The Complexity of Memory Checking with Covert Security*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/358).

title: A56. Proof-checked implementation of assumption-based delegation
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can a practical SNARG whose security rests on standard assumptions be paired with a machine-checked specification that verifies the full pipeline — arithmetization, preprocessing, transcript binding, adaptive statements, and serialization?
status: Currently a proposed engineering target. It is known that verifying an arithmetic kernel alone does not establish end-to-end protocol security. Candidate starting points include Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956), and Guan–Yogev (2025/2026), [Micali's SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2328).
solved_when: A standard-assumption SNARG implementation is connected to a proof-checked specification covering arithmetization, preprocessing, transcript binding, adaptive statements, and serialization.
why: This would close the gap between asymptotic proofs and deployed verifiers, replacing arguments about idealized protocol descriptions with guarantees about the code that actually runs.
key_works: Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956); Guan–Yogev (2025/2026), [*Micali’s SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2328).

title: E01. Sharp entropy threshold for explicit two-source extraction
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can we construct explicit, polynomial-time two-source extractors that work all the way down to the probabilistic existence threshold, with sharp leading constants and optimal error dependence? Formally, the goal is to match the entropy threshold guaranteed by nonconstructive arguments, including constants and the joint dependence between error and output length.
status: Li achieved asymptotically optimal \(O(\log n)\) entropy in 2023; sharp constants and joint error/output guarantees remain stronger targets. See Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802).
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time extractor for two independent \(n\)-bit sources matches the probabilistic existence threshold in its leading constants and error/output guarantees, with entropy \(O(\log n)\) carrying the sharp constant.
why: It determines exactly how little independent randomness suffices for explicit extraction, pinning down the true boundary between what randomness and computation can achieve for this most basic extractor model.
key_works: Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802).

title: E03. Almost-all entropy output at logarithmic entropy
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can an extractor for sources of entropy \(k = O(\log n)\) output nearly all of that entropy — specifically \(k - O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bits — while simultaneously being strong in a designated source and achieving near-optimal constants?
status: Currently, extraction from logarithmic-entropy sources is established only in the one-bit output case, and this does not achieve the simultaneous output length, strength in a designated source, and error guarantee sought here. Relevant work includes Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802), and Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists that, at \(k = O(\log n)\), outputs \(k - O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bits with error \(\varepsilon\), remains strong in a designated source, and achieves near-optimal constants.
why: It would convert very weak sources into useful multi-bit random seeds, which is exactly the bottleneck in bootstrapping minimal randomness into workable randomness.
key_works: Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802); Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).

title: E06. Explicit low-degree extractors for polynomial sources
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can we explicitly construct low-degree extractors for polynomial-map sources of bounded degree that match the entropy and degree bounds achieved by random low-degree polynomials, uniformly across the whole class of allowed source degrees?
status: Random low-degree polynomials are known to be good extractors in important regimes (Alrabiah–Goodman–Mosheiff–Ribeiro, 2025, [Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.38)); removing the randomness from the construction and making it explicit remains open.
solved_when: An explicit (deterministic, efficiently computable) low-degree extractor is constructed for bounded-degree polynomial-map sources, achieving the same regimes of parameters that random low-degree polynomials attain.
why: Randomness generated by algebraic processes pervades coding and cryptography, so explicit extractors for such sources would turn a probabilistic existence fact into usable, derandomized primitives.
key_works: Alrabiah–Goodman–Mosheiff–Ribeiro (2025), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.38).

title: E07. Explicit extraction from bounded-complexity varieties
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Construct deterministic extractors for uniform distributions on common zero sets of bounded-degree polynomials, with useful dimension and degree dependence.
status: Random-polynomial existence results cover new variety-source regimes; uniform explicit constructions remain a target.
why: Would exploit geometric structure in sources beyond affine spaces.
key_works: Alrabiah–Goodman–Mosheiff–Ribeiro (2025), [*Low-Degree Polynomials Are Good Extractors*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2025.38).

title: E08. Two good sources among many adversarial sources
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can randomness be extracted with negligible error from a sequence of many independent sources when only two of them — and we do not know which two — have polylogarithmic entropy, while the rest may be fixed adversarially?
status: Chattopadhyay–Goodman (2025) obtain three good low-entropy sources in 2025; their two-good-source consequence requires higher entropy.
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists that, given such a sequence, outputs bits statistically close to uniform (negligible error) even though only two sources have entropy polylogarithmic in the source length.
why: It would enable robust distributed randomness generation where a system produces near-uniform random bits without needing to identify which contributors are actually supplying entropy.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Goodman (2025), [*Leakage-Resilient Extractors against Number-on-Forehead Protocols*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/075/).

title: E10. Near-optimal low-entropy samplable-source extraction
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can we extract many nearly-uniform bits, with small error, from sources of only near-logarithmic entropy that are samplable by polynomial-size circuits, under a clearly stated standard circuit-hardness hypothesis?
status: Existing results cover only one-bit extraction at low entropy and multiplicative-error extraction at higher entropy, leaving the joint target open. A separate 2026 near-optimality report (ECCC TR26-089) was retracted. Key works: Oh–Shaltiel (2025/2026), *Extractors for Samplable Distributions from the Two-Source Extractor Recipe*; Shaltiel (2025), *Multiplicative Extractors for Samplable Distributions*.
solved_when: An explicit extractor (or a conditional construction under such a hypothesis) is given that outputs many bits with small error from polynomial-circuit-samplable sources at near-logarithmic entropy, with the near-optimality of the parameters established.
why: It would yield strong randomness extraction from sources described by efficient algorithms — such as low-entropy generative models — rather than sources with simple algebraic structure.
key_works: Oh–Shaltiel (2025/2026), [*Extractors for Samplable Distributions from the Two-Source Extractor Recipe*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/107/); Shaltiel (2025), [*Multiplicative Extractors for Samplable Distributions*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.22); [ECCC TR26-089 retraction](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/089/).

title: E11. Simultaneously optimal seeded-extractor parameters
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Can a seeded extractor achieve both the optimal seed length and the optimal entropy loss to within additive O(1) at the same time, across the entire feasible range of (n, k, ε)? Formally, the question asks for uniform polynomial-time strong extractors that simultaneously match the information-theoretic lower bounds on seed length and entropy loss up to an additive constant.
status: Constant-factor-optimal constructions are classical, but sharp simultaneous optimality — additive-constant closeness on both parameters at once — is a stronger demand that remains open. Key frameworks come from Guruswami–Umans–Vadhan (2009), *Unbalanced Expanders and Randomness Extractors from Parvaresh–Vardy Codes* (https://doi.org/10.1145/1538902.1538904), and Vadhan (2012), *Pseudorandomness* (https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/pseudorandomness/).
solved_when: An explicit family of uniform polynomial-time strong seeded extractors exists that, for all feasible (n, k, ε), attains both optimal seed length and optimal entropy loss within additive O(1) simultaneously.
why: It would settle the basic efficiency frontier for converting weak randomness into uniform bits, pinning down exactly how much randomness must be sacrificed in seed and entropy.
key_works: Guruswami–Umans–Vadhan (2009), [*Unbalanced Expanders and Randomness Extractors from Parvaresh–Vardy Codes*](https://doi.org/10.1145/1538902.1538904); Vadhan (2012), [*Pseudorandomness*](https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/pseudorandomness/).

title: E12. Short seeds, low error, and sublinear entropy loss
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Can a seeded extractor take a source with min-entropy k and, using only a seed of length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\), incur entropy loss \(o(k)\) in the negligible-error regime \(\log(1/\varepsilon)=o(k)\) — ideally with nearly linear evaluation time?
status: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), in [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473), achieve \((1-\eta)k\) output for fixed \(\eta>0\) in their regime; sublinear entropy loss remains explicitly open.
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists with seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\), entropy loss \(o(k)\) when \(\log(1/\varepsilon)=o(k)\), and, preferably, nearly linear time evaluation.
why: It would preserve nearly all of the source's available entropy even at cryptographic (negligible) error levels, where current constructions give up a constant fraction.
key_works: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473).

title: E13. Preprocessing-free nearly linear extraction
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Can nearly linear time seeded extractors with short seeds be made to work in very-low-entropy and very-small-error regimes without any parameter-dependent preprocessing? Formally, this asks to remove preprocessing — currently required only in those extreme regimes — while preserving the short-seed, nearly linear time guarantees.
status: The February 2026 revision of Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473), identifies removing preprocessing in these regimes as future work; parameter regimes outside very-low-entropy and very-small-error already avoid preprocessing.
solved_when: An explicit construction achieves nearly linear time extraction with short seeds for very-low-entropy sources and very-small-error parameters, with no step depending on preprocessing tailored to those parameters; other parameter regimes already avoid preprocessing, so success here closes the remaining gap.
why: Preprocessing costs can dominate small deployments or settings where parameters change frequently, so eliminating it makes these extractors practical exactly where they are currently most awkward to use.
key_works: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473).

title: E14. The low-entropy AC⁰ extractor frontier
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: How much randomness extraction can constant-depth (AC⁰) circuits actually perform when the source entropy falls below \(n/\operatorname{polylog}n\)? More precisely, characterize the optimal tradeoffs among entropy, seed length, error, and circuit depth for uniform AC⁰ strong extractors in this low-entropy regime.
status: Cheng–Wu (2024), [*Randomness Extractors in AC⁰ and NC¹*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2024.69), obtain strong parameters in their high-entropy AC⁰ regime and give NC¹ constructions; lower-entropy constant-depth tradeoffs remain incomplete.
solved_when: A characterization of the entropy–seed–error–depth tradeoffs for uniform AC⁰ strong extractors below \(n/\operatorname{polylog}n\) entropy is established, ideally matching upper and lower bounds.
why: It would determine exactly how much extraction can be performed by extremely shallow circuits, with consequences for constant-depth coding and related AC⁰ lower-bound and noise-sensitivity techniques.
key_works: Cheng–Wu (2024), [*Randomness Extractors in AC⁰ and NC¹*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.APPROX/RANDOM.2024.69).

title: E15. Restricted nonmalleability to full nonmalleability
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Does security of a seeded extractor against tampering that permutes the seed — or even tampering by an involution — automatically yield full nonmalleability against arbitrary fixed-point-free tampering, with only controlled losses in parameters?
status: The question was explicitly posed by Cohen–Doron–Samocha in 2025 in *Seed-Protecting Extractors* (https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given that permutation- or involution-tampering security implies full nonmalleability against arbitrary fixed-point-free tampering, with the parameter losses explicitly controlled.
why: A positive answer would simplify both the construction and the analysis of nonmalleable extractors, since permutation-based tampering is far easier to handle than general tampering.
key_works: Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).

title: E16. Small exceptional-seed sets from restricted nonmalleability
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Does restricted nonmalleability of a seeded extractor allow the removal of a small exceptional set of seeds so that every remaining pair of distinct seeds yields jointly near-uniform outputs — or is this implication false?
status: An explicit 2025 question, raised in connection with Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/); it is known that average-over-seed security does not directly imply uniform pairwise guarantees.
solved_when: A proof that a small exceptional seed set can be removed so all remaining distinct seed pairs give jointly near-uniform outputs, or a counterexample refuting the implication from restricted nonmalleability.
why: A positive answer would support reliable seed reuse and yield stronger structural properties for extractors; a refutation would clarify the limits of average-over-seed security.
key_works: Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).

title: P03. Sparse decoding polynomials for all server counts
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: Can the improved \(s\)-server PIR tradeoff of Gupte–Ragavan be made unconditional for every fixed server count \(s\), eliminating the number-theoretic conjecture it currently rests on? Equivalently, one seeks \(\exp(O((\log N)^{1/s}(\log\log N)^{1-1/s}))\) communication via constructions that are uniform in \(s\), for all \(s\).
status: Gupte–Ragavan's July 2026 result conditionally achieves \(\exp(O((\log N)^{1/s}(\log\log N)^{1-1/s}))\) communication, and unconditionally for fixed \(s\le15\); the conditional part rests on number-theoretic conjectures including the generalized repunit conjecture and Schinzel's hypothesis H, with the underlying technique being sparse \(s\)-decoding polynomial support. See Gupte–Ragavan (2026), [*Exponentially Fewer-Server PIR from Sparser S-Decoding Polynomials*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22033).
solved_when: An \(s\)-server PIR scheme unconditionally achieves communication \(\exp(O((\log N)^{1/s}(\log\log N)^{1-1/s}))\) for every fixed \(s\) (not just \(s\le15\)), with constructions that behave uniformly as \(s\) grows.
why: It would remove the dependence on unproven conjectures (the generalized repunit conjecture, Schinzel's hypothesis H) from the fewest-server efficient PIR regime, substantially reducing the number of servers needed for highly efficient PIR.
key_works: Gupte–Ragavan (2026), [*Exponentially Fewer-Server PIR from Sparser S-Decoding Polynomials*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22033).

title: P05. Dynamic information-theoretic PIR with cheap updates
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: Can a quasilinear-space, sublinear-query-time information-theoretic PIR scheme be made dynamic, so that databases undergoing point updates remain queryable without costly rebuilds? Formally, the goal is to support point updates with polylogarithmic amortized update cost while preserving the static guarantees on space and query time, and with the update procedure's leakage made explicit.
status: This is a proposed dynamic extension of recent static preprocessing advances, in particular the sublinear-time, quasilinear-space two-server PIR of Henzinger–Ragavan (2026) and the preprocessing line initiated by Beimel–Ishai–Malkin (2000); no dynamic construction is yet known.
solved_when: An explicit construction achieves quasilinear space and sublinear query time for information-theoretic PIR while handling point updates at polylogarithmic amortized cost, with a stated characterization of what information each update leaks.
why: Real private databases change; if every update forces an expensive rebuild, the query-time gains of modern preprocessing-based PIR are erased in practice.
key_works: Henzinger–Ragavan (2026), [*Two-Server Private Information Retrieval in Sublinear Time and Quasilinear Space*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2008); Beimel–Ishai–Malkin (2000), *Reducing the Servers’ Computation in Private Information Retrieval: PIR with Preprocessing*.

title: P06. Arithmetic two-server PIR below the cube-root bound
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: Can two servers holding an \(N\)-element database over a field answer a private retrieval query while transmitting fewer than \(O(N^{1/3})\) field elements, using only black-box field arithmetic — or is this cube-root barrier optimal for such schemes?
status: The 2026 arithmetic-PIR characterization of Applebaum–Ishai–Shechter, [*On Arithmetic Private Information Retrieval: Why Code-Based PIR (Usually) Fails*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1224), explicitly leaves this two-server boundary open; nontrivial single-server arithmetic PIR is already ruled out.
solved_when: Either a two-server arithmetic PIR scheme communicating \(o(N^{1/3})\) field elements is constructed, or a matching lower bound shows \(\Omega(N^{1/3})\) field elements are necessary for black-box field-arithmetic schemes.
why: It determines the reach and limitations of a broad algebraic design approach to private information retrieval.
key_works: Applebaum–Ishai–Shechter (2026), [*On Arithmetic Private Information Retrieval: Why Code-Based PIR (Usually) Fails*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1224).

title: P07. Tight noninteractive random-index PIR communication
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: What is the true communication cost of retrieving a uniformly random row from a two-server database when each server answers with a single message? Formally, close the gap between the known \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\) lower bound and the existing upper bounds for two-server, one-message-per-server random-index PIR on \(d\) rows of \(w\) bits.
status: Kolby, Roy, Sternad, and Yakoubov (2025) establish the \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\) lower bound and give sublinear constructions in appropriate row-width regimes, in [*Information-Theoretic Random-Index PIR*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2025.5).
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for the communication complexity of two-server, one-message-per-server random-index PIR on \(d\) rows of \(w\) bits, tightening the current \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\) lower bound against the known constructions.
why: Random-index retrieval enables private sampling with an interaction pattern fundamentally different from chosen-index PIR, so tight bounds would pin down the true cost of this sampling primitive.
key_works: Kolby–Roy–Sternad–Yakoubov (2025), [*Information-Theoretic Random-Index PIR*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2025.5).

title: P08. General finite-file MDS-TPIR capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: What is the true download capacity of private information retrieval when files are stored as separate MDS codes and T servers collude? In particular, can the exact capacity be characterized for all feasible parameters, beyond schemes restricted to be linear with full support rank?
status: The original general capacity formula was disproved. Recent 2026 work established new cases and restricted linear-capacity results, but the general problem remains open.
solved_when: An exact capacity formula (or matching achievability and converse proofs) for the download cost is established for separately MDS-coded files with T colluding servers, valid across all feasible parameters and without restricting to linear full-support-rank schemes.
why: It would quantify the optimal download cost of achieving privacy in coded storage, telling designers the fundamental price of privacy in such systems.
key_works: Freij-Hollanti et al. (2017), [*Private Information Retrieval from Coded Databases with Colluding Servers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02062); Sun–Tao–Xu–Zhang (2026), [*A Disguise-and-Squeeze PIR Scheme for the MDS-TPIR Setting and Beyond*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10769).

title: P09. Capacity of joint MDS-coded PIR
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: What is the capacity of private information retrieval when files are jointly MDS-coded across storage nodes rather than stored separately? A complete characterization is sought beyond known systematic-storage patterns and the parameter cases already settled.
status: Joint coding can outperform separate-file schemes; 2026 results determine selected regimes and improve others, notably Xu–Shi–Lan–Fang (2026), [*Private Information Retrieval from Joint Systematic MDS-Coded with Non-Colluding Servers: Bounds and Constructions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22802).
solved_when: The PIR capacity (optimal download cost given storage and privacy constraints) is characterized for jointly MDS-coded storage in general, covering the regimes not settled by prior bounds and constructions.
why: Joint encoding may change the fundamental storage/privacy/download tradeoff, so settling the capacity determines whether known separate-file schemes are fundamentally optimal or can be beaten.
key_works: Xu–Shi–Lan–Fang (2026), [*Private Information Retrieval from Joint Systematic MDS-Coded with Non-Colluding Servers: Bounds and Constructions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22802).

title: C02. Efficient decoding under time-bounded compression promises
subfield: Randomized compression and seed reuse
open: Which sources and decoder classes admit both near-optimal randomized compression and polynomial-time decompression, when the target description length is measured against a time-bounded complexity notion? In other words, characterize when a short encoding produced by a randomized compressor can still be decoded efficiently by the intended receiver.
status: It is known that universal compression can slow decoding, and that unrestricted, uncomputable Kolmogorov complexity cannot supply the required efficient promise. Key works include Bauwens–Zimand (2019/2023), [*Universal Almost Optimal Compression and Slepian-Wolf Coding in Probabilistic Polynomial Time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.04268), and Zimand (2024), [*On One-Way Functions and the Average Time Complexity of Almost-Optimal Compression*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03392).
solved_when: A characterization is given of the source and decoder classes for which near-optimal randomized compression coexists with polynomial-time decompression relative to a time-bounded description measure, together with a proof that the characterization is tight (exhibiting classes outside it where the coexistence fails).
why: A short encoding is operationally useful only when the intended receiver can decode it; without efficient decompression, near-optimal compression rates are a purely information-theoretic ideal.
key_works: Bauwens–Zimand (2019/2023), [*Universal Almost Optimal Compression and Slepian-Wolf Coding in Probabilistic Polynomial Time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.04268); Zimand (2024), [*On One-Way Functions and the Average Time Complexity of Almost-Optimal Compression*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03392).

title: C03. Compression and extraction with reused public seeds
subfield: Randomized compression and seed reuse
open: When a public seed is reused across rounds, how much randomness can we still extract from later weak sources that were generated using outputs derived from that same seed? Determine tight entropy-loss bounds and seed-refresh requirements under explicit bounded-dependence models.
status: Extractor-dependent-source and seed-protection frameworks handle particular dependence classes; arbitrary seed dependence cannot be allowed. Key works include Dodis–Vaikuntanathan–Wichs (2019/2020), [*Extracting Randomness from Extractor-Dependent Sources*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1339), and Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).
solved_when: Tight entropy-loss bounds and seed-refresh schedules are established for later weak sources depending on earlier outputs generated under the same public seed, within explicit bounded-dependence models.
why: Real systems reuse public parameters and continuously process correlated data, so extraction guarantees that break under seed dependence would fail exactly in the settings where they are deployed.
key_works: Dodis–Vaikuntanathan–Wichs (2019/2020), [*Extracting Randomness from Extractor-Dependent Sources*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1339); Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).

title: I01. Practical short-seed extraction at cryptographic error
subfield: Infrastructure for pseudorandomness and assumption research
open: Can strong seeded extractors be made practical enough for high-throughput cryptography — a tenfold time or memory improvement over a pinned short-seed-extractor baseline at identical parameters \((n,k,m,\varepsilon)\), with \(\varepsilon\le2^{-128}\)?
status: A proposed moonshot. Nearly linear short-seed theory — Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473) — and existing extractor libraries — Foreman–Yeung–Edgington–Curchin (2025), [*Cryptomite: A Versatile and User-Friendly Library of Randomness Extractors*](https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2025-01-08-1584) — provide starting points.
solved_when: A demonstrated implementation achieves at least a tenfold improvement in running time or memory over the pinned baseline while maintaining identical \((n,k,m,\varepsilon)\) with \(\varepsilon\le2^{-128}\).
why: It would make strong theoretical extractors usable in high-throughput cryptographic systems rather than remaining purely asymptotic tools.
key_works: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473); Foreman–Yeung–Edgington–Curchod (2025), [*Cryptomite: A Versatile and User-Friendly Library of Randomness Extractors*](https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2025-01-08-1584).

title: I02. Machine-checkable cryptographic implication census
subfield: Infrastructure for pseudorandomness and assumption research
open: Can we build a machine-checkable, versioned census of cryptographic implications and separations — at least 1,000 records strong — that captures, for each entry, the quantifier structure, setup assumptions, uniformity, adversary class, reduction type, and security loss, together with automated consistency checks so the records can be composed safely?
status: Currently a proposed data target; no such census exists. A bibliography alone does not establish that theorem statements can be safely composed. Related work on black-box separations includes Couteau–Farshim–Mahmoody (2021), *Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography*, and Bitansky–Degwekar (2019), *On the Complexity of Collision Resistant Hash Functions: New and Old Black-Box Separations*.
solved_when: A publicly available, versioned dataset contains at least 1,000 implication and separation records, each encoding quantifiers, setup, uniformity, adversary class, reduction type, and security loss, with consistency checks that validate composability.
why: It supplies reusable infrastructure for a much larger cross-linked open-problem census, replacing bibliographies that cannot establish whether theorem statements compose safely.
key_works: Couteau–Farshim–Mahmoody (2021), [*Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2021.47); Bitansky–Degwekar (2019), [*On the Complexity of Collision Resistant Hash Functions: New and Old Black-Box Separations*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-36030-6_17).

title: I03. Reproducible implementations of OWF-to-PRG reductions
subfield: Infrastructure for pseudorandomness and assumption research
open: Can the classical transformations turning one-way functions into pseudorandom generators be implemented reproducibly, so that their true concrete costs can be measured and compared? The goal is at least three foundational OWF-to-PRG reductions, each with symbolic security-loss accounting, runtime and randomness measurements, and controlled preimage-distribution test cases.
status: Proposed as an engineering benchmark; no implementations yet exist for this comparison. The asymptotic constructions of Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby (1999), [*A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function*](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539793244708), and Mazor–Zhang (2024), [*Simple Constructions from (Almost) Regular One-Way Functions*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-024-09507-4), leave concrete constants and crossover points largely unspecified.
solved_when: At least three foundational OWF-to-PRG transformations are implemented, with symbolic accounting of their security loss, measured runtime and randomness usage, and test cases over controlled preimage distributions; the results expose where each reduction's actual costs arise.
why: A solution would reveal which generic reductions are actually usable in practice and where their real costs occur, since asymptotic constructions currently leave concrete constants and crossover points largely unspecified.
key_works: Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby (1999), [*A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function*](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539793244708); Mazor–Zhang (2024), [*Simple Constructions from (Almost) Regular One-Way Functions*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-024-09507-4).

title: G02. Bound the dimension of the worst quantum extractor adversary
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Given a finite extractor table and an accuracy parameter \(\eta\), how much quantum side-information dimension suffices for an adversary to approximate the maximum distinguishing advantage within \(\eta\) — and can this dimension be bounded polynomially?
status: Explicitly posed in 2017 (Berta–Fawzi–Scholz, [*Quantum-proof randomness extractors via operator space theory*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3563)); norm formulations and semidefinite relaxations do not generally control this dimension.
solved_when: A bound, ideally polynomial, is established on the quantum side-information dimension needed to approximate the maximum distinguishing advantage within \(\eta\) for a finite extractor table.
why: It would make finite-instance quantum-security certification computationally tractable.
key_works: Berta–Fawzi–Scholz (2017), [*Quantum-proof randomness extractors via operator space theory*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3563).

title: G03. Classical-quality parameters for quantum-proof Raz extraction
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Can Raz's two-source extractor be made quantum-proof while keeping the same entropy requirements, output length, and error as the best classical construction, at least in the product-source or exact-Markov models? Formally, the question is whether the known quantum-secure variants can be made lossless with respect to the classical parameters.
status: Quantum security and quasilinear implementation of Raz's extractor were established in 2025, but the resulting constructions still incur parameter penalties. Lossless improvements achieved in 2025 by Foreman–Wooltorton–Milner (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15547) concern a different extractor and do not settle Raz's construction; quantum-secure two-source extractors with improved parameters were also given by Miller–Sandfuchs–Ferradini (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05528).
solved_when: A quantum-proof version of Raz's extractor matches the classical entropy thresholds, output length, and error parameters, with no parameter penalties, in the product or exact-Markov source models.
why: Raz's extractor requires only asymmetric entropy from its two sources, so a lossless quantum-proof version would preserve this advantage exactly in settings — such as cryptography against quantum adversaries — where the sources have very different quality and quantum side information is present.
key_works: Foreman–Wooltorton–Milner–Curchod (2025), [*An efficient construction of Raz’s two-source randomness extractor with improved parameters*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15547); Miller–Sandfuchs–Ferradini (2025), [*Improved Two-source Extractors against Quantum Side Information*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05528).

title: G05. Sublinear-entropy extraction from two independent processes
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Can randomness be extracted from two independent channels when the inputs to those channels are arbitrarily correlated — even entangled — and each channel contributes only a sublinear amount of fresh conditional min-entropy?
status: The 2025/2026 independent-process framework (Sandfuchs–Ferradini–Renner, [*Randomness from causally independent processes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05203)) gives inner-product constructions above a high entropy-sum threshold, and this is tight for inner product itself.
solved_when: A construction (with security proof) extracts uniform randomness from two independent channels acting on arbitrarily correlated, possibly entangled inputs, where each channel supplies only sublinear fresh conditional min-entropy.
why: Independent physical processes need not produce independent classical outputs, so existing extraction results that assume independence of the sources can fail exactly in the physical situations they are meant to model.
key_works: Sandfuchs–Ferradini–Renner (2025/2026), [*Randomness from causally independent processes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05203).

title: G06. Generic lifting to causally independent processes
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Can any classical two-source extractor be lifted to work for causally independent processes — sources that influence each other only through their common past — while keeping the entropy and error losses under control? Or is there a fundamental obstruction, exhibitable by counterexamples, that forces extra conditions beyond causal independence?
status: The problem was explicitly posed in 2025 in work by Sandfuchs–Ferradini–Renner (2025/2026) on randomness from causally independent processes; the known exact-Markov lifting does not cover the case of independent channels acting on correlated inputs.
solved_when: Either a general transformation of arbitrary classical two-source extractors into extractors for causally independent processes is given, with explicit quantitative bounds on the entropy and error losses, or counterexamples are constructed that identify which additional conditions are necessary for such a lifting to exist.
why: Success would make the large classical two-source extractor toolkit applicable to broader physical source models, including independent channels acting on correlated inputs.
key_works: Sandfuchs–Ferradini–Renner (2025/2026), [*Randomness from causally independent processes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05203).

title: G07. Seedless device-independent extraction with memoryful devices
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Can one perform secure, seedless (deterministic) privacy amplification on Bell-certified data when the untrusted devices retain quantum memory between rounds and adapt their measurements to all prior inputs and outputs — and still achieve a positive key rate?
