status: Seedless extraction, and the asymptotic one-key-bit-per-singlet one-party rate, are established for memoryless measurements (Foreman–Masanes 2025, *Seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography*; Lin–Foreman–Masanes 2026, *High-rate and computationally-efficient seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography*); the memoryful-device case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or construction) of seedless device-independent extraction secure against memoryful, adaptive devices, with a positive asymptotic key rate (the memoryless case achieving one key bit per singlet per party serving as the benchmark).
why: Device memory is a natural adversarial capability in any repeated Bell-test experiment, so without a proof against it the existing security guarantees do not cover the realistic setting.
key_works: Foreman–Masanes (2025), [*Seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography*](https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2025-03-06-1654); Lin–Foreman–Masanes (2026), [*High-rate and computationally-efficient seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31525).

title: G08. Explicit matrices for high-rate seedless device-independent extraction
subfield: Quantum-proof extraction and independent-process randomness
open: Can we explicitly construct, in polynomial time, the binary matrices whose existence underlies the high-rate seedless device-independent extractor — that is, matrices meeting the required row-space weight conditions at every block length and rate covered by the theorem?
status: The 2026 revision (Lin–Foreman–Masanes, [High-rate and computationally-efficient seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31525)) proves existence of suitable matrices and efficient extractor evaluation given such a matrix; BCH candidates do not achieve all claimed parameters.
solved_when: An explicit, efficiently constructible family of binary matrices satisfies the row-space weight conditions across the full range of block lengths and rates for which the high-rate theorem guarantees existence.
why: Without an explicit construction, the extractor's guarantees hold only nonconstructively, so there is no implementable extractor at every operating point of the theorem.
key_works: Lin–Foreman–Masanes (2026), [*High-rate and computationally-efficient seedless extractors for device-independent quantum cryptography*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31525).

title: G14. Explicit condensing with constant-size online blocks
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Can we explicitly condense a stream of online symbol-fixing blocks of some sufficiently large constant length into nearly full-entropy bits? Formally, given \(\ell\) blocks of which at least \(0.51\ell\) are uniform and good, the goal is an explicit construction condensing them to \(\Omega(\ell)\) bits at rate 0.99 with exponentially small error.
status: Existential constructions achieve the stated parameters; explicit constructions are known only with growing block length (Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5)).
solved_when: An explicit condenser for constant block length exists that, from \(\ell\) online symbol-fixing blocks with at least \(0.51\ell\) uniform good blocks, outputs \(\Omega(\ell)\) bits at rate 0.99 with exponentially small error.
why: It would let many weak contributors, each producing only short messages, be combined reliably — a setting where current explicit tools require blocks to grow in length.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: G16. Exact online-corruption threshold for extraction
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: How much corruption can an online adversary inject before constant-error randomness extraction from a weak collective source becomes impossible? Specifically, determine the optimal corruption thresholds for constant-error online extraction, separately for the model where each participant contributes one bit and the model where contributions are symbols of length at least \(\log\ell\).
status: Constructions tolerate \(\Omega(\ell/\log\ell)\) corrupt bits or \(\Omega(\ell/\log^*\ell)\) corrupt symbols; known lower bounds leave gaps.
solved_when: The exact corruption thresholds are determined in both models, matching constructions with lower bounds for one-bit contributions (currently at \(\Omega(\ell/\log\ell)\) corrupt bits) and for longer symbols (currently at \(\Omega(\ell/\log^*\ell)\) corrupt symbols), closing the gaps left by known lower bounds.
why: Pinning down the maximum adversarial participation still compatible with extracting shared randomness settles when distributed protocols can rely on collectively generated randomness despite online corruption.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115); Ben-Or–Linial (1989), [*Collective Coin Flipping*](https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~nati/PAPERS/coll_coin_fl.pdf).

title: G17. Constant entropy deficiency for online symbol sources
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Can one condense uniform 0.51-good-fraction online symbol-fixing sources so that the output has only constant entropy deficiency? Ideally, such a condenser should achieve fixed small error and an output length that grows with the input while losing only a constant amount of entropy.
status: Even the existence of such condensers is explicitly open in the 2026 formulation; the available deficiency bounds grow with the parameters. See Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).
solved_when: An explicit (or existent) condenser for uniform 0.51-good-fraction online symbol-fixing sources is given with \(O(1)\) output entropy deficiency, fixed small error, and growing output length.
why: Constant deficiency would bring the condenser's outputs close to ideal random seeds, enabling their use where near-perfect randomness is required.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: G22. High-entropy extraction with seed depending on deficiency
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can a source with min-entropy \(n-\Delta\) have almost all of its entropy extracted using a seed of length \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)+f(\Delta)\), with no additional dependence on \(n\)? Formally, the goal is a construction whose seed length is \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)\) plus a function of the deficiency \(\Delta\) alone.
status: Explicitly identified in 2025. Constant-seed optimal-output constructions for symbol-fixing sources exploit structure absent from arbitrary high-entropy sources, leaving the general question open.
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists for sources of min-entropy \(n-\Delta\) with error \(\varepsilon\), output recovering almost all the entropy, and seed length \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)+f(\Delta)\) for some function \(f\), with no dependence on \(n\) beyond these terms.
why: Nearly uniform sources should require randomness proportional only to their deficiency, so settling this determines whether deficiency is the right complexity measure for extraction seed length.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G23. Smaller alphabets for fast nearly-MDS erasure codes
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can we construct explicit codes of rate R that correct \(1-R-\eta\) adversarial erasures with quasilinear-time encoding and decoding, over alphabets whose size approaches \(\exp(O(1/\eta^2))\)?
status: The 2025 fast construction of Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya ([*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090)) achieves alphabet dependence approximately \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^4))\); better nonexplicit tradeoffs are known but do not yield the same uniform algorithms.
solved_when: An explicit rate-R code family exists, with uniform quasilinear-time encoding and decoding algorithms, correcting \(1-R-\eta\) adversarial erasures over alphabets of size \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^2))\) — improving on the current \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^4))\) dependence.
why: Smaller alphabets directly improve the practicality of these erasure codes and strengthen the associated extractor constructions they enable.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G26. Negligible-error affine nonmalleability at polylogarithmic entropy
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can an affine nonmalleable extractor run at polylogarithmic entropy with essentially no error? Formally, construct polynomial-time affine nonmalleable extractors for \(k=\operatorname{polylog}n\), error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\), and output \(k^{\Omega(1)}\).
status: Li–Zhong (2024) achieved polynomial error, and their 2026 follow-up [*Non-Malleable Affine Extractors with Small Error and Complexity Lower Bounds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02407) gives exponentially small error at constant entropy rate and strong near-\(n/\log n\) results — but the low-entropy target remains open.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time affine nonmalleable extractor exists for min-entropy \(k=\operatorname{polylog}n\) with error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\) and output length \(k^{\Omega(1)}\).
why: It would combine very weak algebraic randomness with cryptographic-strength tamper resistance.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108); Li–Zhong (2026), [*Non-Malleable Affine Extractors with Small Error and Complexity Lower Bounds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02407).

title: G14. Explicit condensing with constant-size online blocks
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Can we explicitly condense online symbol-fixing sources whose blocks each have constant length, when only a bare majority of the blocks are good? Formally, for sufficiently large constant block length, construct an explicit condenser for \(\ell\) online blocks with at least \(0.51\ell\) uniform good blocks, outputting \(\Omega(\ell)\) bits at rate 0.99 with exponentially small error.
status: Existential (non-explicit) constructions already achieve the stated parameters; explicit constructions are known only with growing block length. See Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).
solved_when: An explicit condenser is given that, for some constant block length and \(\ell\) online symbol-fixing blocks containing at least \(0.51\ell\) uniform good blocks, outputs \(\Omega(\ell)\) bits at rate 0.99 with exponentially small error.
why: It would allow many weak contributors, each producing only short constant-length messages, to be combined into a reliable near-uniform string — a setting where current explicit constructions fail because they need block length to grow.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: G16. Exact online-corruption threshold for extraction
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: How much of an online-adversarially corrupted source can still be condensed or extracted from at constant error — what is the exact corruption threshold? In particular, determine the optimal thresholds separately for one-bit contributions and for symbols of length at least \(\log\ell\).
status: Known constructions tolerate \(\Omega(\ell/\log\ell)\) corrupt bits or \(\Omega(\ell/\log^*\ell)\) corrupt symbols, but known lower bounds leave gaps in both regimes. See Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115); Ben-Or–Linial (1989), [*Collective Coin Flipping*](https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~nati/PAPERS/coll_coin_fl.pdf).
solved_when: The optimal corruption thresholds for constant-error online extraction are determined, matching upper and lower bounds in both regimes: one-bit contributions and symbols of length at least \(\log\ell\).
why: A solution would identify the maximum adversarial participation compatible with shared randomness, pinning down the exact boundary of feasibility for distributed random selection.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04115); Ben-Or–Linial (1989), [*Collective Coin Flipping*](https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~nati/PAPERS/coll_coin_fl.pdf).

title: G17. Constant entropy deficiency for online symbol sources
subfield: Condensers, online adversaries, and entropy deficiency
open: Does there exist a condenser for uniform \(0.51\)-good-fraction online symbol-fixing sources whose output has only constant entropy deficiency? A construction is sought with fixed small error and output length growing with the input, where the entropy loss does not grow with the source parameters.
status: Even the existence of such condensers is explicitly open in the 2026 formulation of Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5); all available deficiency bounds grow with the parameters.
solved_when: A condenser is constructed for uniform \(0.51\)-good-fraction online symbol-fixing sources with \(O(1)\) output entropy deficiency, fixed small error, and growing output length.
why: Constant deficiency would bring the adversarial-source outputs close to ideal random seeds, making them usable wherever nearly-uniform randomness is required.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Gurumukhani–Ringach–Servedio (2026), [*Condensing and Extracting Against Online Adversaries*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.5).

title: A15. Fully adaptive circuit ABE from ordinary LWE
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can we build attribute-based encryption for general circuits, assuming only the plain Learning with Errors assumption, that remains secure when the adversary chooses both the challenge attribute and its key requests adaptively after seeing the public parameters? In other words, achieve full adaptive security — not merely the output-adaptive intermediate notion — without recourse to witness encryption or stronger tools.
status: The current state of the art is an output-adaptive ABE notion introduced in October 2026 as an intermediate step; fully adaptive constructions exist using witness encryption but do not settle the question under LWE alone. Key works: Waters–Wichs (2024), [*Adaptively Secure Attribute-Based Encryption from Witness Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1486); Cheng–Goyal (2026), [*Revisiting Partitioning: Output-Adaptive ABE for Circuits from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2305).
solved_when: A construction of circuit ABE from ordinary LWE is given, with a proof of full adaptive security in which challenge attributes and secret-key requests may be chosen after the public parameters are published.
why: Real authorization requests are selected after deployment rather than fixed before setup, so constructions secure only against pre-setup choices do not match how ABE is actually used.
key_works: Waters–Wichs (2024), [*Adaptively Secure Attribute-Based Encryption from Witness Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1486); Cheng–Goyal (2026), [*Revisiting Partitioning: Output-Adaptive ABE for Circuits from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2305).

title: A20. Sublinear collusion dependence in lattice registered FE
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can registered functional encryption for general circuits under standard lattice assumptions achieve ciphertext growth that is sublinear in the number of corrupted users \(Q\)? Formally, can the \(Q\)-linear term in the ciphertext size be reduced below linear while supporting general circuits and resting on explicit lattice assumptions?
status: The 2026 construction of Champion–Wu–Yamada ([*Silent Threshold Encryption from Lattices*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1716)) achieves \(Q\widetilde O(d)+\ell\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,d,\log N)\) ciphertext size from decomposed LWE in the random-oracle model.
solved_when: A registered FE scheme for general circuits from explicit lattice assumptions is given whose ciphertext size scales as \(o(Q)\) in the corruption count, improving on the current \(Q\widetilde O(d)+\ell\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,d,\log N)\) bound.
why: Otherwise the collusion bound dominates the compactness budget, so ciphertext size blows up precisely in the regime where many users collude — the setting compactness is meant to control.
key_works: Champion–Wu–Yamada (2026), [*Silent Threshold Encryption from Lattices*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1716).

title: A22. Adaptive registered ABE with linear CRS in the plain model
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can a pairing-based registered attribute-based encryption scheme for monotone span programs achieve a linear-size CRS together with adaptive security and independent, stateless user key generation, all in the plain model?
status: The 2026 linear-CRS construction of Stracovsky–Waters–Wu, [*Pairing-Based Registered ABE for Boolean Formulas with a Linear-Size CRS*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1062), achieves static plain-model security under a \(q\)-type assumption and adaptive security in random oracles.
solved_when: A construction exists that is pairing-based, supports monotone span programs, has linear-size CRS, is proven adaptively secure in the plain model (no random oracles), and allows users to generate keys independently and statelessly.
why: It would combine compact setup with realistic adaptive use, removing the gap between the compactness of the CRS and the security model needed in practice.
key_works: Stracovsky–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Pairing-Based Registered ABE for Boolean Formulas with a Linear-Size CRS*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1062).

title: A28. Function privacy without universal-circuit inflation
subfield: Functional encryption, attribute-based encryption, and compactness
open: Can a compiler take a declared private-key functional-encryption workload and hide both the functions and the messages, while inflating the underlying circuit work by at most a factor of two and preserving adaptive security and the original leakage profile?
status: Proposed engineering target. Generic function-privacy transformations already establish feasibility (see Brakerski–Segev, [*Function-Private Functional Encryption in the Private-Key Setting*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/550), 2014/2015).
solved_when: A compilation procedure exists for private-key FE that achieves function and message privacy with at most \(2\times\) additional circuit work, retains adaptive security, and matches the original leakage profile.
why: Function descriptions handed to an FE scheme can leak proprietary algorithms or sensitive query intent; a cheap compilation route makes function privacy practical for real workloads rather than a theoretical add-on.
key_works: Brakerski–Segev (2014/2015), [*Function-Private Functional Encryption in the Private-Key Setting*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/550).

title: G22. High-entropy extraction with seed depending on deficiency
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can an arbitrary source of min-entropy \(n-\Delta\) be converted into one that is close to uniform using a seed of only \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)+f(\Delta)\) random bits, with no dependence on the source length \(n\)? In other words, is randomness extraction from nearly uniform sources possible with seed length proportional to the deficiency \(\Delta\)?
status: The problem was explicitly identified in 2025 (Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya, [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090)). Constant-seed optimal-output constructions for symbol-fixing sources exist, but they exploit structure absent from arbitrary high-entropy sources.
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists that, for sources of min-entropy \(n-\Delta\), outputs almost all of the entropy with error \(\varepsilon\) using a seed of length \(2\log(1/\varepsilon)+f(\Delta)\), where \(f\) depends only on the deficiency and the seed has no additional dependence on \(n\).
why: Nearly uniform sources should require randomness proportional to their deficiency, so such an extractor would show that the last few bits of missing entropy — not the source length — govern the cost of extraction.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G23. Smaller alphabets for fast nearly-MDS erasure codes
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can we build explicit codes of rate R that correct \(1-R-\eta\) adversarial erasures, with quasilinear-time encoding and decoding, over alphabets whose size approaches \(\exp(O(1/\eta^2))\)?
status: The 2025 fast construction of Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya ([*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org//abs/2504.03090)) achieves alphabet dependence approximately \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^4))\); better nonexplicit tradeoffs are known but do not yield comparable uniform algorithms.
solved_when: An explicit rate-R code family is given that corrects \(1-R-\eta\) adversarial erasures, has quasilinear-time uniform encoding and decoding algorithms, and alphabet size \(\exp(\widetilde O(1/\eta^2))\) or better.
why: Smaller alphabets make such erasure codes more practical and directly improve the associated extractor constructions built from them.
key_works: Chen–Cheraghchi–Shagrithaya (2025), [*Optimal Erasure Codes and Codes on Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03090).

title: G26. Negligible-error affine nonmalleability at polylogarithmic entropy
subfield: Further extractor–coding frontiers
open: Can one construct, in polynomial time, an affine nonmalleable extractor that works when the source has only polylogarithmic entropy in \(n\), while achieving negligible error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\) and output length \(k^{\Omega(1)}\)?
status: Polynomial error was achieved in 2024 (Li–Zhong, [Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108)). The October 2026 result of Li–Zhong ([Non-Malleable Affine Extractors with Small Error and Complexity Lower Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02407)) gives exponentially small error at constant entropy rate and strong near-\(n/\log n\) results, leaving the low-entropy target open.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time affine nonmalleable extractor exists for entropy \(k=\operatorname{polylog}n\), with error \(n^{-\omega(1)}\) and output length \(k^{\Omega(1)}\).
why: It would combine very weak algebraic randomness with cryptographic-strength tamper resistance, bringing nonmalleable extraction down to the entropy regimes where such sources actually arise.
key_works: Li–Zhong (2024), [*Two-Source and Affine Non-Malleable Extractors for Small Entropy*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2024.108); Li–Zhong (2026), [*Non-Malleable Affine Extractors with Small Error and Complexity Lower Bounds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02407).

title: P06. Arithmetic two-server PIR below the cube-root bound
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: Can two servers implementing a private information retrieval scheme transmit fewer than \(O(N^{1/3})\) field elements to retrieve one item from an \(N\)-element database, when the servers are restricted to black-box field arithmetic — or is \(O(N^{1/3})$ essentially optimal for this model?
status: The 2026 arithmetic-PIR characterization explicitly leaves this two-server boundary open; nontrivial single-server arithmetic PIR is already ruled out (Applebaum–Ishai–Shechter (2026), [*On Arithmetic Private Information Retrieval: Why Code-Based PIR (Usually) Fails*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1224)).
solved_when: Either an arithmetic two-server PIR scheme communicating \(o(N^{1/3})$ field elements is constructed, or a lower bound is proved showing that \(\Omega(N^{1/3})\) field elements must be transmitted by any two-server scheme using only black-box field arithmetic.
why: It settles the boundary of what algebraic, code-based design techniques can achieve for PIR, either opening a route to more efficient schemes or proving a fundamental barrier.
key_works: Applebaum–Ishai–Shechter (2026), [*On Arithmetic Private Information Retrieval: Why Code-Based PIR (Usually) Fails*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1224).

title: P05. Dynamic information-theoretic PIR with cheap updates
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: Can a quasilinear-space, sublinear-query-time information-theoretic PIR scheme be made dynamic, so that it supports point updates to the database at polylogarithmic amortized cost while keeping query performance? A satisfactory construction should also make explicit what information each update leaks.
status: The problem is a proposed dynamic extension of recent static preprocessing advances, namely Henzinger–Ragavan (2026), [*Two-Server Private Information Retrieval in Sublinear Time and Quasilinear Space*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2008), building on the preprocessing paradigm of Beimel–Ishai–Malkin (2000), *Reducing the Servers’ Computation in Private Information Retrieval: PIR with Preprocessing*; related lines include dynamic data-structure lower bounds and update/query tradeoffs.
solved_when: An explicit information-theoretic PIR construction achieves quasilinear space and sublinear query time while handling point updates with polylogarithmic amortized update cost, together with a stated characterization of update leakage.
why: Real private databases change; without cheap updates, the entire structure must be rebuilt after each change, which can erase the query-time gains of static preprocessing.
key_works: Henzinger–Ragavan (2026), [*Two-Server Private Information Retrieval in Sublinear Time and Quasilinear Space*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2008); Beimel–Ishai–Malkin (2000), *Reducing the Servers’ Computation in Private Information Retrieval: PIR with Preprocessing*.

title: P07. Tight noninteractive random-index PIR communication
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: What is the true communication cost of privately retrieving a uniformly random row from a database when the client sends each of two servers just one message? Formally, close the gap between the known \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\) lower bound and existing upper bounds for two-server, one-message-per-server random-index PIR on \(d\) rows of \(w\) bits.
status: Kolby–Roy–Sternad–Yakoubov (2025), [*Information-Theoretic Random-Index PIR*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2025.5), establish the \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\) lower bound and give sublinear constructions in appropriate row-width regimes.
solved_when: Matching (up to constants) upper and lower bounds are proved for the communication complexity of two-server, one-message-per-server random-index PIR over \(d\) rows of \(w\) bits, with the lower bound remaining \(\Omega(\sqrt{d}\,w)\).
why: Random-index retrieval enables private sampling with a different, noninteractive-with-each-server pattern from chosen-index PIR, so tight bounds would pin down exactly when this cheaper interaction pattern is possible.
key_works: Kolby–Roy–Sternad–Yakoubov (2025), [*Information-Theoretic Random-Index PIR*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2025.5).

title: P08. General finite-file MDS-TPIR capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic private information retrieval
open: What is the exact download capacity for private information retrieval from separately MDS-coded files when T servers collude, for all feasible parameter regimes? In particular, the answer should be established without restricting attention to linear schemes with full support rank.
status: The originally proposed general capacity formula was disproved. Recent 2026 results (Sun–Tao–Xu–Zhang, "A Disguise-and-Squeeze PIR Scheme for the MDS-TPIR Setting and Beyond") provide new cases and capacity results restricted to linear schemes, but the general problem remains open; the setting was introduced by Freij-Hollanti et al. (2017), "Private Information Retrieval from Coded Databases with Colluding Servers."
solved_when: A formula (or matching achievability and converse arguments) for the download capacity is established across all feasible parameters of the separately MDS-coded, T-colluding-server setting, with no linearity or full-support-rank restriction on schemes.
why: A solution would quantify the exact download cost of preserving privacy in coded storage systems, telling designers the fundamental overhead that collusion among servers forces on any retrieval scheme.
key_works: Freij-Hollanti et al. (2017), [*Private Information Retrieval from Coded Databases with Colluding Servers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02062); Sun–Tao–Xu–Zhang (2026), [*A Disguise-and-Squeeze PIR Scheme for the MDS-TPIR Setting and Beyond*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10769).

title: I01. Practical short-seed extraction at cryptographic error
subfield: Infrastructure for pseudorandomness and assumption research
open: Can short-seed extraction be made genuinely practical at cryptographic security levels? Formally, demonstrate at least a tenfold time or memory improvement over a pinned short-seed-extractor baseline while keeping the parameters \((n,k,m,\varepsilon)\) identical, with \(\varepsilon\le2^{-128}\).
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no demonstrated solution. Nearly linear short-seed theory [Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), *Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*, arXiv:2411.07473] and existing extractor libraries [Foreman–Yeung–Edgington–Curchod (2025), *Cryptomite: A Versatile and User-Friendly Library of Randomness Extractors*, doi:10.22331/q-2025-01-08-1584] provide starting points.
solved_when: A construction achieves a tenfold reduction in running time or memory relative to the pinned baseline at identical \((n,k,m,\varepsilon)\), with error \(\varepsilon\le2^{-128}\).
why: It would make strong theoretical extractors usable in high-throughput cryptographic systems rather than remaining objects of pure theory.
key_works: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473); Foreman–Yeung–Edgington–Curchod (2025), [*Cryptomite: A Versatile and User-Friendly Library of Randomness Extractors*](https://doi.org/10.22331/q-2025-01-08-1584).

title: A01. Indistinguishability obfuscation from ordinary LWE
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size classical circuits be built from ordinary LWE alone? That is, without resorting to evasive, circular-evasive, succinct-sampling, or other obfuscation-specific assumptions.
status: Open since general-purpose iO candidates appeared in 2013. Constructions from well-founded assumptions, such as Jain–Lin–Sahai (2020/2021), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09317), combine multiple assumptions; current lattice-only general-purpose candidates remain heuristic, and recent work such as Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932), addresses obfuscating non-evasive programs without resolving the ordinary-LWE goal.
solved_when: A construction of iO for all polynomial-size classical circuits is given, with a proof of security reducing solely to ordinary LWE and no obfuscation-specific assumptions.
why: It would give a conventional, post-quantum foundation for a large fraction of advanced cryptography, replacing today's multi-assumption or heuristic bases with a single standard hardness assumption.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai (2020/2021), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09317); Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A03. General iO from polynomial-security assumptions
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can general-purpose indistinguishability obfuscation be built from assumptions secure only against polynomial-time adversaries? Formally, construct iO whose reduction loses at most polynomial factors, so that no subexponential hardness is needed to absorb exponential proof losses.
status: Short-equivalence-proof promises (Jain–Jin 2022, *Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence*) permit improved reductions, but arbitrary equivalent circuits do not necessarily satisfy those promises.
solved_when: A construction of general iO is given whose security reduces to assumptions with polynomial hardness, i.e., the reduction's security loss is polynomially bounded.
why: It would let obfuscation rest on the same standard quantitative hardness as ordinary cryptography, rather than requiring much stronger subexponential assumptions.
key_works: Jain–Jin (2022), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation via Mathematical Proofs of Equivalence*](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00100).

title: A04. Minimum truth-table savings sufficient to bootstrap XiO
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: How much must an obfuscator shrink a truth table before that compression alone yields full indistinguishability obfuscation — in particular, do polynomial savings such as \(2^n/n^c+\operatorname{poly}(|C|,\lambda)\) suffice to bootstrap to polynomial-time iO?
status: XiO with \(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\)-type size can be amplified to full iO under subexponential XiO and LWE assumptions (Lin–Pass–Seth–Telang, 2016, [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation with Non-trivial Efficiency*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/006)); polynomial savings remain a weaker, unamplified starting point.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given that XiO achieving size \(2^n/n^c+\operatorname{poly}(|C|,\lambda)\) for some constant \(c\) implies polynomial-time iO (under stated assumptions), or an impossibility separating such polynomial-savings XiO from full iO.
why: It would lower the efficiency threshold required for a general obfuscation breakthrough, telling us how close to trivial an "efficient" obfuscator must be before amplification takes over.
key_works: Lin–Pass–Seth–Telang (2016), [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation with Non-trivial Efficiency*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/006).
aliases: XiO amplification threshold; exponentially efficient iO.

title: A07. Secret-oblivious private-coin evasive LWE
subfield: Obfuscation: assumptions, restricted notions, and efficiency
open: Can private-coin evasive LWE be proven secure when the sampler is secret-oblivious and useful for obfuscation applications, or does a genuine attack exist within exactly those sampler restrictions?
status: The 2026 Huang–Hung–Yamada correction invalidates a previously claimed obfuscation attack in this regime while leaving the security of the assumption unresolved; Vaikuntanathan–Wee–Wichs (2022), [*Witness Encryption and Null-IO from Evasive LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1140), motivates the assumption's use.
solved_when: A security proof is given for a useful class of secret-oblivious samplers in private-coin evasive LWE, or an attack is exhibited that satisfies the exact sampler restrictions of the assumption.
why: Several advanced lattice constructions rely on the precise scope of evasive LWE assumptions, so settling this determines which of them can be soundly based on it.
key_works: Huang–Hung–Yamada (2026), [*A Note on Obfuscation-Based Attacks on Private-Coin Evasive LWE*](https://cic.iacr.org/p/2/4/20); Vaikuntanathan–Wee–Wichs (2022), [*Witness Encryption and Null-IO from Evasive LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1140).

title: E03. Almost-all entropy output at logarithmic entropy
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can we extract essentially all of the entropy from a source with only logarithmic entropy — specifically, at \(k=O(\log n)\), can we output \(k-O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bits while remaining strong in a designated source, with near-optimal constants?
status: Existing one-bit logarithmic-entropy extraction does not establish this simultaneous output, strength, and error guarantee; the problem remains open.
solved_when: An explicit construction achieves, at \(k=O(\log n)\), output of \(k-O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bits that is strong in the designated source, with near-optimal constants.
why: It would turn very weak sources into useful multi-bit random seeds rather than single bits of randomness.
key_works: Li (2023), [*Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06802); Cohen–Doron–Samocha (2025), [*Seed-Protecting Extractors*](https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v021a008/).

title: E08. Two good sources among many adversarial sources
subfield: Randomness extractors for structured sources
open: Can randomness be extracted with negligible error from a sequence of many independent sources when only two of them — and we do not know which two — have polylogarithmic entropy, while all the others may be adversarially fixed?
status: Chattopadhyay–Goodman (2025), [*Leakage-Resilient Extractors against Number-on-Forehead Protocols*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/075/), obtain three good low-entropy sources; their two-good-source consequence requires higher entropy.
solved_when: An explicit extractor is constructed that works with negligible error for independent sources where exactly two (unidentified) sources have polylogarithmic entropy and the remaining sources are arbitrarily fixed.
why: It would enable robust distributed randomness generation where honest, high-quality contributors are a small unknown subset amid potentially malicious participants.
key_works: Chattopadhyay–Goodman (2025), [*Leakage-Resilient Extractors against Number-on-Forehead Protocols*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/075/).

title: R3-011. Optimal exceptional integer-matrix cliques
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the largest possible size of a family of \(d\times d\) integer matrices such that every pairwise difference has determinant \(\pm1\) — and how tight can we make the current bounds? Formally, determine the optimal size, or close the asymptotic gap between the best known upper and lower bounds.
status: The 2026 work of Boutros, Cascudo, Cramer, van Gent and Xing constructs families of size \(d^2\) for infinitely many \(d\) and resolves several small dimensions exactly; the general optimal sizes remain unknown.
solved_when: The maximum size of such a family is determined as a function of \(d\), or matching (up to lower-order terms) asymptotic upper and lower bounds are established.
why: Larger such families directly improve the algebraic challenge spaces available for hidden-order-group proofs and black-box secret sharing.
key_works: Milan Boutros, Ignacio Cascudo, Ronald Cramer, Daniël van Gent and Chaoping Xing (2026), [*On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24586).
aliases: Exceptional sets; subtractive sets; admissible sets in related formulations.

title: R3-030. Construct Strong Off-the-Record Deniability
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we build an interactive encryption protocol in which both parties can withstand coercion that arrives while the protocol is still executing, each producing mutually consistent fake claims? Formally, construct a protocol achieving Strong Off-the-Record Deniability (SORD) as defined by Abapour.
status: Abapour (2026) defines SORD and explicitly leaves the construction open; the same paper's threshold fully deniable encryption addresses only post-execution deniability.
solved_when: An interactive encryption protocol is constructed and proven to satisfy SORD: both parties can answer mid-execution coercion with fake claims that are mutually consistent.
why: It would make deniability survive coercion even while a conversation is ongoing, rather than only after execution has finished.
key_works: Navid Abapour (2026), [*Threshold Fully Deniable Interactive Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1900), SSS 2026.

title: R3-042. Standard-model decisional proofs of no intrusion
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a classical client obtain, in the standard model and from LWE alone, a reusable and nondestructive proof that no intrusion into stored data has occurred, where the plaintext bits remain everlastingly indistinguishable in the residual state of an outside attacker?
status: Goyal–Raizes posed the decisional-security question. Kalai–Raizes's September 2026 preprint achieves classical upload and everlasting search security from LWE, but its decisional construction still relies on the QROM.
solved_when: A construction is given, secure under LWE in the standard model (no QROM), that is reusable, nondestructive, and achieves everlasting indistinguishability of plaintext bits in an outside attacker's residual state.
why: An accepted audit would certify the absence of even partial-message leakage while leaving the stored data intact for future use.
key_works: Vipul Goyal and Justin Raizes (2025; EUROCRYPT 2026), [*Proofs of No Intrusion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06432v1), §2.4; Yael Tauman Kalai and Justin Raizes (2026), [*Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion*](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38915v1).

title: R3-077. Exact one-neighbor private retrieval on a path
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the exact capacity of private information retrieval on a path of \(N\) servers, \(N\ge6\), when each message is stored at its edge's two endpoints and each server must be kept ignorant of requests for messages held by itself or either immediate neighbor?
status: Bounds on the capacity follow from the September 2026 two-sided-neighbor theorem at \(h=1\), due to Mohamed Nomeir, Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Private Information Retrieval With Arbitrary Privacy Requirements: Introduction and Capacity Results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15875), Theorem 7; the exact capacity remains undetermined.
solved_when: The capacity of this \(N\)-server path model is determined exactly for all \(N\ge6\).
why: A solution quantifies the price of extending privacy one hop beyond a file's storage locations.
key_works: Mohamed Nomeir, Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Private Information Retrieval With Arbitrary Privacy Requirements: Introduction and Capacity Results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15875), Theorem 7.

title: R3-080. Leaky joint demand-and-side-information privacy beyond one known file
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the minimum download cost of single-server retrieval that keeps both the demanded file and the set of cached side-information files private up to an \(\varepsilon\)-differential-privacy guarantee, when the user holds \(M\ge2\) side-information files and the \(N\) replicas of the \(K\) files cannot communicate?
status: Huangfu–Bai's January 2026 construction handles \(M=1\), recovering perfect-privacy limits as \(\varepsilon\to0\); general \(M\ge2\) costs and matching converses remain explicitly open (Huangfu & Bai 2026, [*On the Leaky Private Information Retrieval with Side Information*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09960), §5).
solved_when: A complete characterization of the optimal download cost for all \(M\ge2\), with matching achievability and converse bounds.
why: It quantifies how much privately cached knowledge is worth when a small, controlled leakage is tolerated, and it extends the exact \(M=1\) theory to the regime relevant to realistic caches.
key_works: Yingying Huangfu and Tian Bai (2026), [*On the Leaky Private Information Retrieval with Side Information*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09960), §5.

title: R3-085. Closing the Lean-verified koalaIRS12 soundness interval
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we close the gap between the proved soundness bound and the known attack bound for the fixed koalaIRS12 protocol, with every step machine-checked in Lean? Formally, either strengthen the verified proof or produce a matching attack so that the Lean-verified soundness interval collapses.
status: The live board as of 9 October 2026 reports 68.15 proved security bits against a 116.13-bit attack bound, with 81 promoted submissions; all figures concern this particular formalized protocol. Key works: Yukon and zkSecurity (2026), [The Proximity Prize companion challenge](https://better.codes/); Arnon, Boneh and Fenzi (2026), [Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/680), Construction 6.9.
solved_when: The Lean-verified interval for koalaIRS12 is closed — i.e., the proved security bits meet the 116.13-bit attack bound, or an attack matching the current 68.15 proved bits is formalized and accepted by the checker.
why: It provides a machine-checkable target where any improvement directly moves an auditable security estimate, making progress verifiable rather than rhetorical.
key_works: Yukon and zkSecurity (2026), [*The Proximity Prize companion challenge*](https://better.codes/); Arnon, Boneh and Fenzi (2026), [*Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/680), Construction 6.9.

title: R3-002. Polynomial shares for slice access structures
subfield: Round 3
open: Does every slice access structure admit a secret-sharing scheme with polynomially many total share bits for a one-bit secret, or is there a slice that forces superpolynomial size? Here a slice structure is arbitrary on one cardinality layer, rejects all smaller sets, and accepts all larger sets.
status: One-bit constructions give \(2^{\widetilde O(\sqrt n)}\) shares. Polynomial information ratios are known for sufficiently long secrets, including September 2026 multislice results, but these leave the one-bit question open.
solved_when: Either a construction achieving polynomial total share size for every slice access structure with a one-bit secret is given, or a specific slice access structure is proven to require superpolynomial total share size.
why: It tests whether a complicated single layer of an authorization policy admits substantial compression, separating what is achievable for one-bit secrets from the long-secret case.
key_works: Tianren Liu and Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2018), [*Breaking the Circuit-Size Barrier in Secret Sharing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/333), DOI:10.1145/3188745.3188936; Benny Applebaum and Oded Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/); Amos Beimel and Oded Nir (2026), [*The Power of Multislices in Monotone Computation*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/213/).

title: R3-003. Efficient information-theoretic sharing for monotone circuits
subfield: Round 3
open: Can every polynomial-size monotone circuit be compiled into a perfectly secure secret-sharing scheme whose sharing and reconstruction run in polynomial time and whose total number of shares is polynomial? In other words, is there an efficient information-theoretic realization of any efficiently evaluable monotone access structure?
status: Efficient schemes are known for monotone formulas, but the case of general monotone circuits remains unresolved. Near-quadratic separations between circuit size and the required number of shares already rule out very low overhead; see Benaloh–Leichter (1988), Beimel (2023), and Applebaum–Nir (2025).
solved_when: A construction is given that maps any polynomial-size monotone circuit to a perfectly secure secret-sharing scheme with polynomial-time sharing and reconstruction algorithms and a polynomial total number of shares (or a proof that no such construction exists).
why: It would make information-theoretic access control scale with any efficiently evaluable policy, replacing reliance on computational assumptions for expressive access structures.
key_works: Josh Cohen Benaloh and Jerry Leichter (1988), *Generalized Secret Sharing and Monotone Functions*; Amos Beimel (2023), [*Lower Bounds for Secret-Sharing Schemes for k-Hypergraphs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2023.16); Applebaum–Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/).

title: R3-004. Graph access structures beyond the logarithmic lower bound
subfield: Round 3
open: How large must shares be for the simplest possible graph-based secret-sharing, where a set of parties may reconstruct the secret exactly when it contains an edge of the graph? Formally, determine the worst-case information ratio: either prove an \(\omega(\log n)\) lower bound on maximum share size relative to secret size, or substantially improve the known \(O(n/\log n)\) upper bound.
status: The gap between the logarithmic lower bound and the \(O(n/\log n)\) upper bound persists in the checked 2020 and 2025 treatments. Stronger lower bounds are known for linear schemes, but these do not settle unrestricted nonlinear sharing. Key works: Amos Beimel and Oriol Farràs (2020), [*The Share Size of Secret-Sharing Schemes for Almost All Access Structures and Graphs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/664); László Csirmaz (2009), *An Impossibility Result on Graph Secret Sharing*; Applebaum–Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/).
solved_when: The asymptotic gap is closed: either an \(\omega(\log n)\) lower bound is established for the maximum share size (relative to secret size) of schemes realizing graph access structures, or the \(O(n/\log n)\) upper bound is substantially improved.
why: It isolates a maximally simple authorization rule — reconstruct exactly on an edge — whose storage complexity is still poorly understood, so any progress here would sharpen the basic techniques of secret sharing.
key_works: Amos Beimel and Oriol Farràs (2020), [*The Share Size of Secret-Sharing Schemes for Almost All Access Structures and Graphs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/664); László Csirmaz (2009), *An Impossibility Result on Graph Secret Sharing*; Applebaum–Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/).

title: R3-006. Truth-table recognition of extremely cheap secret sharing
subfield: Round 3
open: Given a monotone truth table of size \(N=2^n\), can one efficiently recognize whether the underlying access structure admits maximum share size two, versus requiring shares of size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) — a promise gap for which the hard instances are known to exist? Formally, distinguish maximum share size two from \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) in \(\operatorname{poly}(N)\), or even \(N^{O(\log N)}\), time.
status: Explicitly posed in 2025 by Applebaum and Nir in *The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing* (ECCC 2025/001, §2.5, Question 1); existing hardness results leave this coarse promise gap unresolved.
solved_when: An algorithm, given the full truth table of a monotone function on \(n\) variables (size \(N=2^n\)), decides in \(\operatorname{poly}(N)\) or \(N^{O(\log N)}\) time whether the maximum share size is two or \(2^{\Omega(n)}\), under the promise that one of the two cases holds.
why: It would identify authorization policies admitting unexpectedly small shares, revealing access structures whose secret-sharing cost is far lower than coarse complexity measures suggest.
key_works: Benny Applebaum and Oded Nir (2025), [*The Meta-Complexity of Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/001/), §2.5, Question 1.

title: R3-009. Exact black-box shares when n is not a power of two
subfield: Round 3
open: For two-out-of-n black-box secret sharing over arbitrary finite abelian groups of unknown order, what is the minimum average number of group elements per share when n is not a power of two? Formally, the question asks for the exact optimum in the black-box model, where shares must be computed without knowledge of the group structure beyond its abelian group operations.
status: The known bounds are \(\log_2 n\) from below and \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) from above; for n a power of two the scheme is known to be optimal. The remaining gap for other n was reposed in 2026 (Boutros, Cascudo, Cramer, van Gent and Xing, *On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*, §13), building on the black-box secret sharing literature of Cramer and Fehr (2002) and Cramer, Fehr and Stam (2005).
solved_when: The exact minimum average share size (in group elements) is determined for every n that is not a power of two, closing the gap between the known lower bound of \(\log_2 n\) and the known upper bound of \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\).
why: It resolves the integrality gap between the fractional lower bound and the rounding-based upper bound in threshold group cryptography, pinning down whether the ceiling is truly necessary for exact black-box shares.
key_works: Ronald Cramer and Serge Fehr (2002), *Optimal Black-Box Secret Sharing over Arbitrary Abelian Groups*; Cramer, Fehr and Martijn Stam (2005), *Black-Box Secret Sharing from Primitive Sets in Algebraic Number Fields*; Milan Boutros, Ignacio Cascudo, Ronald Cramer, Daniël van Gent and Chaoping Xing (2026), [*On Exceptional Cliques in Matrix Rings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24586), §13.

title: R3-012. Optimal linear sharing for low-density upslices
subfield: Round 3
open: For a fixed density \(0<\alpha<1/2\), what is the minimum total length of a linear secret-sharing scheme over \(\mathbb F_2\) realizing the monotone DNF whose minterms are all sets of size \(\lceil\alpha n\rceil\)? Specifically, can every such DNF be realized with total length \(2^{H_2(\alpha)n/2+o(n)}\), where \(H_2\) is the binary entropy function, or is a larger exponent necessary?
status: Nir's September 2026 preprint (Oded Nir, 2026, [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), §1.3 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4) analytically bounds the exponent between \(H_2(\alpha)/2\) and \(H_2(\alpha)/(1+H_2(\alpha))\); numerical improvements leave the gap open.
solved_when: Either a construction achieves total length \(2^{H_2(\alpha)n/2+o(n)}\) for every fixed \(0<\alpha<1/2\), or a lower bound proves that some \(\alpha\) requires a strictly larger exponent.
why: Determining the optimal exponent for low-density upslices is the route to lowering the unrestricted worst-case exponent for linear secret sharing below \(0.491\).
key_works: Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), §1.3 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4.

title: R3-013. The quadratic secret-sharing exponent
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the worst-case share-size exponent for perfect one-bit secret sharing when sharing and reconstruction are computed by degree-at-most-two polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\)? Formally, determine the infimum exponent \(c\) such shares must have in the worst case.
status: As of September 2026, the exponent is bracketed between \(1/3\) and \(0.4994\), and quadratic sharing is known to strictly improve on linear sharing. Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), Theorem 1.6.
solved_when: The exponent is determined exactly, pinning it down to a single value within the currently known interval \([1/3, 0.4994]\).
why: It quantifies the concrete savings in share size gained by allowing one extra algebraic degree beyond linear secret sharing.
key_works: Oded Nir (2026), [*Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/146/revision/1/download), Theorem 1.6.

title: R3-019. Almost-universal hashing with leading constant two and subexponential error
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we construct an almost-universal hash family on \(n\)-bit inputs achieving collision probability \(\exp(-n^{\Omega(1)})\) and output length \(o(n)\) using only \(2n+o(n)\) gates over the basis \(B_2\) of all two-input Boolean functions?
status: Fan–Li–Yang (2022) gave a partial result with \(3n\) gates nonuniformly. Chen–Li–Yang (2022) achieve \(2n+o(n)\) gates with improved uniformity and seed length, but their collision error is only \(\exp(-\Omega(\log^2 n/\log\log n))\), falling short of the desired \(\exp(-n^{\Omega(1)})\).
solved_when: An explicit (or nonexplicit) construction attains all three targets simultaneously: collision probability \(\exp(-n^{\Omega(1)})\), output length \(o(n)\), and circuit size \(2n+o(n)\) over \(B_2\).
why: It would preserve stronger PRF security while driving evaluation cost down to its optimal leading constant.
key_works: Zhiyuan Fan, Jiatu Li and Tianqi Yang (2022), [*The Exact Complexity of Pseudorandom Functions and the Black-Box Natural Proof Barrier for Bootstrapping Results in Computational Complexity*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/125/revision/1/download), DOI:10.1145/3519935.3520010; Lijie Chen, Jiatu Li and Tianqi Yang (2022), [*Extremely Efficient Constructions of Hash Functions, with Applications to Hardness Magnification and PRFs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2022.23).

title: R3-021. Adaptive compute-and-compare CPRFs in the standard model
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a collusion-resistant compute-and-compare constrained PRF built from ordinary LWE be proven adaptively secure in the standard model, where the adversary may choose constrained predicates after seeing earlier keys and outputs?
status: Cheng–Goyal (2026) establish selective security in the standard model and discuss adaptive security in the random-oracle model; the gap between selective standard-model security and adaptive security remains unresolved.
solved_when: A construction from ordinary LWE is proven adaptively secure in the standard model, with the relevant predicates allowed to depend on previously obtained constrained keys and PRF outputs.
why: It removes the need for users to commit in advance to predicates, making fine-grained pseudorandom delegation practical in scenarios where queries arrive adaptively.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng and Rishab Goyal (2026), [*Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1874).

title: R3-023. Remove one input-dimension factor from registered quadratic FE setup
subfield: Round 3
open: Can the common reference string of registered quadratic functional encryption be shrunk by one factor of the input dimension — from \(O(n^2L^2\log L)\) to \(O(nL^2\log L)\), where \(n\) is the input dimension and \(L\) the number of registration slots — while keeping ciphertexts compact and the scheme secure?
status: The target was explicitly posed in 2024; ciphertexts of size \(O(n+\log L)\) are already achieved, but the CRS retains the \(O(n^2L^2\log L)\) dependence. Ziqi Zhu, Jiangtao Li, Kai Zhang, Junqing Gong and Haifeng Qian (2024), [*Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13), DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13.
solved_when: A registered quadratic functional encryption scheme is given whose CRS size is \(O(nL^2\log L)\), with ciphertexts remaining of size \(O(n+\log L)\) and full security retained.
why: It removes the quadratic dependence on the data dimension from the public setup, making registration-based deployment practical for higher-dimensional data.
key_works: Ziqi Zhu, Jiangtao Li, Kai Zhang, Junqing Gong and Haifeng Qian (2024), [*Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13), DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13.

title: R3-025. The expressive power of pre-constrained registration
subfield: Round 3
open: Which restrictions can a registration authority impose before any ciphertext exists, and does this power match what ordinary pre-constrained encryption can express? Formally, characterize when pre-constrained registered inner-product functional encryption realizes ordinary pre-constrained encryption, and when a compiler in the converse direction exists — with slot \(i\) registering only functions of the form \(M_i f_i\) for CRS-fixed \(M_i\), even against malicious registration.
status: Zhu–Li–Zhang–Gong–Qian (2024), in *Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*, explicitly pose the question of clarifying this relationship and developing general definitions and constructions beyond their specialized pairing-based tool; no characterization or converse compiler is known.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the class of pre-constrained encryption functionalities realizable by pre-constrained registered inner-product FE, together with a converse compiler or a proof that none exists in general, all under malicious registration with the \(M_i f_i\) restriction preserved.
why: It identifies exactly which restrictions on decryption power can be enforced at registration time, independently of the functionality later encrypted, separating the roles of the registering authority and the encryptor.
key_works: Ziqi Zhu, Jiangtao Li, Kai Zhang, Junqing Gong and Haifeng Qian (2024), [*Registered Functional Encryptions from Pairings*](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-031-58723-8_13).

title: R3-026. Dishonest-registration lattice NIKE at polynomial noise ratio
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a lattice-based noninteractive key exchange be proven secure against users who register maliciously crafted public keys, even when the modulus-to-noise ratio is only polynomial? The question asks for dishonest-key-registration security in a model where registered keys may be malformed or maliciously correlated.
status: Langrehr–Tran (2026) explicitly pose this question. Their optimal linear-in-users reduction loss includes a polynomial-ratio regime with inverse-polynomial correctness error, but does not supply dishonest-registration security there.
solved_when: A lattice NIKE scheme is constructed and proven secure against dishonest key registration, with security holding at a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio (the regime with inverse-polynomial correctness error), tolerating malformed and maliciously correlated registered public keys.
why: It closes the gap between the security model and the realistic setting where public keys come from untrusted users, so that lattice NIKE does not silently assume honestly generated keys.
key_works: Roman Langrehr and Si An Oliver Tran (2026), [*Lattice-based NIKE with optimal tightness*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1845).

title: R3-027. Non-black-box time-lock puzzles from VDFs alone
subfield: Round 3
open: Can time-lock puzzles be built from any ordinary verifiable delay function alone, using non-black-box techniques and no additional cryptographic assumption — or is there a stronger impossibility showing this cannot be done? Any construction should keep puzzle generation fast and remain secure against parallel solvers.
status: A EUROCRYPT 2026 result (Abusalah, Aggarwal, Azari, Kamath, von Consbruch, *Separating Verifiable Delay Functions and Time-Lock Puzzles*) rules out fully black-box constructions in both directions and explicitly leaves non-black-box constructions open. Renawi's 2020 thesis (*Time-Lock Puzzles from Verifiable Delay Functions and Witness Encryption*) achieves such puzzles only using additional witness-encryption assumptions.
solved_when: Either a non-black-box construction of time-lock puzzles from arbitrary ordinary VDFs is given (with fast puzzle generation and security against parallel solvers, and no assumption beyond the VDF), or an impossibility is proven that is strictly stronger than the existing black-box separation.
why: The answer determines whether publicly verifiable sequential work inherently supports encryption to the future, i.e., whether the ability to prove elapsed time suffices to send messages unlockable only after that time.
key_works: Hamza Abusalah, Nivesh Aggarwal, Karen Azari, Chethan Kamath and Maximilian von Consbruch (2026), [*Separating Verifiable Delay Functions and Time-Lock Puzzles*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-25330-9_2); Omar Renawi (2020; repository deposit 2025), [*Time-Lock Puzzles from Verifiable Delay Functions and Witness Encryption*](https://publications.cispa.de/articles/thesis/Time-Lock_Puzzles_from_Verifiable_Delay_Functions_and_Witness_Encryption/30866072).

title: R3-031. Separate strong and ordinary off-the-record deniability
subfield: Round 3
open: Do ordinary off-the-record deniability and strong off-the-record deniability (SORD) capture genuinely different security notions? A proof of formal separation—or, alternatively, a compiler establishing their equivalence under specified assumptions—would settle the question, with any distinction hinging on adaptive mid-execution coercion and consistency across fake claims.
status: Explicitly left open alongside the SORD construction in Navid Abapour (2026), [*Threshold Fully Deniable Interactive Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1900); introducing the definition does not establish a separation.
solved_when: A formal separation between ordinary off-the-record deniability and SORD is proven, or a compiler demonstrating their equivalence under specified assumptions is established; in either case the distinction must turn on adaptive mid-execution coercion and consistency across fake claims.
why: It determines whether existing deniability guarantees fundamentally miss a stronger coercion threat.
key_works: Navid Abapour (2026), [*Threshold Fully Deniable Interactive Encryption*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1900).

title: R3-037. Classical deletion certificates for CE-NIZK in the CRS model
subfield: Round 3
open: Can a CRS-model certified-everlasting NIZK for NP accept a purely classical deletion certificate in place of a returned quantum state, while still retaining statistical soundness?
status: The question is explicit as of September 2026; the current CRS construction requires quantum revocation, and the shared-EPR alternative does not resolve this setup-specific target (Nikhil Pappu, 2025; revised 2026, *Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*, https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4, §2.7).
solved_when: A construction in the CRS model is given where deletion is certified by a classical certificate, with statistical soundness preserved.
why: It would allow deletion certificates to be transported and handled classically, removing the need for quantum communication in the revocation step.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-038. Plain-model certified-everlasting NIWI
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we build noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs in the plain model whose everlasting security is certified — statistically sound, computationally WI before deletion, and statistically WI once the verifier accepts a deletion request? The aim is a construction achieving this without any shared setup.
status: Explicitly posed in September 2026; the natural approach of replacing the outer ZK proofs in the CE-NIZK construction by WI proofs defeats its current simulation argument. See Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), *Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*, §2.7.
solved_when: A plain-model, statistically sound noninteractive WI proof system exists with computational WI before accepted deletion and statistical WI after accepted deletion.
why: It removes the shared setup required by current certified-everlasting constructions, letting everlasting deletion security hold without trusted common parameters.
key_works: Nikhil Pappu (2025; revised 2026), [*Certified-Everlasting Quantum NIZK Proofs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13628v4), §2.7.

title: R3-045. Does unitary iO imply stateful quantum iO?
subfield: Round 3
open: Can stateful quantum indistinguishability obfuscation be constructed from ordinary unitary iO alone? Formally, derive stateful quantum iO while replacing the currently assumed ideal-obfuscation component.
status: The problem was posed explicitly in October 2026 by Gupte, Liu, Qian, Raizes, Roberts and Zhandry (2026), *On Best-Possible One-Time Programs* (arXiv:2603.00544v2), §1.9. The known unresolved step is protecting the authentication key that hides the evolving state register.
solved_when: A construction of stateful quantum iO is given whose only underlying assumption is unitary iO, with the ideal-obfuscation assumption eliminated and the authentication key protecting the evolving state register secured unconditionally relative to that assumption.
why: It would connect the two obfuscation models, showing the stateful quantum setting adds no intrinsic power beyond unitary iO.
key_works: Gupte, Liu, Qian, Raizes, Roberts and Zhandry (2026), [*On Best-Possible One-Time Programs*](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00544v2), §1.9.

title: R3-054. The reverse SZK–instance-hiding oracle separation
subfield: Round 3
open: Is there an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in IHIP, or does the containment hold relative to every oracle? That is, construct an oracle \(O\) with \(\mathrm{SZK}^O\not\subseteq\mathrm{IHIP}^O\), or prove the corresponding containment.
status: Mu–Vasudevan establish an oracle with \(\mathrm{IHIP}^O\not\subseteq\mathrm{SZK}^O\) (Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan, 2024; journal 2026, [Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w)); the reverse direction remains open.
solved_when: An oracle \(O\) is explicitly constructed with \(\mathrm{SZK}^O\not\subseteq\mathrm{IHIP}^O\), or a proof is given that \(\mathrm{SZK}^O\subseteq\mathrm{IHIP}^O\) for all oracles \(O\).
why: It would cleanly separate the notion of hiding a verifier's instance from that of hiding a prover's witness, delineating the limits of instance-hiding interactive proofs as a proof system.
key_works: Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w).

title: R3-055. Complement closure with a simulatable prover
subfield: Round 3
open: Is the class of instance-hiding interactive proofs with a simulatable prover closed under complement — that is, can every statement whose rejection is efficiently provable also have its acceptance efficiently provable (and vice versa) within this model?
status: Ordinary IHIP has complement closure; the simulatable variant remains open in 2026. The question is posed as Question 3 in §1.4 of Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w), where it was earlier termed Strong-IHIP complement closure.
solved_when: A proof that Simulatable-IHIP is closed under complement, or a separation showing a complement class strictly outside it.
why: It determines whether privately proving rejection is as feasible as proving acceptance in the simulatable setting.
key_works: Changrui Mu and Prashant Nalini Vasudevan (2024; journal 2026), [*Instance-Hiding Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-026-09573-w), §1.4, Question 3.
aliases: Strong-IHIP complement closure in the earlier terminology.

title: R3-059. Perfectly correct statistical additive encodings
subfield: Round 3
open: Can every finite multiparty function be encoded by a statistically private additive randomized encoding that is perfectly correct — so that decoding always returns the true output, never a failure symbol?
status: The STOC 2026 universality theorem of Bitansky, Erabelli, Garg, and Ishai (2026) ([Shuffling Is Universal: Statistical Additive Randomized Encodings for All Functions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1442), DOI:10.1145/3798129.3800890) achieves statistical correctness only with error and explicitly leaves perfect correctness open; computational perfect correctness does not establish this information-theoretic target.
solved_when: A construction exists for every finite multiparty function achieving statistical privacy and perfect correctness (decoding always outputs the true function value with no error or failure symbol).
why: It removes errors and aborts from anonymous computation based on summing encodings, making such protocols fully reliable.
key_works: Nir Bitansky, Saroja Erabelli, Rachit Garg and Yuval Ishai (2026), [*Shuffling Is Universal: Statistical Additive Randomized Encodings for All Functions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1442), DOI:10.1145/3798129.3800890.

title: R3-060. Statistical robust additive encodings for finite functions
subfield: Round 3
open: Can every fixed finite multiparty function be encoded robustly, in the information-theoretic sense? That is, for every fixed finite \(f\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), construct a robust additive randomized encoding with statistical correctness and privacy errors at most \(\varepsilon\), revealing only the residual function determined by the honest parties' inputs, with the encoding size allowed to depend arbitrarily on \(f\).
status: The STOC 2026 universality paper (Bitansky, Erabelli, Garg and Ishai, *Shuffling Is Universal*) explicitly leaves finite-function robustness open. The September robust constructions (Freizeit and Bitansky, *Robust Additive Randomized Encodings With Transparent Setup*) rely on computational assumptions and do not settle the statistical case; the foundational framework is Halevi, Ishai, Kushilevitz and Rabin (2023), *Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*.
solved_when: A construction exists for every fixed finite multiparty function \(f\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\) achieving statistical correctness error at most \(\varepsilon\), statistical privacy error at most \(\varepsilon\), revealing only the residual function determined by honest inputs, with no restriction on how the encoding size grows with \(f\).
why: It would bridge anonymous computation and information-theoretic MPC, extending security to larger coalitions without computational assumptions.
key_works: Halevi, Ishai, Kushilevitz and Rabin (2023), [*Additive Randomized Encodings and Their Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/870); Bitansky, Erabelli, Garg and Ishai (2026), [*Shuffling Is Universal*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1442); Sapir Bekerman Freizeit and Nir Bitansky (2026), [*Robust Additive Randomized Encodings With Transparent Setup*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1937).

title: R3-067. Explicit distributions resisting AC0-with-parity samplers
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we exhibit an explicit, polynomial-time samplable distribution on \(n\) bits that no polynomial-size, constant-depth \(\mathrm{AC}^0[\oplus]\) circuit can sample, even given arbitrarily many uniform input bits? Formally, the distribution should have total-variation distance \(1-o(1)\) from the output of every such sampler, with even a nontrivial constant separation counting as progress.
status: Explicitly open as of July 2026, posed by Farzan Byramji, Daniel M. Kane, Jackson Morris and Anthony Ostuni (2026), [*Hard-to-Sample Distributions from Robust Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26179), §5, Question 1. Strong sampling lower bounds are known for ordinary \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) and for bounded-degree polynomial maps, but these do not extend to \(\mathrm{AC}^0[\oplus]\) samplers.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time samplable distribution on \(n\) bits is constructed whose total-variation distance from every polynomial-size, constant-depth \(\mathrm{AC}^0[\oplus]\) sampler (with arbitrarily many uniform input bits) is \(1-o(1)\); a constant separation strictly bounded away from 0 is recognized partial progress.
why: It would separate general efficient distribution generation from generation by shallow parallel circuits with parity gates, delineating the power of depth-bounded samplers.
key_works: Farzan Byramji, Daniel M. Kane, Jackson Morris and Anthony Ostuni (2026), [*Hard-to-Sample Distributions from Robust Extractors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26179), §5, Question 1.

title: R3-069. Breaking the logarithm-squared seed barrier at width four
subfield: Round 3
open: Can we construct an explicit pseudorandom generator that fools every length-n, width-four read-once branching program to fixed constant error using seed length o(log² n), with no regularity, permutation, or commutativity restriction on the program?
status: Nisan's 1992 bound remains unbroken for width four; the 2026 weighted-generator treatment of Ben Chen, Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Yuval Khaskelberg and Amnon Ta-Shma ([*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3) identifies this as the smallest outstanding width. Width three admits improvements.
solved_when: An explicit generator is exhibited that fools all length-n, width-four read-once branching programs to fixed constant error with seed length o(log² n).
why: It tests whether small-space derandomization extends beyond specially structured transitions, and would break the long-standing width-four barrier.
key_works: Ben Chen, Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Yuval Khaskelberg and Amnon Ta-Shma (2026), [*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3; Noam Nisan (1992), *Pseudorandom Generators for Space-Bounded Computation*.

title: R3-070. Additive width dependence in weighted pseudorandom generators
subfield: Round 3
open: Can one construct a space-efficient weighted pseudorandom generator for length-\(n\), width-\(w\) branching programs whose seed length depends only additively on the width, namely \(O(\log^2 n+\log(w/\varepsilon))\)? Signed weights are allowed, and both generation and evaluation must meet the derandomization's space requirements.
status: Hoza's 2021 bound is \(O(\log n\log(nw)+\log(1/\varepsilon))\); 2026 work by Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma ([*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3, §1) improves the case of very large widths, but does not achieve additive width dependence in general.
solved_when: A weighted PRG for length-\(n\), width-\(w\) branching programs (with signed weights) is constructed with seed length \(O(\log^2 n+\log(w/\varepsilon))\), where generation and evaluation satisfy the space requirements of the derandomization.
why: Such a generator would imply \(\mathrm{BPL}\subseteq\operatorname{DSPACE}(\log^{4/3}n)\), improving the Saks–Zhou simulation.
key_works: Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma (2026), [*Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/064/), revision 3, §1.
