title: R3-072. Optimal small-error generators for S3 products
subfield: Round 3
open: Can one explicitly construct a pseudorandom generator with seed length O(log(n/ε)) for read-once products over S3 — and in particular, achieve logarithmic seed at inverse-polynomial error?
status: Lee–Viola (2025) attain the optimal bound for every fixed p-group but identify S3, of order six, as unresolved; the 2026 general permutation-program INW bound of Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber still incurs a seed length multiplying log n by log(1/ε).
solved_when: An explicit ε-error generator for read-once products over S3 is constructed with seed length O(log(n/ε)), including logarithmic seed for inverse-polynomial ε.
why: It isolates the obstruction arising from mixing prime factors in a small noncommutative group, a bottleneck beyond the fixed p-group case.
key_works: Chin Ho Lee and Emanuele Viola (2025), [*Pseudorandom Bits for Non-Commutative Programs*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.9), §1.2; Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber (2026), [*A Forward-Backward Weight Analysis of INW for Permutation Branching Programs*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/123/).
aliases: Optimal small-error PRGs for width-three permutation branching programs.

title: R3-074. Finite-file capacity of X-secure T-private retrieval
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the exact download capacity of X-secure, T-private information retrieval when the database holds a finite number K of files? The asymptotic answer is known, but the finite-K capacity — with jointly optimized storage encoding — remains undetermined.
status: The 2018/2019 result of Jia, Sun, and Jafar determines the asymptotic capacity 1 − (X + T)/N for N > X + T, along with selected finite-K cases. The 2026 storage paper of Nomeir and Ulukus confirms that even general finite-file T = 1 remains open.
solved_when: The exact download capacity is characterized for K files on N servers with X-secure storage and T-private queries, for N > X + T and finite K, including the jointly optimized storage encoding.
why: It quantifies the exact combined cost of hiding both the stored data and the requested index, rather than only in the many-file limit where that cost is 1 − (X+T)/N.
key_works: Zhuqing Jia, Hua Sun and Syed Ali Jafar (2018/2019), [*Cross Subspace Alignment and the Asymptotic Capacity of X-Secure T-Private Information Retrieval*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07457); Mohamed Nomeir and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*Storage-Rate Trade-off in A-XPIR*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14202).

title: R3-076. Addition-only multi-message PIR when demand size does not divide file count
subfield: Round 3
open: What is the best download rate achievable by addition-only linear PIR when a user wants to retrieve any \(D\)-subset of \(K\) replicated files from \(N\) noncolluding servers and \(D\) does not divide \(K\)? In formal terms, settle the exact capacity of this coefficient-restricted class by matching an achievability scheme with a tight converse.
status: A 2025 linear-programming construction (Heidarzadeh, Wang, and Sprintson, [A Linear Programming Approach to Private Information Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12286)) improves on previous rates but leaves gaps in the nondivisible regime; both the constructions and the converse bounds may be improvable.
solved_when: A construction and a matching converse establish the optimal download rate of addition-only linear PIR for arbitrary \(D\)-subset retrieval from \(K\) files across \(N\) servers in the nondivisible regime \(D\nmid K\).
why: It settles whether inexpensive addition-only schemes can already achieve optimal batch-retrieval rates, or whether the restriction to additions fundamentally costs rate in the nondivisible regime.
key_works: Anoosheh Heidarzadeh, Ningze Wang and Alex Sprintson (2025), [*A Linear Programming Approach to Private Information Retrieval*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12286).

title: R3-078. Joint rate–randomness–subpacketization region for structured subset retrieval
subfield: Round 3
open: For a specified family of \(D\)-element demands, what is the full achievable region of retrieval rate, shared randomness, and subpacketization in balanced \(\{0,1\}\)-linear schemes that keep the demand subset hidden from each server and all unrequested files hidden from the user?
status: May 2026 work by Issa and Heidarzadeh solves the optimal-rate corner: rate \(1-1/N\), randomness ratio \(D/(N-1)\), and subpacketization \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\) [*Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368), §VII. The constrained region remains open.
solved_when: The joint rate–randomness–subpacketization region is characterized under simultaneous budgets on shared randomness and subpacketization; the optimal-rate corner with rate \(1-1/N\), randomness ratio \(D/(N-1)\), and subpacketization \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\) is already settled.
why: It makes secure retrieval guarantees usable when packet sizes and key storage are independently limited, showing exactly what rate is attainable under realistic resource budgets.
key_works: Maha Issa and Anoosheh Heidarzadeh (2026), [*Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368), §VII.

title: R3-079. Asymmetric subpacketization in secure structured-subset retrieval
subfield: Round 3
open: When servers may return fixed-length linear answers of unequal sizes, what is the minimum subpacketization needed for secure structured-subset retrieval at rate \(1-1/N\) — and can allowing such asymmetry beat the balanced bound \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\)?
status: Explicitly posed in May 2026 (Maha Issa and Anoosheh Heidarzadeh (2026), *Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368, §VII). The proven minimum applies only to balanced schemes and does not establish the asymmetric minimum.
solved_when: A scheme with asymmetric answer lengths is shown to achieve subpacketization strictly below \((N-1)/\gcd(D,N-1)\) at rate \(1-1/N\), or the bound is proven tight even among asymmetric fixed-length linear schemes.
why: Asymmetric answer lengths could reduce subpacketization — easing fragmentation constraints in practice — without sacrificing request privacy or database secrecy.
key_works: Maha Issa and Anoosheh Heidarzadeh (2026), [*Secure and Private Structured-Subset Retrieval: Fundamental Limits and Achievable Schemes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09368), §VII.

title: R3-081. Can graph-replicated secret randomness beat rate 1/N?
subfield: Round 3
open: Can the topology of a storage graph do more than the trivial replication count for symmetric PIR — specifically, does any connected graph on \(N\ge3\) servers admit a symmetric PIR rate above \(1/N\) when each edge-message has independent secret randomness shared only by its endpoints? Any answer must retain the paper's stronger database-privacy condition, including privacy conditioned on the other message-specific secrets.
status: As of 2026, rate \(1/N\) is universally achievable and is optimal for paths and regular graphs [Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), *The Role of Common Randomness Replication in Symmetric PIR on Graph-Based Replicated Systems*, Theorems 1–3 and §7]. Whether any graph admits higher capacity remains explicitly unresolved.
solved_when: A scheme (or an impossibility proof) is exhibited for some connected graph on \(N\ge3\) servers under edge-local secret randomness, either achieving symmetric PIR rate strictly greater than \(1/N\) while satisfying the strengthened database-privacy condition, or showing no such graph exists.
why: It determines whether topology can help when masks cannot be shared globally, separating graph structure from mere replication in symmetric PIR capacity.
key_works: Shreya Meel and Sennur Ulukus (2026), [*The Role of Common Randomness Replication in Symmetric PIR on Graph-Based Replicated Systems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16700), Theorems 1–3 and §7.

title: M11. Guaranteed output delivery without the depth surcharge
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can constant-round honest-majority MPC with guaranteed output delivery be achieved with communication that does not grow with the multiplicative depth of the computed circuit — or is there an inherent depth-dependent lower bound on communication in this setting?
status: The September 2026 Li–Song revision ( [*Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296)) achieves constant rounds but retains this depth surcharge.
solved_when: Either a constant-round, honest-majority MPC protocol with guaranteed output delivery removes the \(Dn^3\lambda^3\) communication term, or a matching depth-dependent communication lower bound is proved for this setting.
why: Deep computations otherwise pay a substantial extra communication cost for guaranteed completion, so settling this determines whether circuit depth is a fundamental price of guaranteed output delivery.
key_works: Li–Song (2026), [*Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296).

title: M08. Circuit-linear communication with only one honest participant
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can constant-round malicious secure computation tolerating a single honest party achieve communication linear in the circuit size? Formally, obtain constant-round malicious MPC tolerating \(n-1\) corruptions with communication \(O(|C|\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))+\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda)\), under weak assumptions such as ordinary OT and without stronger general-purpose primitives.
status: Current round-collapsing techniques require a constant fraction of honest parties. A 2024 DDH-based construction (Goyal et al., 2024, *Dishonest Majority Constant-Round MPC with Linear Communication from DDH*) tolerates \(n-1\) corruptions but retains an \(O(|C|n)\) circuit term; round collapsing from minimal assumptions (Goyal–Li–Ostrovsky–Song, 2025/2026, *Towards Building Scalable Constant-Round MPC from Minimal Assumptions via Round Collapsing*) remains tied to the honest-majority setting.
solved_when: A construction exists meeting the stated bound: constant rounds, \(n-1\) corruptions tolerated, communication \(O(|C|\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))+\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda)\), assuming only weak primitives like OT.
why: It would settle whether almost-total collusion inherently forces per-gate communication proportional to the number of parties, determining the true communication cost of secure computation in the dishonest-majority extreme.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2024), [*Dishonest Majority Constant-Round MPC with Linear Communication from DDH*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1466); Goyal–Li–Ostrovsky–Song (2025/2026), [*Towards Building Scalable Constant-Round MPC from Minimal Assumptions via Round Collapsing*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/508).

title: M10. Efficient guaranteed output delivery from OWFs without random oracles
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Match constant-round honest-majority MPC with guaranteed output delivery and circuit-linear-in-\(n\) communication using ordinary OWFs in the standard model.
status: Li–Song’s 2026 protocol achieves the relevant combination in the random-oracle model, with communication \(O(|C|n\lambda+Dn^3\lambda^3+W_I\operatorname{poly}(n,\lambda))\).
why: Would place low-latency, availability-preserving MPC on an explicit minimal assumption.
key_works: Li–Song (2026), [*Achieving Guaranteed Output Delivery MPC with Constant Rounds and Linear Communication in Minicrypt*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1296).

title: M12. Network-agnostic MPC with near-quadratic setup
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can perfectly secure MPC that tolerates both synchronous and asynchronous adversaries be set up with only near-quadratic communication, independent of the circuit being computed? Formally, reduce the circuit-independent overhead to \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) bits while preserving polynomial computation and the optimal synchronous/asynchronous corruption thresholds.
status: Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song's October 2026 revision achieves \(O((|C|n+(D+C_I)n^2+n^6)\log n)\) bits under the optimal threshold \(n>2\max(t_s,t_a)+\max(2t_a,t_s)\); see [*Perfectly Secure Network-Agnostic MPC Comes for Free*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/377).
solved_when: A perfectly secure network-agnostic MPC protocol with circuit-independent communication overhead of \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) bits, polynomial computation, and optimal corruption thresholds is constructed and proved.
why: It would remove an enormous startup cost from protocols designed for settings where network timing is uncertain.
key_works: Ji–Liu-Zhang–Song (2026), [*Perfectly Secure Network-Agnostic MPC Comes for Free*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/377).

title: M16. Asynchronous MPC within tenfold synchronous throughput overhead
subfield: Secure computation: rounds, honesty, and communication
open: Can asynchronous secure computation be made to pay, in practice, only a small constant premium over its synchronous counterpart? Specifically, construct asynchronous MPC with guaranteed output delivery against \(t<n/3\) Byzantine faults whose throughput — counting preprocessing and measured under adversarial scheduling — stays within \(10\times\) that of a matched synchronous implementation at \(n=32,64,128\).
status: Currently a proposed moonshot benchmark with no demonstrated result. Theoretical starting points exist: linear-amortized-communication theory from Goyal–Liu-Zhang–Song (2024), [*Towards Achieving Asynchronous MPC with Linear Communication and Optimal Resilience*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/243), and the practical preprocessing improvements of Meng et al. (2026), [*RondoMPC*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1261).
solved_when: A demonstrated asynchronous MPC protocol with guaranteed delivery at resilience \(t<n/3\) achieves throughput within \(10\times\) a matched synchronous implementation for each of \(n=32,64,128\), with the accounting including preprocessing and adversarially delayed messages.
why: It would quantify — and potentially sharply reduce — the practical cost of dropping synchrony assumptions, turning a widely believed overhead into a measured engineering budget.
key_works: Goyal–Liu-Zhang–Song (2024), [*Towards Achieving Asynchronous MPC with Linear Communication and Optimal Resilience*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/243); Meng et al. (2026), [*RondoMPC*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1261).

title: E11. Simultaneously optimal seeded-extractor parameters
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Can a single seeded extractor be optimal in both seed length and entropy loss at once — matching each to within an additive constant — across the entire feasible range of input length, min-entropy, and error? Formally, construct strong seeded extractors, uniform and polynomial-time, whose seed length and entropy loss are simultaneously optimal to additive \(O(1)\) for all \((n,k,\varepsilon)\).
status: Constant-factor-optimal constructions are classical, but sharp simultaneous optimality — additive-constant optimality in both parameters at once — is a strictly stronger requirement that remains open. See Guruswami–Umans–Vadhan (2009), [*Unbalanced Expanders and Randomness Extractors from Parvaresh–Vardy Codes*](https://doi.org/10.1145/1538902.1538904); Vadhan (2012), [*Pseudorandomness*](https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/pseudorandomness/).
solved_when: An explicit uniform polynomial-time strong seeded extractor exists whose seed length and entropy loss are each within an additive \(O(1)\) of the respective information-theoretic optima, simultaneously for every feasible \((n,k,\varepsilon)\).
why: It would settle the basic efficiency frontier for converting weak randomness into uniform bits, closing the gap between what is information-theoretically possible and what explicit constructions achieve.
key_works: Guruswami–Umans–Vadhan (2009), [*Unbalanced Expanders and Randomness Extractors from Parvaresh–Vardy Codes*](https://doi.org/10.1145/1538902.1538904); Vadhan (2012), [*Pseudorandomness*](https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/pseudorandomness/).

title: E12. Short seeds, low error, and sublinear entropy loss
subfield: Seeded extraction: sharp parameters and computational complexity
open: Can a seeded extractor for min-entropy \(k\) sources on \(n\) bits achieve seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) while losing only \(o(k)\) bits of entropy at negligible error, in the regime \(\log(1/\varepsilon)=o(k)\)? Ideally the construction should also admit nearly linear-time evaluation.
status: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), in [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473), achieve \((1-\eta)k\) output for fixed \(\eta>0\) in their regime; achieving sublinear entropy loss is explicitly stated as open.
solved_when: An explicit extractor exists with seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\), entropy loss \(o(k)\), and negligible error \(\varepsilon\) satisfying \(\log(1/\varepsilon)=o(k)\); preferably with nearly linear evaluation time.
why: Such an extractor would preserve nearly all of the source's available entropy even at cryptographic error levels, which current constructions forfeit.
key_works: Doron–Ribeiro (2025/2026), [*Nearly-Linear Time Seeded Extractors with Short Seeds*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07473).

title: A43. SNARGs for all NP from polynomially hard LWE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we construct succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for all of NP assuming only standard polynomial hardness of LWE? More precisely, the goal is a construction with polynomial-time preprocessing, proof length polynomial in the security parameter, and verification time growing only logarithmically in the computation.
status: LWE-based SNARGs are known for P and for special NP languages that admit suitable bounded-space nonmembership proofs (Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan, 2024, [SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956)); the general NP case remains open.
solved_when: A SNARG for arbitrary NP languages is constructed from polynomially hard LWE, with polynomial preprocessing, proof length polynomial in the security parameter, and logarithmic verification time.
why: It would yield general-purpose succinct verification of arbitrary NP statements from a conventional, post-quantum lattice assumption, removing the need for stronger or nonstandard hardness in succinct-argument foundations.
key_works: Jin–Kalai–Lombardi–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*SNARGs under LWE via Propositional Proofs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/956).

title: A46. Remove derandomization from unprovability-based SNARGs
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can the 2026 unprovability-based SNARG for NP be rebuilt without assuming promise-class derandomization? More precisely, can the \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) premise be eliminated while keeping the construction's other explicitly stated assumptions intact?
status: The 2026 construction of Hsieh–Jain–Li–Mathialagan rests on LWE, SXDH, promise-class derandomization, and a formal unprovability assumption involving hard Extended Frege tautologies; no derandomization-free variant is known.
solved_when: An NP-SNARG construction is given that matches the 2026 result but drops the \(\mathrm{prBPP}=\mathrm{prP}\) assumption, retaining the remaining premises (LWE, SXDH, and the formal unprovability assumption involving hard Extended Frege tautologies).
why: It isolates whether derandomization contributes essential cryptographic power, or whether the unprovability assumption alone suffices.
key_works: Hsieh–Jain–Li–Mathialagan (2026), [*SNARGs for NP from Unprovability of Mathematical Theorems*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/098/).

title: A47. Adaptive public delegation from plain WE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we build publicly verifiable SNARGs for arbitrary NP, with adaptive soundness, assuming only plain witness encryption plus ordinary LWE? The target is a construction that avoids strengthening the witness encryption assumption to extractable witness encryption or instantiating indistinguishability obfuscation.
status: Universal constructions yield nonadaptive results, and stronger guarantees are known only for restricted languages; positional witness encryption alone does not establish the full target. Key works: Jin et al. (2025), [Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718104); Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).
solved_when: A publicly verifiable, adaptively sound SNARG for arbitrary NP is constructed and proved sound from plain witness encryption and LWE alone.
why: It would turn a comparatively weak advanced primitive into a broadly usable adaptive delegation scheme, giving succinct delegation of arbitrary computation without the strong assumptions currently required.
key_works: Jin et al. (2025), [*Universal SNARGs for NP from Proofs of Correctness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718104); Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A53. Quasioptimal concrete delegation from polynomial LWE
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can we build, from polynomial hardness of Learning With Errors, a practical delegation system for deterministic computations — SNARGs or IVC — whose prover runs in quasilinear time, whose proofs stay below 1 MB, and whose verification costs under 1% of simply redoing the computation on the declared large workloads?
status: Proposed as a moonshot retaining polynomial-hardness assumptions; theoretical LWE-based SNARGs and IVC for P already exist. Key works: Chen–Freitag–Jin–Wichs (2025), [Unambiguous SNARGs for P from LWE with Applications to PPAD Hardness](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718159).
solved_when: An implemented LWE-based SNARG or IVC for deterministic computations achieves quasilinear prover work, proofs below 1 MB, and verification time below 1% of recomputation on the declared large workloads.
why: It would give a concrete alternative to pairing-based or hash-based delegation, resting only on polynomial-hardness lattice assumptions.
key_works: Chen–Freitag–Jin–Wichs (2025), [*Unambiguous SNARGs for P from LWE with Applications to PPAD Hardness*](https://doi.org/10.1145/3717823.3718159).

title: A54. A fully doubly efficient IP equals PSPACE theorem
subfield: Succinct arguments, delegation, and computation checking
open: Can every polynomial-space computation be proved interactively with truly doubly efficient costs — a prover that runs in time polynomial in the computation's time, and a verifier that runs in time polynomial in the original input length? For general time \(T\), construct such information-theoretic interactive proofs.
status: Chen–Hong–Kalai–Xi reach \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\) in 2026, improving the earlier \(n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}\) regime; see [*Towards a Doubly Efficient IP=PSPACE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1287).
solved_when: An information-theoretic interactive proof for general polynomial-space computations of time \(T\) exists with prover time polynomial in \(T\) and verifier time polynomial in the input length.
why: It would align the honest prover's cost with the actual computation throughout PSPACE, making delegation of computation checking practical even for long-running computations.
key_works: Chen–Hong–Kalai–Xi (2026), [*Towards a Doubly Efficient IP=PSPACE*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1287).

title: A32. Concrete parameters for group-based WE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can a group-based witness encryption scheme be made concretely usable — encrypting for realistically large relations in practice? Formally, build a reproducible candidate that handles \(10^5\)-gate relations with ciphertexts below 1 GB and encryption/decryption running in under one hour on a specified workstation, while targeting 128-bit classical attack cost.
status: Currently a proposed moonshot. The existing polynomial-time and quasipolynomial generic-security statements for group-based witness encryption (Hair–Sahai 2026, *Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*; Jin 2026, *Witness Encryption for NP from SNARGs and Groups*) do not establish these concrete bounds.
solved_when: A reproducible candidate construction is exhibited that encrypts \(10^5\)-gate relations, produces ciphertexts below 1 GB, completes encryption and decryption in under one hour on the specified workstation, and targets 128-bit classical attack cost.
why: A solution would reveal whether the new group-based route to witness encryption can actually support substantive applications, rather than remaining an asymptotic existence result.
key_works: Hair–Sahai (2026), [*Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275); Jin (2026), [*Witness Encryption for NP from SNARGs and Groups*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2063).

title: A36. Breaking the half-exponent in LWE-based XWE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can the encryption exponent for general witness encryption built from standard (subexponential) LWE assumptions be pushed below \(1/2\), with an explicit dependence on the witness size and security parameter?
status: The current reference point is a verified construction with a \(2^{m/2}\) encryption exponent (Brakerski et al. 2017/2018, [Non-Trivial Witness Encryption and Null-iO from Standard Assumptions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/874)); exponents that are arbitrarily small positive constants remain a strictly stronger, open target, with meet-in-the-middle barriers and fine-grained reductions as related obstructions.
solved_when: A construction achieves a general XWE encryption exponent strictly smaller than \(1/2\) — in particular, approaching arbitrarily small positive exponents — under ordinary subexponential LWE, with the witness-size and security dependence made explicit.
why: It would improve the best available weak-assumption route to non-trivial witness encryption, even before a full polynomial-time witness encryption is achieved.
key_works: Brakerski et al. (2017/2018), [*Non-Trivial Witness Encryption and Null-iO from Standard Assumptions*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/874).

title: A39. Polylogarithmic public tracing from plain WE
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can we build publicly traceable broadcast encryption from plain witness encryption whose ciphertexts are only polylogarithmic in the number of users? Formally, reduce the ciphertext size to poly(λ, log N) while retaining collusion resistance and the applicable independent-key guarantees.
status: The best known result, the September 2026 cutoff-iO construction of Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), *Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional* (https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932), achieves ciphertext size N^ε·poly(λ) for every fixed positive ε, from WE plus LWE — still polynomial in N rather than polylogarithmic.
solved_when: A construction from plain WE (with standard assumptions) achieves ciphertext size poly(λ, log N) for N users, security parameter λ, with collusion resistance and applicable independent-key guarantees.
why: It would make public traitor tracing scale to very large populations, where current ciphertexts growing with N are prohibitive.
key_works: Nassar–Waters–Wu (2026), [*Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs: Making Witness Encryption Positional*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1932).

title: A42. Efficient public certification of condition ciphertexts
subfield: Witness encryption and condition-based cryptography
open: Can a special-purpose witness-encryption ciphertext be accompanied by a compact, publicly verifiable certificate that it indeed encodes the declared payload commitment under the declared condition — cheap enough to add at most a 10× overhead to encryption, and secure even against a malicious encryptor?
status: This is a proposed engineering target. General-purpose proofs can certify encryption computations, but an integrated, efficient envelope achieving the stated overhead and malicious-encryptor security remains to be demonstrated. Key works: Garg et al. (2025), [*A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364).
solved_when: A construction exists that produces compact public certificates for WE ciphertexts encoding the declared payload commitment and condition, incurs at most 10× encryption overhead, and provably withstands malicious encryptors.
why: Without such certificates, users cannot trust what a conditional ciphertext promises to release, undermining the reliability of condition-based cryptographic systems.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), [*A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364).

title: M51. High-error ZK-to-OWF implications beyond constant rounds
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Does weak zero knowledge for public-coin protocols with polynomially many messages already force one-way functions under the same complexity premise? Formally, derive OWFs whenever the combined completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge errors satisfy \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_z\le1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), independent of the number of messages.
status: Constant-round protocols satisfy the unweighted criterion \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_z\le1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\). For protocols with \(m\) messages, the known general criterion is \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+(m-1)\varepsilon_z<1\); removing the message-dependent coefficient remains open. See Chatterjee–Li–Vasudevan (2026), [Weak Zero-Knowledge and One-Way Functions](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.5); Chakraborty et al. (2026), [Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651).
solved_when: An implication from polynomial-round public-coin ZK to OWFs is established under the criterion \(\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_s+\varepsilon_z\le1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), with no message-dependent coefficient such as the \((m-1)\) factor multiplying \(\varepsilon_z\).
why: It would show whether interaction dilutes the hardness forced by weak privacy — i.e., whether longer protocols can satisfy weaker privacy while still implying one-way functions.
key_works: Chatterjee–Li–Vasudevan (2026), [*Weak Zero-Knowledge and One-Way Functions*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.5); Chakraborty et al. (2026), [*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651).

title: M33. Exact rounds for fully black-box nonmalleable ZK from OWFs
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: What is the fewest number of messages needed to build fully black-box simulation-extractable nonmalleable zero knowledge from arbitrary one-way functions? In particular, does a five-message protocol exist achieving delayed-input one-many security?
status: Constant-round feasibility was established in 2024 by Botta–Ciampi–Orsini–Siniscalchi–Visconti ([*Black-Box (and Fast) Non-Malleable Zero Knowledge*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/432)), but the exact message count remains open. On the lower-bound side, an earlier barrier of Hazay–Pass–Venkitasubramaniam (2020) ([*Which Languages Have 4-Round Fully Black-Box Zero-Knowledge Arguments from One-Way Functions?*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-45727-3_20)) shows four-round fully black-box ordinary ZK from arbitrary OWFs is out of reach.
solved_when: A fully black-box nonmalleable (simulation-extractable) zero-knowledge argument is constructed from arbitrary one-way functions in five messages with delayed-input one-many security, or a matching lower bound shows five messages are impossible; the minimal round count is thereby pinned down exactly.
why: It would separate the inherent round cost of nonmalleability from the overhead introduced by compilation techniques, telling us whether current constructions are optimal or wasteful.
key_works: Botta–Ciampi–Orsini–Siniscalchi–Visconti (2024), [*Black-Box (and Fast) Non-Malleable Zero Knowledge*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/432); Hazay–Pass–Venkitasubramaniam (2020), [*Which Languages Have 4-Round Fully Black-Box Zero-Knowledge Arguments from One-Way Functions?*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-45727-3_20).

title: M36. Negligible nonmalleability error in three-round weak ZK
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can a three-round weak zero-knowledge argument in the plain model achieve negligible nonmalleability error while keeping a precisely stated weak-ZK quantifier? That is, can the current inverse-polynomial nonmalleability error be driven down to negligible without adding rounds or strengthening the simulation notion beyond the intended weak-ZK guarantee?
status: A September 2026 preprint (Zhang et al. 2026, *Three-Round Weak Non-Malleable Zero-Knowledge Argument*, https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1964) achieves three rounds with weak ZK and parameterized inverse-polynomial nonmalleability error, building from primitives including OT and circuit-private FHE.
solved_when: A construction of three-round, plain-model weak-ZK arguments is given whose nonmalleability error is negligible (rather than parameterized inverse-polynomial), with the weak-ZK quantifier explicitly stated and retained.
why: It would give tamper-resistant (man-in-the-middle-secure) arguments at the minimal three-round round complexity, without paying for the extra interaction that strong non-malleable ZK typically requires.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), [*Three-Round Weak Non-Malleable Zero-Knowledge Argument*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1964).

title: M40. End-to-end partial-reset experiments
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Can a zero-knowledge prover be hardened, at negligible cost, against partial-reset faults such as VM rollback and fault injection that force selective reuse of its masks and keys? Concretely, this asks for end-to-end experiments demonstrating a defense that keeps proof size and verification unchanged while adding under 10% prover overhead, evaluated across three proof architectures.
status: Proposed experimental target; no experiments yet. The 2026 work of Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), [Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036), gives the attacks and a generic randomness-generation defense.
solved_when: Benchmarks show the defense withstands selective reuse of prover masks and keys under fault injection and VM rollback, across three proof architectures, with unchanged proof size and verification and under 10% prover overhead.
why: Ordinary transcript-validity tests do not reveal many reset-induced witness leaks, so empirical evidence of this kind is needed to show whether realistic reset faults actually break provers and whether cheap defenses suffice.
key_works: Abdolmaleki et al. (2026), [*Resettable Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge: Attacks and Defenses*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1036).

title: M50. Ordinary OWFs from high-error private-coin ZK
subfield: Zero knowledge: assumptions, round limits, and robust composition
open: Does every constant-round private-coin zero-knowledge proof for NP with high error already imply the existence of ordinary one-way functions? Formally, assuming \(NP\not\subseteq ioP/poly\), derive ordinary OWFs whenever completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge errors sum to at most \(1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\).
status: The 2026 result of Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer ([*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651)) yields ordinary OWFs for public coins, but only auxiliary-input OWFs for private coins.
solved_when: Ordinary (not merely auxiliary-input) one-way functions are derived from constant-round private-coin NP zero-knowledge proofs whose completeness, soundness, and ZK errors sum to at most \(1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n)\), under the assumption \(NP\not\subseteq ioP/poly\).
why: It would identify the weakest meaningful private-coin privacy guarantee that already forces cryptographic hardness.
key_works: Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer (2026), [*Non-Trivial Zero-Knowledge Implies One-Way Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17651).
